Barbuda is distant from the civil-society and institutional resources of St John's, has limited medical, legal and administrative services, fewer gendered facilities than Antigua, no trans community or advocacy body, and medical care beyond a small clinic requires referral to Antigua — combining to give thin local recourse after discovery, including birth-sex ward or custody placement if something goes wrong. Daily enforcement and visitor-facing scrutiny appear lighter than on the main island, and police, healthcare and border functions follow national standards with no known local facility, custody or care restrictions.

regions.name: Redonda
regions.merged_summary:
Redonda is an uninhabited, guano-covered islet and protected nature reserve within Antigua and Barbuda, with no permanent population, settlements, accommodation, clinics, police, courts or civil-registration services. Visits are brief expedition or yacht landings staged from Antigua and cleared under Antiguan officials, so a trans visitor encounters no local society or institutions and nothing local adds to or subtracts from the national framework; any dispute, document check, complaint or medical evacuation is handled by Antiguan authorities on Antigua or Barbuda, where the same legal position applies. There is no Redonda-specific record of trans targeting, tolerance or enforcement in either direction, and the absence of a resident community does not itself indicate local acceptance. Entry clearance means informal document checks against paperwork showing birth-sex markers, with no local recourse and reliance on national authorities. Emergency medical care would require evacuation to Antigua.

Under the inherited national regime, a 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling struck down the buggery and gross-indecency provisions, and the courts read constitutional sex-discrimination protection to cover sexual orientation and gender identity — but this is constitutional rather than statutory, with no explicit statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection. There is no route to change legal sex markers, so foreign-issued documents retain birth-sex markers, and same-sex unions or relationships are not recognised. Conservative social attitudes persist, and the national record includes past anti-LGBT violence (the litigant's assault) with no documented enforcement response. For a visitor who is out or discovered, this combines into document mismatch at clearance, no operative protections and no local complaint mechanism, leaving recourse dependent entirely on national authorities, with discretion being the practical course.

regions.name: Saint George
regions.merged_summary: Saint George parish has no separate legal regime and operates entirely under Antigua and Barbuda's national framework, though it contains St. John's, the cruise port and V.C. Bird International Airport, where most visitors first arrive and where document checks, hotel registration and police presence are most concentrated. Consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court in 2022, and that ruling read constitutional sex-discrimination protection to cover gender identity and sexual orientation, but the interpretive holding has not been enacted as statutory protection: there is no explicit anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute, no statutory gender-identity protection, and same-sex unions are not recognised. There is no administrative or judicial route to change the sex marker on local identity documents, so a visitor's foreign passport remains the operative document and will show a birth-sex marker at border, hotel, bank, transport and police checks, potentially creating mismatches with presentation. No parish-level ban or organised targeting is known, and no local enforcement, facility rules, policing, access-to-facilities or social-hostility patterns specific to Saint George are documented — that absence reflects lack of documentation rather than established safety, and no documented remedy operates for a trans person who is outed. The parish is predominantly residential and rural, with fewer large resort operations and a smaller police and health infrastructure than the country's main tourism nodes, which may make strangers more noticeable and reduce familiar complaint pathways, leaving a visibly trans visitor outside the tourist zones exposed to stares, comment, service refusal and, at the margins, confrontation with little realistic recourse; its tourist-facing economy and steady foreign traffic nonetheless mean resort, airport and cruise-terminal staff are comparatively accustomed to diverse travellers, and a short-stay visitor in those zones is buffered by foreignness and generally treated courteously. Conditional on discovery or being outed, the likely result is intrusive questioning, misgendering and occasional service friction rather than criminal liability for identity, with social friction and document mismatch weighing somewhat more heavily than in a major resort area, but without reaching severe legal exposure and with formal recourse largely absent.

regions.name: Saint John
regions.merged_summary:
Saint John, Antigua and Barbuda's capital and main air, sea and cruise-port entry point, inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct has not been criminal since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling and the constitution's sex-discrimination language has been read to cover gender identity, but there is no enacted statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination or hate crime, no legal route to change a sex marker on identity documents, and no recognition of same-sex relationships (which affects a visitor travelling with a same-sex partner). Because documents continue to record sex assigned at birth, any identity check — at borders, hotels, banking or police stops — can mismatch a visitor's presentation and produce involuntary outing, bureaucratic friction, service denial or awkwardness, and possible police questioning, with remedies remaining informal rather than statutory, policing and service discretion unregulated, and any custody or hospital placement following birth-sex records. No local ordinance, facility ban, documented pattern of police targeting, trans-specific violence, or campaign of detention, violence, deportation or execution against transgender visitors is known here, so risks conditional on discovery or being outed centre on harassment, service refusal and misgendering rather than detention or prosecution.

Assessments differ on local texture: Saint John is described both as the country's most urban, tourism-dependent and internationally visible place — a visitor-facing hospitality economy whose staff deal routinely with foreigners, giving a trans visitor in resort and cruise corridors less scrutiny and a milder everyday reaction to gender nonconformity than in close-knit rural villages where gossip circulates quickly — and, in one account, a largely rural, less tourist-served parish shaped by Caribbean social conservatism, staring or curiosity and variable local tolerance. In either reading, formal recourse for service refusal or harassment is thin and resolved informally.

regions.name: Saint Mary
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Mary is a largely rural, socially conservative parish on Antigua with limited tourism infrastructure, coastal villages and few services, so a transgender visitor has less anonymity and fewer local institutions to turn to than in St. John's; village-level attitudes away from tourist strips may be somewhat more conservative, with small-community visibility raising the likelihood that anyone outed is noticed. No parish-level provision creates a separate regime or local protection, and there is no documented pattern of trans-specific enforcement, policing, service denial or violence of its own. Conditions otherwise mirror the national picture: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court in July 2022, and that court also read constitutional sex-discrimination protections to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, but no statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime regime has followed, no mechanism exists to change a legal gender marker, and same-sex unions are not recognised. The judgment's extension of protection to gender identity is interpretive and largely unenforced in practice.

For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, home-country documents govern every identity check, so a passport showing sex assigned at birth can surface a mismatch at hotels, police stops, clinics or transport, potentially prompting intrusive questioning, with no local recognition or complaint recourse beyond ordinary police response and thin formal protection. The tourism economy moderates everyday treatment, but social conservatism in a small parish can still produce staring, gossip, service refusal or police friction; no documented pattern of trans-specific state targeting, imprisonment or lethal violence is known.

regions.name: Saint Paul
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Paul parish — which includes the English Harbour and Falmouth yachting and tourism area — inherits Antigua and Barbuda's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct has not been an offence since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling that voided the buggery and gross-indecency provisions, and that court read constitutional sex-discrimination protection to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No statute spells out anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on those grounds, the ruling has not been turned into a statutory regime, same-sex relationships are not recognised (affecting a visitor travelling with a partner), and there is no legal route to change the sex marker on identity documents, so passports and local identity checks at hotels, banks, clinics or with police will show sex assigned at birth. No local law targets transgender expression, and no region-specific information distinguishes Saint Paul from the national picture on border checks, policing, facilities, health care or documented violence, arrests, organised targeting or state detention of transgender visitors; there is no criminal penalty for being transgender and no credible risk of imprisonment or execution. The parish's economy is heavily visitor- and expatriate-facing around English Harbour, luxury accommodation, yacht tourism and retail, with visible LGBTQ advocacy (ECADE, Outright International), though accounts differ on its tourism intensity — describing it both as a principal tourism hub and as quieter, largely residential and rural with far less tourism than St John's and the northwest coast. That transient, foreign-visitor economy can reduce everyday scrutiny and make gender-nonconforming foreign visitors a familiar rather than exceptional presence, but it creates no local transgender-specific protections, services or police practice. One account notes the parish's lower visitor familiarity and stronger small-community conformity pressure as sitting slightly below the national picture, with no evidence of worse local conditions.

If discovery occurs — through document checks, hotels, clinics, transport or police contact — social conservatism, church influence, small communities and informal scrutiny combine with the national regime's thin practical recourse: exposure is primarily outing through document mismatch, leading to questioning, bureaucratic friction, misgendering, service friction or refusal, indifference, harassment or social awkwardness rather than arrest or severe hostility. The interpretive ruling remains unenforced by statute, leaving recourse uncertain; there is no documented pattern of police or public hostility toward transgender visitors, though an incidental 2022 public attack on the decriminalisation litigant illustrates the social climate.

regions.name: Saint Peter
regions.merged_summary: Saint Peter is a small, largely rural parish on Antigua's north-central coast centred on Parham, with a tiny, tight-knit population, low anonymity, and far less of the tourist-facing infrastructure found in the St John's area; its coastal, resort and expatriate-facing economy may make street-level reactions somewhat more guarded than in strongly rural or church-centred areas. It has none of the capital's advocacy or complaint-handling presence, no local trans-specific advocacy, and no known local ordinances, policing campaigns or trans-specific cases that distinguish it from Antigua and Barbuda's national picture on enforcement, border screening, custody, health care or social treatment. Consensual adult same-sex conduct was decriminalised by the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court in 2022, but that ruling's reading of constitutional sex-discrimination protections to cover gender identity remains interpretive rather than statutory, and there is no statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, no route to change a recorded sex marker, and no formal recognition of a same-sex partner relationship. Everyday life is conservative and church-influenced. A visibly transgender or outed visitor would likely draw intense curiosity and possible social friction or refused service with thin practical recourse, and police recourse is uncertain; identity documents cannot be changed, so home-country documents govern every check and will show sex assigned at birth at border, hotel, emergency-care and detention encounters, leaving a visitor exposed, especially when travelling with a same-sex partner. That resident-facing limitation does not itself mean officials reject foreign-issued documents, and such treatment is not documented. No criminal exposure, documented police targeting or recorded pattern of anti-trans violence is known in the parish, and no visitor-facing document risk has been documented; one trans litigant nationally reported being bullied and physically attacked, an isolated case that does not establish the frequency of violence against visitors.

regions.name: Saint Philip
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Philip is a rural eastern parish of Antigua, centred on Willikies with coastal resort and tourism areas, and it has no parish-level rules, ordinances, or documented trans-specific enforcement pattern that depart from the national picture. Antigua and Barbuda decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in a July 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling, which also read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, but this remains an interpretive holding rather than a statutory anti-discrimination, harassment, or hate-crime regime. Same-sex unions are not recognised nationwide, which matters for a trans visitor travelling with a partner, and there is no route anywhere in the country to change the sex marker on identity documents — only name changes — so a visitor's own passport governs every identity check, and how local officials handle a mismatch between a foreign document's marker and presentation is not documented.

Because the parish is agricultural, socially conservative, and comparatively less resort-centred than St John's or St Mary, with fewer hotels, clinics, and advocacy or complaint channels, smaller close-knit communities may reduce anonymity and amplify personal scrutiny, gossip, misgendering, or service friction, and any refusal of service or police friction would leave thinner practical recourse. No parish-level hostility, facility ban, police targeting of gender-nonconforming people, organised targeting, or serious anti-trans violence is documented — nor is any local tolerance; the absence of records reflects thin local data rather than demonstrated safety, and resort presence is not evidence of protection. The reported bullying and assault of a transgender litigant shows social harm but does not establish a pattern specific to this parish. Conditional on discovery or being outed, a trans visitor would face no criminal penalty for being trans, and Antigua's tourism dependence gives foreign visitors some buffer, but also no formal recourse against discrimination, harassment, or refusal of service, with police indifference rather than arrest the more likely outcome.

regions.name: Niederösterreich
regions.merged_summary:
Niederösterreich operates under Austria's national framework: no criminalisation of trans identity, gender expression or same-sex conduct; legal gender change without surgery, though conditional on a psychiatric opinion, with 'X' and 'diverse' markers available; same-sex marriage and family protections; and anti-discrimination protection in goods and services, which Lower Austria was the last federal state to extend and which has been in force since 2017. Prejudice-motivated offences and hate speech are treated as aggravating, security police are bound to avoid biased action, and foreign passports are accepted without a local gender-recognition requirement. Detention and care follow national gender-recognition principles rather than local criminalisation, screening at the Schwechat gateway and along the eastern Schengen border follows national practice with otherwise ordinary Schengen/EU border controls, and no distinct regional facility, border or police rule targeting trans visitors is known. Regional courts, police, oversight bodies and hate-crime recourse function as elsewhere in Austria.

The state is Austria's largest and most rural, more socially conservative than Vienna, with strong ÖVP and FPÖ presence and an ÖVP–FPÖ governing coalition — a reason to expect more social friction, not in itself evidence of official targeting — alongside documented hate violence and political debate about the FPÖ. Dedicated LGBTQ infrastructure is thin and there are fewer LGBT-specific venues outside the St. Pölten, Wiener Neustadt and Krems areas and the Vienna commuter belt, while spa, wine-country and alpine tourism economies remain visitor-facing though smaller than in Vienna's. For a trans visitor who is outed or discovered, exposure is therefore mostly visibility and friction rather than hostility: more staring, curiosity, misgendering and occasional service friction in small towns and outside resort centres, with fewer local support options, and consequences that typically mean social discomfort or bureaucratic document mismatches rather than detention or violence. No state-level hostile measure, local restrictive ordinance, or documented pattern of police targeting, facility bans, birth-sex custody of trans visitors, or care or family-intervention risk for a travelling minor is recorded — though the lack of documented regional incidents does not establish that hostility is absent, and experiences vary outside larger towns. National rather than local exposures still apply, including the 2025 documented fake dating-profile ambushes by neo-Nazis against LGBTQ people — chiefly gay and bisexual men, prosecuted but amid under-recorded hate-crime statistics — with no established trans-specific pattern or Niederösterreich rate, plus a rising far-right political climate.

regions.name: Contiguous Azerbaijan
regions.merged_summary:
Contiguous Azerbaijan — the mainland, including the capital Baku — operates under Azerbaijan's national framework with no known local protective law, practice or safer exception: there is no legal prohibition of discrimination on grounds of gender identity, no legal change of gender marker on official documents, no gender-identity criminal statute, and ILGA-Europe ranks the country last in Europe, while social conservatism is widespread and state-affiliated and private media carry hostile coverage. The documented abuses occur directly on this mainland: police raids in Baku in 2017 targeting trans and queer people involved beatings, forced medical examinations, electric shocks, blackmail, fines and short imprisonment, and a July 2023 raid on a private party involved forced examinations and threats of outing, with other raids in connection with prostitution and private gatherings reported to involve beatings, sexual harassment, threats of outing, blackmail, fines and imprisonment. A trans woman was killed in Baku in March 2024 and the police investigation was inadequate. Baku also holds the country's only visible queer infrastructure and offers greater anonymity to foreigners, but it is where security operations and media hostility are concentrated and is also the most tolerant setting; outside the capital, communities are smaller and more conservative, with fewer support services, less visibility, thinner recourse and weaker institutional cover, so local variation does not improve on the national picture. Accountability for abuses has relied largely on outside bodies such as the European Court of Human Rights.

For a transgender visitor, exposure to police therefore does not depend on domestic protections: the operative consequences after discovery or being outed are arbitrary police custody, humiliation, extortion, blackmail, fines or short imprisonment, forced medical examinations, detention and threats of outing, with little practical recourse, and official responses to violence against trans people have been inadequate. The evidence does not establish a routine capital-punishment pathway for trans visitors, and no distinct rule for a travelling family or a minor is documented, so family-specific outcomes remain uncertain.

regions.name: Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic
regions.merged_summary:
Nakhchivan has no documented rule of its own that softens or hardens Azerbaijan's national framework: no region-specific raids, prosecutions or trans-visitor incidents were identified, and no distinct rule applies to travelling minors. The inherited national picture is the one that governs — gender identity is not covered by anti-discrimination law, the gender marker on official documents cannot be changed, and documented police action against queer people has involved detention, beatings, forced medical examinations, extortion and blackmail, including the 2017 Baku detentions and a 2023 Baku party raid. Investigations of anti-trans violence, among them the 2024 murder of a trans woman in Baku, have been inadequate; annual European legal comparisons place the country last for protection, and state-affiliated and private media output has been measured at 77% hateful or biased. No documented execution or immigration-exclusion campaign specifically targets trans travellers.

Locally, the exclave's small, rural and socially conservative population, close community ties and tight security apparatus mean a foreign visitor is conspicuous, anonymity is limited, and discovery is more likely to invite informal confrontation. There is no visible LGBTIQ infrastructure, community organisation, legal aid or local recourse, and weaker independent media, NGO and monitoring presence than in Baku, so police abuse reported nationally is unlikely to be disciplined and assistance may be harder to reach; police and security authorities retain broad discretion and are not known to have developed visitor-protective practice. The territory is isolated, with little independent scrutiny and limited foreign tourism: entry is restricted to the Turkish and Iranian borders and flights from Baku, with heightened security and document checks at crossings and the airport under national rules. These conditions offer no known local exception softening the national regime, so a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed faces the same hostile institutional environment as elsewhere in Azerbaijan with a greater probability of sanction and little effective recourse — an absence of documented local incidents is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Bubanza
regions.merged_summary: Bubanza is a rural province in northwestern (western) Burundi with close-knit agricultural communities, conservative Catholic social norms and little anonymity outside its small urban centre, and no documented local laws, protections or enforcement patterns distinct from the national picture. Burundi's national regime therefore applies in full: the Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct with imprisonment of three months to two years and a fine, and the provision targets same-sex conduct rather than transgender identity itself, though it may expose a trans visitor if officials interpret their relationships or presentation through that lens. Same-sex conduct carries documented arrests, convictions and prison sentences, with enforcement intensifying in 2023. There is no legal gender recognition, so visitors cannot obtain identity documents matching their gender, and LGBTIQ organisations are not registered. In December 2023 the president publicly called for people found engaging in gay sex to be stoned, remarks described by advocates and exile groups as licensing violence or a license to kill; no later enforcement case or official statement is documented here. LGBT people face documented discrimination, harassment, stigmatisation and family rejection with no government protection, in a setting that includes arbitrary arrest and torture. Border and document checks usually occur in Bujumbura, but onward travel into Bubanza offers few safe recourse options if identity is questioned: local police and administrative officials exercise wide discretion, the province is distant from Bujumbura's smaller advocacy and consular presence and weaker institutional oversight, and a visibly trans visitor would likely be known and scrutinised quickly. There is no documented Bubanza-specific trans enforcement case, tolerance or sheltering mechanism, and local authorities may lack capacity to investigate anti-trans violence or curb extortion, leaving an outed trans visitor with little practical recourse beyond arbitrary detention, informal sanction or unremedied social hostility; the absence of local information is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Bujumbura Mairie
regions.merged_summary: Bujumbura Mairie, Burundi's former capital and its main urban, commercial, diplomatic and airport zone, operates under the national regime: same-sex conduct remains an offence under Penal Code Article 567 carrying up to two years' imprisonment, there is no legal gender recognition, LGBTIQ associations cannot register, and the state offers no protection from discrimination. Enforcement and hostile rhetoric concentrate here, including the 2009 arrest of a man in Bujumbura in which police sought money for his release (he was freed after advocacy secured it), the March 2023 arrest waves, and the seven convictions that followed, alongside the president's December 2023 call for people found engaging in gay sex to be stoned in stadiums — remarks rights groups described locally as a licence for violence. Police presence, checkpoints, ID and immigration spot-checks, hotel registration, airport, hospital and court checks are denser than elsewhere in the country, and the law does not expressly criminalise transgender identity or presentation, with no documented direct targeting of trans visitors — a gap that reflects uncertainty rather than assurance given the official climate. There is no trans-specific local data, no local exception, protective law or documented tolerance, and conditions differ from the national picture mainly in the intensity of policing and visibility; the capital's operative risk for a transgender visitor is at least as severe as elsewhere in Burundi. The law's absence of gender recognition means a visitor's foreign documents may not match their presentation, and a visitor whose gender marker, medication, documents or presentation attract attention could face questioning, confiscation, arrest under morality or sexuality offences, bribery demands, detention violence and deportation, while family or neighbourhood discovery carries real risk of ejection, extortion, assault or arrest; local NGOs are constrained, legal remedies are minimal, and some health services operate discreetly. Offsetting this only modestly, the city's urban anonymity, foreign and diplomatic presence, tourist-facing venues and small NGO footprint offer some informal support and institutional attention greater than in provinces such as Cibitoke or Karuzi.

regions.name: Bujumbura Rural
regions.merged_summary:
Bujumbura Rural has no documented local legal exception, protective measure, or trans-specific enforcement pattern, so Burundi's national regime applies: same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code (cited as Article 567 or Article 250) with prison terms of three months to two years and fines, with enforcement intensified in 2023 through arrests and convictions carrying one-to-two-year sentences. Legal gender recognition does not exist, so local documents cannot be made to match a transgender visitor's gender, LGBTIQ associations cannot register, and there is no anti-discrimination protection. In December 2023 the president publicly called for people found engaging in same-sex conduct to be stoned, remarks LGBTQ Burundians described as a licence to kill and followed by reports of terror and fear of lynching. Reporting across the country describes arbitrary detention, extrajudicial killings, torture and documented impunity, with police under national command aligned with the hostile executive line. The documented law concerns sexual conduct rather than transgender identity itself, but it creates exposure for a trans visitor who is discovered.

Locally, the province is largely rural and agricultural, made up of peri-urban hills and communes surrounding Bujumbura city, with limited tourist infrastructure, tight-knit and conservative communities, close social scrutiny, foreigners who are conspicuous, and checkpoints, local administrators and police harassment. This combination means a transgender visitor who is outed faces the same criminal exposure as elsewhere in Burundi but with less anonymity, a higher probability of being outed, and less access to advocacy, legal aid and consular help — though proximity to the capital does bring some consular, NGO and hospital presence, these resources are constrained and do not change the risk. Community and youth-militia presence is stronger, while institutional oversight and state enforcement capacity are thinner, raising the risk of community hostility, extortion or detention with little practical recourse; relative to the capital's greater anonymity, visibility and social exposure are higher here. No documented region-specific trans case, local incident, or information about visitor facilities, border treatment or protective remedies is recorded.

regions.name: Cankuzo
regions.merged_summary:
Cankuzo is a small, remote and poor, predominantly rural province in eastern Burundi near the Tanzanian border, lying outside the capital's greater concentration of services and advocacy. It has no urban queer infrastructure, no known tolerant venues or community organisations, and no documented local exceptions, protections, enforcement records, court outcomes or tourism-facing tolerance that distinguish it from the rest of the country; equally, there is no province-specific record of violence or of relief available to a transgender visitor, no documented province-specific targeting or protective practice — an absence of local data rather than evidence of safety. Tight small-community networks and conservative social and religious norms mean a visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitor has little anonymity, and discovery is likely to spread quickly through neighbours, lodging staff, local administrators, chiefs and religious authorities, adding social surveillance and reducing the chance of discreet handling.

The country's national rules supply the operative exposure: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code with imprisonment of up to two years and fines, with documented arrests, prosecutions and multi-year convictions in 2023; no legal gender recognition exists, so a visitor cannot obtain documents matching their gender identity; and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. Criminalisation does not itself target transgender identity, but if a visitor is outed or perceived as violating gender norms, arrest, detention, extortion and violence become possible alongside documented harassment, family rejection and societal stigma, with no effective government protection. In December 2023 the president publicly urged stoning of people found in same-sex acts — described by exile groups as a license to kill, with no documented official repudiation. In Cankuzo these conditions combine with weak policing often dominated by routine extortion, thinner institutional oversight, a weaker advocacy presence and greater reliance on police discretion than in the capital, plus no functioning local recourse or transgender-specific support network: discovery can bring detention or shakedowns, hostile community exposure, and a state climate that legitimises vigilante violence, an operating environment described as harsher than even Bujumbura, though no province-specific execution of a transgender visitor is documented.

regions.name: Cibitoke
regions.merged_summary:
Cibitoke is a rural, conservative northwestern border province of Burundi, bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo along the Rusizi and far from the Bujumbura tourism economy, with no tourism-facing tolerance or documented local protections. No region-specific information was found that clearly lowers or raises the national picture, and no trans or LGBTI organisation, shelter or legal-aid capacity operates in the province. Burundi criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under the Penal Code, punishable by up to two years' imprisonment and a fine, with enforcement intensifying in 2023 through arrests, prosecutions and convictions; there is no legal gender recognition, no government protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. Visitor documents cannot be changed to match gender, so mismatches at borders and checkpoints remain an exposure point. In December 2023 the president publicly dehumanised gay people and called for them to be stoned, remarks advocates said incited violence and that were widely read as licence for hostility. These are not trans-specific rules, but officials may interpret a trans visitor's relationships or presentation through them; police and local officials are likely to treat document or appearance mismatches as moral or public-order matters, and a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming visitor has little anonymity. Provincial exposure would probably come through a clinic, hotel, checkpoint or neighbourhood rumour, with arrest and abusive custody plausible and community violence poorly investigated; the broader setting includes documented harassment, stigma, family rejection, arbitrary detention, torture and extrajudicial killings with limited or no meaningful recourse.

The province is itself a documented enforcement site: in November 2016 the High Court of Cibitoke Province convicted a person reported as a 15-year-old minor on homosexuality charges alongside rape charges. This shows the statutory risk is operative locally, though the case is dated, involved a sexual-violence charge rather than trans-specific enforcement, and does not establish targeting of trans visitors or consensual conduct. Rural isolation and weaker institutional scrutiny plausibly reduce, rather than improve, protection for an outed visitor, including one travelling with a minor, while border-area security conditions and thin local oversight add uncertainty; visitor-specific document, facility, care and police practices, and effective protections, are not documented, and no known local difference materially mitigates the national risks.

regions.name: Gitega
regions.merged_summary: Gitega is Burundi's political capital and seat of government in the central interior, a small, administratively heavy second city with a prominent security presence, few international visitor services and limited anonymity for outsiders. It is generally more socially conservative and less cosmopolitan than Bujumbura, with a heavier concentration of state security, administrative checkpoints and party-linked surveillance around official institutions, so document checks by police, hotels or officials are more likely to draw attention than in the commercial hub; a visibly transgender foreigner has no local network or remedy. No Gitega-specific protections, sanctuary policy, tolerant venue network, community infrastructure, complaint mechanism or distinct police or court practice are known, and the hardline rhetoric emanates from the national leadership based there. Local conditions therefore add visibility and security scrutiny rather than mitigation. The national regime applies: Article 567 (or 250) of the Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct — punishable by three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine — though it does not criminalise transgender identity itself, it can create additional vulnerability if a visitor is perceived as engaging in same-sex conduct. Enforcement intensified markedly in 2023 with mass arrests, prosecutions, convictions and one- to two-year sentences, alongside documented arrests, extortion and convictions; the arrests have concentrated in Bujumbura, and while Gitega has fewer visible queer institutions and fewer documented local cases, that absence is not evidence of safety. No legal gender recognition exists, so a visitor's documents cannot be changed locally, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register, leaving no anti-discrimination recourse or government protection. In December 2023 the president publicly called for stoning people engaging in gay sex, described by activists, LGBTQ Burundians and the Iteka League as a licence to kill, with no later enforcement case documented; the remarks operate locally alongside reported stigma and discrimination. For a transgender visitor discovered or outed there, detention would follow birth-sex placement amid reported abuse and impunity, with arrest leverage under the morality statute, police extortion, humiliation, and mob or security violence credible in a setting of weak rule of law and documented impunity, and no recourse.

regions.name: Karuzi
regions.merged_summary:
Karuzi Province has no separate legal regime: Burundi's national rules apply in full, criminalising same-sex conduct with imprisonment of three months to two years and fines, denying legal gender recognition, and barring registration of LGBTIQ organisations. Enforcement intensified across the country in 2023, with arrests and convictions for same-sex conduct and inciting debauchery, and presidential remarks that people found engaging in gay sex should be taken to stadiums and stoned, which activists described as a licence to kill; senior officials have endorsed severe hostility, and reporting documents stigma, discrimination, harassment, arbitrary arrest and detention, and no effective government protection. In Karuzi itself, a 2014 case involving a foreign employee and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence, showing that perceived sexual-minority conduct can draw police attention and detention locally even when charges fail, but it does not establish how authorities treat transgender visitors, and no trans-specific local enforcement or protective practice is documented. The absence of such reports is not evidence of safety, and consequences may be serious if a visitor is treated as violating the law.

As a largely rural, agricultural province, Karuzi has tight community networks, limited anonymity, social conservatism, and scarce legal or LGBTIQ support, so discovery or being outed is harder to contain than in Bujumbura. A transgender visitor whose documents or presentation attract attention could face forced outing or community exposure, questioning, arbitrary detention, extortion, mistreatment in custody and violence, in a context of documented detention deaths elsewhere in Burundi, general impunity and weak rule of law; the province has no documented sanctuary, protective service or independent monitoring, leaving little recourse.

regions.name: Kayanza
regions.merged_summary:
Kayanza is a densely populated, largely rural province in Burundi's northern highlands, with a coffee- and tea-growing economy, close-knit communities shaped by strong Catholic and Anglican influence, limited anonymity, no visible LGBT community infrastructure, no trans-specific advocacy, legal aid or health expertise (support would require travel to Bujumbura), and no tourist-facing institutions. Local police and administrators exercise wide discretion under weak oversight, and no documented local exception — protective or hostile — distinguishes the province from the national picture; Kayanza-specific police practices, facility rules, violence patterns and treatment of foreign documents are not documented, and that uncertainty is not evidence of safety, as is the absence of any distinct rule for travelling minors.

Burundi's national framework therefore governs a visit: same-sex conduct is criminalised with imprisonment of up to two years and fines, enforcement intensified in 2023 with arrests, convictions, prison sentences and a death in custody and no later relief documented, and in December 2023 the president publicly called for stoning people found engaging in same-sex acts, which domestic advocates described as a licence to kill and which prompted documented fear among LGBTQ Burundians. There is no legal gender recognition, so a visitor cannot obtain documents matching their gender, and no government protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is documented, while LGBTIQ associations cannot register. For a trans visitor discovered or outed — through document checks, hospital care, lodging or public visibility — these provisions are not trans-specific but may expose them to suspicion or enforcement, and the hostile official climate, rural conservatism and absence of civil-society or consular monitoring mean social hostility, document mismatch, police extortion, arbitrary detention, service exclusion and local harassment with little reliable remedy; tourism does not create a protective local exception.

regions.name: Kirundo
regions.merged_summary: Kirundo is a remote, densely settled and farmed rural province in Burundi's north near the Rwandan and Tanzanian borders, with small-town social networks that offer little anonymity, limited tourism, and strong community and local-authority scrutiny. No Kirundo-specific rules, policing practice, enforcement campaign, protective exception, local trans organisation, or documented relief distinguish it from Burundi's national picture. Under that national framework, consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code with imprisonment of up to two years and a fine (sources cite different article numbers), enforcement intensified in 2023 with mass arrests, convictions and sentencing, and arrests for homosexuality and debauchery have included detention abuse and extortion. Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so a visitor's documents cannot be aligned with gender identity, LGBTIQ organisations cannot register, and discrimination receives no government protection, amid broader arbitrary arrest, weak rule of law, impunity for extrajudicial killings, and documented harassment, family rejection and stigmatisation. In December 2023 the president called publicly for people found engaging in same-sex conduct to be stoned, remarks described locally as licensing lethal violence and prompting fear among LGBTQ Burundians. The laws do not specifically criminalise transgender identity, and how they would be applied to a trans visitor is not established — that uncertainty is not evidence of safety. A visibly transgender visitor would likely be identified quickly, and because these laws do not address trans identity directly, discovery would rest on local scrutiny and official hostility rather than any documented local enforcement practice; given rural scrutiny, distance from oversight institutions and thin recourse, such discovery would carry a high risk of outing, hostile questioning, arbitrary detention, violence and little practical recourse, making it more consequential than in Bujumbura.

regions.name: Makamba
regions.merged_summary: Makamba is a remote, socially conservative rural province in southern Burundi on the Tanzanian border, where small, closely connected communities, frequent checkpoints, police stops and document checks, and low tourism limit anonymity for a foreign visitor. Its distance from the capital and international organisations, weak local institutions, sparse service infrastructure and limited advocacy or consular resources mean fewer protective bodies and little recourse, while its stronger administrative and security presence and local police discretion operate without meaningful oversight. No Makamba-specific transgender incident is documented, and no local exception, tolerant enclave or safeguard to national law and practice is known. The province falls squarely under Burundi's national regime: same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 567 with up to two years' imprisonment, there is no legal gender recognition or protection from discrimination, and enforcement intensified in 2023 through mass arrests and convictions, police use of such charges for extortion, and the president's December 2023 public call for people engaging in same-sex acts to be stoned in stadiums, with no subsequent reform on record. For a transgender visitor who is outed or read as gender nonconforming — including through a document or appearance mismatch, or trans-related documents or medication — these conditions combine to make police questioning by under-supervised officers, short-term detention in misgendered custody, extortion, referral under morality provisions and communal hostility more likely than protection, with weak independent remedies, risk of mistreatment in custody and severe escalation possible.

regions.name: Muramvya
regions.merged_summary:
Muramvya is a small, rural highland province in central Burundi with no documented local exceptions, protective practices, tolerance record, tourism-facing accommodation practice, or region-specific institutions that would soften the national picture for a transgender visitor; province-level enforcement practice is not documented beyond the national regime, and such gaps do not establish safety. Burundi's penal code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under Article 567, with imprisonment of three months to two years and a fine; arrests have been documented in 2009, 2012 and repeatedly in 2023, with convictions and prison sentences in 2023. The law targets conduct rather than transgender identity itself, and legal gender recognition, official protection from societal discrimination, and registration of LGBTIQ associations are all unavailable, so a visitor's foreign documents are the only gender marker. In December 2023 the president publicly called for people found engaging in gay sex to be stoned, described by exile monitors as a licence to kill or harm, amid reports of fear among LGBTQ Burundians, and a March 2026 monitoring entry records ongoing harassment, arbitrary arrests and torture in a setting without meaningful legal reform; nationally reported harassment, family rejection and stigmatisation also apply. Whether authorities would interpret a trans visitor's relationship or handle foreign documents is uncertain, and trans-specific facility rules, border practices and police targeting in Muramvya are not documented.

In Muramvya's close-knit, conservative communities a visibly transgender or outed visitor would have little anonymity and few avenues of recourse, so discovery would carry at least the national level of criminal exposure, societal hostility and official hostility, and would likely be harder to mitigate locally. Conditional on discovery or being outed, a visitor could face questioning, detention, coercive searches, violence, refusal of care, or exposure through police or local authorities, with no dependable state protection or effective remedy; the absence of documented local mitigations leaves the national severe-risk pattern in place.

regions.name: Muyinga
regions.merged_summary:
Muyinga is a largely rural, agricultural province in north-eastern Burundi near the Tanzanian border, and no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture for transgender visitors: there are no known trans-specific services, advocacy infrastructure or protective local practice, no documented trans-specific border checkpoint regime, and no visitor-specific protection from health, lodging or transport staff. Burundi's national framework criminalises same-sex conduct, with penalties of three months to two years' imprisonment and fines, and enforcement intensified in 2023 with mass arrests and prison sentences; police discretion and detention extortion are also reported. There is no legal gender recognition, LGBTIQ organisations cannot register, and constitutional provisions bar same-sex marriage. The law targets same-sex conduct rather than transgender identity, no trans-specific visitor enforcement is documented in Muyinga, and the resident-facing gap in gender recognition does not itself affect a visitor's foreign documents.

A visibly trans or outed visitor in this small, socially conservative provincial centre would attract notice, with hotel registration and police checks creating outing risk and little anonymity, and in close-knit communities discovery can lead to arbitrary detention, harassment, extortion or mob hostility, with recourse for harassment or detention effectively absent. State and social hostility is underscored by the president's December 2023 call for gay people to be stoned in stadiums, described by exile monitoring groups as a license to kill and followed by reports of fear among LGBTQ people, alongside reporting of extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, torture and societal discrimination with no government protection. Local conditions add scrutiny and isolation rather than mitigation.

regions.name: Mwaro
regions.merged_summary:
Mwaro is a small, densely populated rural highland province in Burundi's interior with no tourist-facing economy, no anonymous urban space, no visible LGBT community infrastructure, and strong church and community scrutiny, so a visibly transgender or gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to be noticed and discussed quickly. No region-specific information documents local protections, enforcement exceptions, or police or administrative practice differing from the national picture, and absence of such information is not evidence of safety. Policing in the province is thin, locally embedded and discretionary, and detention conditions are poor. One assessment notes that the criminal provision addresses sexual conduct rather than transgender identity or gender expression by itself, and that the effects of discovery in local facilities or police encounters remain uncertain rather than indicative of safety. The record for the most recent period is limited.

Burundi's national regime supplies the operative conditions: Article 567 of the Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine, enforcement intensified from 2023 with arrests and prison sentences, legal gender recognition does not exist so documents matching a visitor's gender cannot be obtained, LGBTIQ organisations cannot register, and the state offers no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. In December 2023 the president publicly called for people engaged in same-sex conduct to be stoned in stadiums, reported to have produced terror and perceived licence for violence or lynching among LGBTQ Burundians. Documented discrimination, family rejection and harassment are widespread, and a March 2026 entry records ongoing harassment, arbitrary arrest and torture amid no meaningful legal reform. Conditional on discovery or being outed, a transgender visitor faces police or community questioning, likely detention in an abusive custodial system, extortion, and violence with impunity, alongside expulsion and no meaningful protection, complaint channels, or reliable consular recourse.

regions.name: Ngozi
regions.merged_summary:
Ngozi is a largely rural, agricultural northern province whose capital shares its name, with tightly knit, conservative, family-centred and religiously observant communities, little tourist infrastructure and no visible LGBTIQ community life. It inherits Burundi's national regime: same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code, with imprisonment and fines, and documented arrests, convictions and police extortion for release since 2009 have intensified since 2023, including mass arrests. There is no legal gender recognition, so documents cannot match a transgender person's gender; there is no protection against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity; and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. In December 2023 the president publicly called for people engaging in same-sex sex to be stoned, remarks Burundian and exile activists described as a licence to kill. Documented enforcement has been concentrated in Bujumbura, and no Ngozi-specific cases, protections, targeting practices or distinct enforcement differences are known; that lack of information does not establish safety, and the criminal provisions concern same-sex conduct rather than transgender identity itself.

A transgender visitor who is visibly transgender or is outed here would face the same criminal exposure, official hostility and absence of recourse as nationally, with conditions that locally reduce anonymity and support: small-community visibility means discovery would likely spread through neighbours, local officials and police; there is no tourist-facing anonymity and no local LGBTIQ organisation, advocacy infrastructure or safe support network; and the province is less connected to Bujumbura's advocacy and legal-assistance interventions that have occasionally secured releases, leaving fewer reachable routes to help. Any detention would occur under the same weak rule-of-law conditions documented nationally, with community hostility adding to police exposure, and the likely operative exposure is questioning, detention or arrest under morality-related law, mistreatment in custody and little effective recourse.

regions.name: Rumonge
regions.merged_summary: Rumonge is a rural, socially conservative and religious lakeshore province on Lake Tanganyika in southern Burundi, centred on a small agrarian and fishing town that grew from a port, with limited foreign tourism, a tight social fabric, thin police and judicial presence relative to Bujumbura, and limited access to consular or legal aid; one account places it near the Congolese border. No regional exception to Burundi's national regime is documented: same-sex conduct remains criminalised under the Penal Code (Article 567, cited elsewhere as Article 250) with prison terms and fines, there is no legal gender recognition so foreign-issued documents carry the traveller's gender marker, there is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register. There is no documented local tolerance, sanctuary practice, protective enforcement, or LGBTIQ community infrastructure. Enforcement of the national law has included arrests, convictions, short prison sentences, extortion, arbitrary detention and detention abuse, escalating sharply in 2023, alongside stigmatising official rhetoric, including the president's December 2023 remarks — described as calling for people found engaging in gay sex to be stoned and as licensing violence against gender and sexual minorities — which advocates said encouraged violence. National reporting also documents harassment, family rejection and extrajudicial violence, societal discrimination acknowledged by the state without government protection, and no effective remedy or meaningful reform; the most recent documented incident nationally dates from early 2024. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, the national pattern combines with the local setting: possible charges, police or administrative questioning, hostile custody, community hostility, and extortion, with few institutional buffers and little practical recourse — in a small town where they are likely to be known quickly — while the law is not trans-specific and available national evidence does not establish a routine practice of targeting transgender visitors, an uncertainty that is not evidence of safety. Regarding how local conditions compare, accounts differ: Rumonge's weaker oversight and rural visibility are described as offering neither added protection nor documented added hostility, and in one account as leaving consequences at least as severe as nationally (though no region-specific execution pathway is known), while another describes conditions there as somewhat harsher than the national picture; no local enforcement pattern or protective practice for Rumonge itself is recorded.

regions.name: Rutana
regions.merged_summary:
Rutana is a poor, rural province in south-eastern Burundi with a low institutional presence, dense community-level surveillance in its hill settlements, and discovery more likely to run through local administration, neighbourhood gossip, customary or community authorities than through specialist police. It inherits Burundi's national regime without any documented local offset: same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code (Article 567 or 250), carrying up to two years' imprisonment and a fine, with documented enforcement including mass arrests in 2023, convictions for inciting debauchery, and one-to-two-year sentences in August 2023; there is no legal gender recognition, LGBTIQ organisations cannot register, and there is no government protection against discrimination based on gender identity. In December 2023 the president publicly endorsed stoning people engaging in gay sex in stadiums, remarks reported by Human Rights Watch in January 2024 and described by exile groups and LGBTQ Burundians as a licence for lethal violence. Rutana's deeper rural conservatism, near-total absence of trans community, advocacy or legal support, and thin formal state services add no trans-specific protections or favourable enforcement record; remedies would sit in Bujumbura, and the province's border and rural character is not documented as either easing or worsening exposure.

For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these laws are not trans-specific but operate as a secondary exposure alongside reported discrimination, with the weaker rule-of-law environment compounding rather than moderating the national picture. The likely pathway runs from discovery through police harassment, extortion, brief detention under morality-adjacent provisions, forced outing or violence, with courts unreliable, no effective recourse, and consular support limited; for travelling families, guardianship or community pressure could add coercion and separation from familiar supports. No region-specific anti-trans incidents are documented here, but no local protective practice or reliable remedy is documented either; the evidence does not establish that a trans visitor would be prosecuted or face lethal violence, and the consequences of discovery remain uncertain and potentially serious. Recourse is effectively nil.

regions.name: Ruyigi
regions.merged_summary: Ruyigi is a predominantly rural, remote province in eastern Burundi with a small-town and agrarian character, limited tourist infrastructure, close community scrutiny that makes foreign visitors conspicuous, strong local administration and party-linked youth networks, and thinner institutional presence than the capital. No region-specific information distinguishes it from Burundi's national picture: there is no documented local enforcement pattern, local exception, local protection or trans-specific support, and access to legal aid, advocacy organisations, anonymous services or sympathetic official recourse is very limited. Discovery there would more plausibly play out through municipal or customary authorities, police stations and moralistic community scrutiny than in neutral service settings. The rural setting may mean less documented police activity, but it also means less protection and less recourse, and local enforcement conditions have been described as making risk slightly higher than the national baseline; there are no documented Ruyigi-specific death sentences, and the consequences and frequency of targeting trans visitors there remain uncertain.\n\nThese conditions sit atop Burundi's national regime: Article 567 of the Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with three months to two years' imprisonment and fines, and it has been enforced through arrests, extortion for release and 2023 convictions carrying one- to two-year sentences, with enforcement intensifying in 2023 and the most recent documented event in January 2024. There is no legal gender recognition, although the law does not specifically criminalise being transgender and a visitor's documents are issued abroad, so the absence of local recognition is not itself a document rule visitors face; LGBTIQ organisations cannot be registered, no anti-discrimination protection exists, and LGBT people face societal discrimination with no government protection. In December 2023 the president publicly endorsed stoning people found engaging in gay sex — remarks read by exile monitors and LGBTQ advocates as a license to kill — after which LGBTQ Burundians reported terror. The wider documented environment includes arbitrary arrests, arbitrary detention, extrajudicial killings, torture and sexual violence, with advocacy and legal intervention concentrated in Bujumbura. For a transgender visitor who is outed or perceived to be in a same-sex relationship, the realistic exposure is police detention, extortion, abuse in custody, community rejection and possible violence enabled by official hostility, with weak practical remedy and no realistic recourse.

regions.name: Atlanique
regions.merged_summary:
Atlantique is Benin's southern coastal department, taking in Cotonou's peri-urban fringe (including Abomey-Calavi), the tourist town of Ouidah, Allada and surrounding smaller towns and rural communes. It is the country's most urbanised and most visitor-facing zone, with greater anonymity, business and foreign presence, and some service providers more accustomed to foreign visitors; the harsher enforcement documented nationally is described as mainly a rural and northern phenomenon. Cotonou has hosted public gatherings (the most recent documented in 2013) and a small survivor-support shelter network. However, no region-specific protective statute, remedy or facility policy distinguishes the department, and local trans-specific enforcement and violence patterns are not documented — much of the department lies outside the capital's urban core, and surrounding rural and traditional communities, police, hospitals and religious institutions remain hostile or indifferent.

The national regime therefore governs. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is legal and there is no trans-specific offence, imprisonment or capital penalty, so custody is not a credible outcome for an outed visitor — but discovery carries documented severity: no legal gender recognition and no protection on grounds of gender identity; documented refusal of hormone therapy and routine medical care such as treatment for malaria; employment refusal singling out transgender people; religious hostility from churches, mosques and traditional healers, including coerced conversion therapy; and LGBTI organisations unable to register. Anti-LGBTQ lynchings are described as commonplace and largely unpunished, with police rarely pursuing perpetrators and victims hiding their identity when reporting. The result for an outed trans visitor is denial of care, harassment, extortion or mob violence, with police unlikely to intervene, though with less street-level scrutiny than in more rural areas.

regions.name: Borgou
regions.merged_summary:
Borgou is a largely rural, predominantly Muslim department in north-eastern Benin centred on Parakou, a commercial city rather than a tourist hub. It inherits Benin's national framework, in which same-sex conduct between adults is legal but there is no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and an indecency provision that can be used against same-sex conduct. The department is more socially and religiously conservative than the southern coast, closely knit, and less developed for tourism, with thin police presence; documented country-wide reporting notes greater hostility outside major urban areas, and religious and conversion-therapy hostility applies throughout the country. No Borgou-specific incidents, no separate local statute or organized state campaign against trans visitors, and no local protective services are documented, and the absence of such records is not evidence of safety, while the local frequency of hostility remains uncertain. The few national support structures — shelters and youth groups — are concentrated in Cotonou and the south rather than in Parakou or rural Borgou, leaving no local recourse or shelter, and distance from Cotonou compounds isolation.

For a trans visitor who is visibly trans or outed, these conditions combine with the national pattern of documented refusals of hormone therapy and general medical care, civilian anti-LGBTQ violence including lynchings described as commonplace, and police who rarely pursue perpetrators, act with indifference or hostility toward those who report, and prompt victims to conceal their identity from officers. Greater community scrutiny, family and community exposure, conversion pressure, and stigma reinforced by religious and traditional authority elevate the risks of hostile social reaction, refusal of care, extortion and violence, with no sympathetic institutional contact and little effective recourse.

regions.name: Littoral
regions.merged_summary:
Littoral, centered on Cotonou and Porto-Novo, is Benin's most urban, cosmopolitan and tourism-facing coastal department, home to the main port, airport, universities, foreign residents, embassies, NGOs and nightlife, with denser and more anonymous street life than rural areas. Consensual adult same-sex conduct is not criminalized, but the country provides no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no reliable police remedy. The documented urban/rural split in hostility applies favourably here: foreigner status in the commercial capital and the city's cosmopolitan character reduce social scrutiny compared with rural districts where hostility is strongest, and a small urban LGBT community plus the country's only documented support infrastructure — the Hirondelles Club shelter at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre in Cotonou, and the 2013 Cotonou IDAHOT gathering that drew 200 people — offers some practical access to sympathetic services and limited community space. No specific local rule or protection for trans visitors is documented, and no region-specific incident record distinguishes Littoral from the national picture; local protections are largely on paper, and urban visibility does not provide enforceable recourse. Border treatment of foreign documents, facility access and custody placement are not documented, leaving uncertainty rather than established safety.

If discovered or outed, the national conditions still govern: documented refusal of medical care including hormone therapy and general treatment, harassment, extortion, public humiliation, civilian violence and lynchings that police rarely pursue, with victims often concealing their identity for fear of mistreatment, and religious condemnation from churches, mosques and traditional healers including conversion therapy, alongside family and community pressure that persists in the city. The same visibility that improves access to services can also increase exposure in hotels, clinics, beaches and bars, where a transgender visitor may still face refusal of care, harassment or assault with limited reliable official recourse. Cotonou's cosmopolitan character may reduce overt hostility and improve practical access to help, but police inaction, healthcare refusals and street violence recorded nationally are not documented as absent there.

regions.name: Oueme
regions.merged_summary:
Oueme is a southern coastal department containing Porto-Novo, the administrative capital, and bordering Cotonou, the country's most urbanised and socially open area. No local legal protections distinguish it from Benin's national framework: consensual adult same-sex acts are legal, but indecency provisions have been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and there is no gender-identity protection, no anti-discrimination law covering employment, services or public life, no legal gender recognition and no hate-crime recourse. Urban settings are described as offering only modest mitigation, with hostility recorded especially outside major urban areas and surrounding rural communities more socially conservative; the more urban, multilingual and cosmopolitan character of Porto-Novo and the southern corridor may offer somewhat more anonymity and a slightly more varied service environment than rural northern departments, and foreigner status may blunt some local scrutiny, though Oueme is less documented as an LGBTQ-friendly hub than Cotonou. The department's Yoruba and Vodun cultural mix has historically accommodated more fluid gender presentation than much of the north, but visitors should not assume this offsets the national conditions. Community infrastructure exists nearby — support centres, small survivor-support shelters and a documented Cotonou gathering and shelter network — but it serves residents rather than visitors, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. The Children's Code bars foreign same-sex couples from adoption, and no organized state campaign targeting trans visitors is documented. Region-specific knowledge is limited to urban character and proximity to that infrastructure; trans-targeted police or visitor incidents, border-document friction, facility rules and custody practices in Oueme are not documented, and no documented incidents appear after 2013 in the available record — gaps that do not establish that such risks are absent.

If discovered or outed, a transgender visitor here faces refusal rather than arrest, but the consequences remain civic and medical: documented denial of general and hormone-related healthcare, employer discrimination, possible lodging refusal, intrusive questioning at security or health desks, and forced outing at any document or care checkpoint. Civilian anti-LGBTQ violence, including lynchings, is reported as largely unpunished, with police rarely pursuing perpetrators, victims concealing their identity when reporting, and fear of mistreatment deterring reporting; police protection is weak, so seeking help may expose the visitor further, and private actors may cause harm. Religious actors — Evangelical, Catholic and Muslim preaching alongside traditional-healer coercion — are a documented source of hostility, including demonising rhetoric and coerced conversion practices.

regions.name: Centre
regions.merged_summary:
Centre is Burkina Faso's capital region, dominated by Ouagadougou, which concentrates the government, the junta's political apparatus, police headquarters, the gendarmerie, embassies, major hospitals and the main international airport. Document checks are denser here than in rural areas, with the airport, hotels and government offices the places where papers are examined, and any morality enforcement would begin in the capital. No local exemption, protective ordinance or documented trans-specific enforcement pattern distinguishes the region from the national picture. The capital's size, foreign-resident and diplomatic presence and informal queer networks offer more anonymity than upcountry towns, where a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner would draw far more attention, but this does not reduce the consequences of discovery. Conservative religious and traditional disapproval persists, and older reports describe social rejection and abuse without establishing current local prevalence.

Since September 2025, consensual same-sex conduct carries two to five years' imprisonment and fines, promotion is banned, and the justice minister has stated that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported. The statute targets conduct rather than transgender identity, but it is framed by birth-sex status, so a trans visitor's relationship may fall within its terms and exposure depends on how conduct is interpreted. There is no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, no documented mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence, and LGBTQ organisations have no legal presence. No arrests or prosecutions under the new law had been reported by late September 2025, which does not establish safety or current non-enforcement; under military rule and with recourse absent, a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed can face police questioning, detention, expulsion or removal, with exposure remaining statutory and discretionary rather than remedied.

regions.name: Centre-Est
regions.merged_summary:
Centre-Est has no documented trans-specific protections, enforcement exceptions or support infrastructure setting it apart from Burkina Faso's national regime, and accounts differ on the region's composition, naming Tenkodogo, Koudougou and Manga in one case and describing it as the capital region centred on Ouagadougou in another. Since 1 September 2025, consensual same-sex relations carry two to five years' imprisonment and a fine, promotion of homosexuality is banned, and foreign nationals face deportation — Justice Minister Bayala has stated this explicitly. No arrests under the framework were reported as of late September 2025, so enforcement appears statutory and discretionary rather than documented, and the absence of reported arrests does not establish safety; local remedies and visitor experiences are likewise undocumented. The constitutional non-discrimination clause omits sexual orientation and gender identity, there is no legal gender recognition, no documented mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence, and religious and traditional opinion remains hostile, alongside reported fear of a witch hunt and self-censorship. Exposure for a trans visitor arises if a relationship or presentation is read locally as same-sex conduct rather than being trans as such; once discovered or outed, that national regime applies with little practical remedy.

Locally, the region is described as a settled, agriculturally dense southern zone with lighter direct jihadist activity than the eastern and Sahelian regions, and its towns have functioning police, courts and ordinary hotel and clinic services, while urban anonymity, hotels, international organisations and a larger expatriate presence may offer somewhat more privacy than rural areas. Against this, police checkpoints, hotel registration and document scrutiny remain everyday features, and in the Tenkodogo area reported insecurity, displacement, checkpoints and strained state authority make encounters with security actors or armed groups less predictable. There is no local trans-specific exception, protective facility practice or tourist-facing shield, so a visibly trans or outed visitor may face discretionary police attention, arbitrary questioning, extortion, community hostility or detention as well as statutory removal, compounding the national exposure with weak recourse.

regions.name: Centre-Nord
regions.merged_summary:
Centre-Nord — a largely rural, socially conservative region centred on Kaya with no known local exception to national law — inherits Burkina Faso's regime criminalising consensual same-sex conduct since 1 September 2025, punishable by two to five years' imprisonment and a fine, alongside a ban on promotion and stated deportation of foreign nationals; no arrests were reported in the initial weeks. The constitution and anti-discrimination provisions do not reference sexual orientation or gender identity, and no mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented. A transgender visitor is not criminalised for being trans as such, but a relationship read locally as same-sex on birth-sex grounds creates exposure. Religious and traditional opinion does not accept homosexuality, and national evidence describes social rejection and occasional abuse together with fear of a witch hunt and self-censorship following criminalisation, although that pattern is old and consequences for visitors remain uncertain; no Centre-Nord-specific record of trans prosecutions, targeted enforcement or targeted violence is documented.

What differentiates the region is institutional fragility under conflict: much of it is an epicentre of jihadist insurgency, with JNIM- and Ansarul Islam-affiliated groups acting as de facto authorities enforcing strict religious norms, government-aligned VDP militia violence occurring with near-total impunity, mass displacement, common military and gendarmerie checkpoints, and uneven state authority, leaving police presence sparse, courts barely functioning, and legal or advocacy support scarce. A visibly trans visitor discovered at a checkpoint, clinic or lodging could therefore face discretionary enforcement, possible detention and expulsion under the national statute, with any accusation of moral or religious violation potentially escalating to militia detention or armed-group punishment, and no working remedy, documented local tolerance of visible gender nonconformity, or protective infrastructure for visitors.

regions.name: Centre-Ouest
regions.merged_summary:
Centre-Ouest, with Koudougou as its principal town, is described as a predominantly rural, mostly Mossi region under conservative religious and traditional authority, with state authority uneven across parts of the region, armed groups operating with impunity, and displacement worsening protection gaps. One account instead describes the region as containing Ouagadougou, the capital and most cosmopolitan part of the country, historically hosting the country's small unofficial LGBTQ networks and constituting its mildest enforcement geography; the same account notes that this does not neutralise the inherited criminal statute, while another holds that insecurity places the region below the national baseline without implying execution-level punishment. There are no documented transgender-specific services or advocacy, LGBTQ organisations have no legal presence, and foreign visitors have little anonymity outside Ouagadougou; police discretion and weak oversight make discovery at hotels, checkpoints or hospitals unpredictable, with extortion or detention plausible, and displacement and conservative norms raise the chance of informal policing, community accusation or detention.
