Public services, transport and accommodation in Tampere generally operate without identity-based exclusion, and the region is among the more socially liberal parts of Finland; no Pirkanmaa-specific hostile legislation, facility or border restriction, enforcement practice, or documented police hostility toward trans visitors is known, and no local deviations from the national picture are documented. Rural municipalities within the region are more socially conservative, where a visitor who is out or discovered may encounter staring, misgendering or occasional service friction shaped by individual providers or communities rather than regional policy — not formal arrest, entry refusal, or severe legal consequence tied to being trans.

The operative regime remains Finland's: trans identity and consensual same-sex activity are not criminalised, gender identity and expression have been covered by criminal, equality and anti-discrimination law since 2005, and legal gender recognition has been available on a self-declaration basis since 2023. Police record sexual-orientation and gender-identity hate-crime motives, though there is no separate hate-crime offence, and nationally reported suspected hate-crime incidents are rising without any established Pirkanmaa-specific rate; national reports of difficult access to gender-affirming care, concentrated gender-care waiting lists, restrictive clinical recommendations for under-25s (which may matter to travelling families seeking care for a trans minor but are not a general restriction on visiting) and pending conversion-practice legislation also apply. Police, courts and anti-discrimination remedies are documented as functioning for trans people, so exposure conditional on discovery amounts to residual hate incidents, uneven local service practice and conservative attitudes rather than any state-imposed restriction.

regions.name: Päijät-Häme
regions.merged_summary:
Päijät-Häme is a southern Finnish region centred on Lahti, roughly an hour from Helsinki, mixing a mid-sized city with smaller and more traditional, partly rural municipalities such as Heinola, Hollola and Orimattila. It operates under the same national framework as the rest of Finland: no region-specific laws, facility restrictions, policing practices or other local departures governing transgender visitors are documented, and no local pattern of violence or official targeting is recorded. Lahti provides the region's main accommodation, transport, policing and social venues and offers some organised queer visibility, while surrounding municipalities are smaller and more conservative, and the region is less metropolitan than Uusimaa with thinner trans community infrastructure. The absence of locally distinguishing information does not by itself establish safety.

Under the inherited national regime, trans identity and consensual same-sex activity are not criminalised, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity and expression has been a criminal offence since 2005, with the Equality Act covering employment, goods and services, education and health care. A 2023 reform made legal gender recognition self-declaration based and removed sterilisation and diagnosis requirements, though those resident-facing rules do not determine a visitor's documents. Police record sexual-orientation and gender-identity motives in suspected hate crimes, while the Criminal Code contains no separate hate-crime offence or dedicated sentencing provision; nationwide reporting of such suspicions has risen in recent years from a low base, mainly defamation and assault, alongside recorded hate-motivated offences and violence, against a backdrop of conservative social attitudes in parts of the interior. Police and courts generally protect rather than target trans people. For a visitor who is outed or discovered, exposure is essentially the same as Finland generally plus local conditions: no plausible risk of imprisonment or state persecution, and no documented border, custody, health-care or law-enforcement practice in the region imposing consequences beyond the national picture, but possible staring, curious or awkward misgendering, uneven staff awareness, informal discomfort around gendered services, and — where visibility is local in close-knit areas and service networks are smaller and vary in trans competence — social friction and administrative inconvenience rather than legal danger, with no evidence of organised hostility. Wider climate and service signals, including extended waits in gender-affirming care and 2020 clinical recommendations restricting such care for minors and prioritising psychosocial therapy, are national rather than regional and operate as no visitor-facing restriction here.

regions.name: Satakunta
regions.merged_summary:
Satakunta, on Finland's west coast around Pori and Rauma as well as smaller municipalities, operates under the national framework: no criminalisation of trans identity or expression or of consensual same-sex activity (legal since 1971); gender-identity discrimination a criminal offence since 2005 and covered by the Discrimination Act and the Act on Equality between Women and Men across employment, services, education and health care; legal gender recognition reformed in 2023, removing prior sterilisation and diagnosis requirements; police recording gender identity or expression as a hate-crime motive amid rising reported suspected offences, though the Criminal Code has no standalone hate-crime offence; and functioning courts and generally professional policing. No region-specific record of violence, police hostility, service refusal, institutional exclusion, targeted policing, moral-police activity or anti-trans organising distinguishes Satakunta, and no distinct local protection or trans visitor restriction is known either.

What differs locally is visibility and everyday friction rather than legal or state exposure. The region is smaller, more rural and more socially conservative than the capital area, with less anonymity and a Lutheran-influenced small-town climate, so a visibly trans or outed visitor may draw more curiosity, misgendering, awkward service encounters or gaps in local knowledge than in Helsinki. Trans-specific support infrastructure is thinner, rural familiarity with trans visitors is limited, and specialised trans-affirming health services and trained frontline staff are less concentrated than in the capital region, which can produce bureaucratic delays or awkwardness if ongoing gender-affirming care or crisis support is needed. Nationally, gender-affirming care for minors is restricted by 2020 recommendations, waiting lists and slow care are documented, and a survey found many trans respondents unable to access needed care, with some harassment reported; these national shortcomings, rather than any local escalation, remain the main exposures. Arrest, state violence or denial of basic emergency care are not the identified risks.

regions.name: South Karelia
regions.merged_summary: South Karelia, the southeastern border region centred on Lappeenranta and Imatra, operates under Finland's national framework: transgender identity and expression are not criminalised, discrimination on grounds of gender identity is an offence under law in force since 2005, the Equality Act protections apply, and police record hate motives and courts handle complaints. No region-specific trans-related statute, restriction, policing campaign, facility ban, or documented pattern of anti-trans violence, targeting, or official hostility is known here. What distinguishes the region is that it is more rural, older, smaller and socially conservative than Helsinki, with less anonymity, fewer LGBTQ venues and smaller-service provision that can bring unfamiliarity with trans documents and care pathways, alongside rising national hate-crime reporting. Public attitudes are generally less internationally exposed, so curiosity, staring, misgendering, verbal harassment, or occasional service friction are more plausible than in the capital, and specialist gender-affirming care is centralised outside the region, meaning a visitor needing continuity may face travel or waiting, while routine local services, emergency care, hotels and transport remain generally accessible under national protections. In practical terms, a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed faces at most discrimination, service friction, or verbal harassment, with functioning legal recourse through police and courts; there is no credible risk of detention, imprisonment, or lethal consequences. The Russian border and Schengen external controls add ordinary document scrutiny, which can be greater for travellers whose passport marker or name differs from their presentation, but border crossings follow Finnish rules rather than Russian ones, trans-specific checks are not a known local practice, cross-border traffic brings no documented trans-specific exposure, and Finland's restrictions on gender care for minors apply here as elsewhere. Local conditions suggest somewhat less predictable everyday acceptance than the national average, without severe or systemic exposure.

regions.name: Southern Savonia
regions.merged_summary: Southern Savonia — a rural, sparsely populated lake region of eastern Finland centred on Mikkeli and Savonlinna, with small towns, an older and more socially traditional population than Helsinki or Finland's larger cities, and a seasonal tourism economy around Savonlinna's opera and festival — has no distinct local law, ordinance, enforcement practice, pattern of violence or official abuse affecting transgender visitors; national rules on documents, facilities and medical care apply. Finland does not criminalise transgender identity, expression or same-sex conduct, and discrimination based on gender identity has been a criminal offence since 2005, with the Discrimination Act and Equality Act covering gender identity and expression, including discrimination based on assumption; legal gender recognition has run on a non-sterilisation, self-declaration basis since 2023, and police and courts function as neutral institutions, record gender-identity motive in hate-crime reports (though there is no standalone hate-crime offence) and give access to meaningful legal recourse. Public venues, hotels, lake cruises and the Savonlinna festival operate under that same national equality framework, and emergency and hospital care follows national non-discrimination obligations. Conditions differing from metropolitan Finland include fewer LGBT organisations and services, thinner local trans-specific and peer networks, narrower specialised health and administrative expertise, less experience with gender-diverse residents, less anonymity in small towns and villages, and gender-affirming care that is centralised elsewhere with waiting times that can be long — so a visitor needing routine or specialist care may encounter unfamiliarity or delay. Region-specific information is absent: no local incident record or local prevalence data was identified, and recorded national trends — rising hate-crime suspicions involving sexual orientation or gender identity, and a 2018 rise in violent attacks against LGBT people — do not establish the local picture. Conditional on discovery or being outing, the likely experience is social curiosity, awkwardness, staring, misgendering, occasional friction or isolated insults rather than state hostility or organised targeting, with institutions generally enforcing protections; no credible pathway to detention, imprisonment or violence above background is known locally. Local social reactions and service experiences beyond this remain uncertain.

regions.name: Tavastia Proper
regions.merged_summary: Tavastia Proper — a largely rural, small-town province of southern inland Finland centred on Hämeenlinna, Riihimäki, Forssa and Lahti, and now without separate legal status — has no local ordinance, facility restriction, border or checkpoint practice, shelter or custody rule, policing pattern, official campaign or documented incident targeting transgender visitors, so a traveller inherits Finland's national framework: no criminalisation of transgender identity or expression, criminal and civil anti-discrimination protection on gender-identity grounds since 2005 covering employment, goods and services, education and health, police recording of hate motive (with 241 reported suspicions in the sexual-orientation and gender-identity category, counts that remain low and have risen in recent years), functioning police and courts that investigate and prosecute anti-LGBT violence, and the same access to equality complaints and legal aid as elsewhere — although the Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence or sentencing aggravator for hate motive. Police and health staff are trained nationally, and emergency and routine public services are generally accessible under standard Finnish administrative practice. Social acceptance is documented alongside reported anti-LGBT incidents, but the cited figures are not specific to Tavastia Proper or necessarily to transgender people and do not establish a local pattern of targeting visitors. Nothing indicates a credible legal, custodial or violent threat arising from discovery; consequences stay at social friction and bureaucratic delay.

regions.name: Uusimaa
regions.merged_summary: Uusimaa, containing Helsinki, Espoo and Vantata, operates within Finland's national framework: there is no criminal penalty for being transgender or for gender expression, discrimination on grounds of gender identity and expression has been prohibited since 2005, and equality statutes covering goods, services and health have applied since 2014, backed by functioning police, courts and equality oversight, with a 2023 legal-gender-recognition reform ending forced sterilisation. Police record hate-crime motives, though the Criminal Code has no standalone hate-crime offence, so motive is logged rather than charged; reported suspected hate crimes with sexual-orientation or gender-identity motives have risen nationally, with no Uusimaa-specific rate established, and most recorded cases are concentrated in the metropolitan area, where anti-LGBT incidents are investigated and prosecuted rather than met with impunity. Uusimaa is Finland's most urban, internationally diverse and socially liberal region, holding the country's largest concentration of foreign visitors, public services, hospitals, LGBTQ venues, trans advocacy organisations, the central gender identity units, and large Pride events with official participation, alongside Seta-linked services. Everyday exposure for a trans visitor is therefore generally limited to mild curiosity, occasional service friction or street-level harassment of low severity, and routine document questions; document checks in hotels, transport, clinics and at Helsinki-Vantaa follow standard EU practice with no trans-specific screening and no requirement to disclose medical history, and border staff are reported to handle differing markers professionally. Should a visitor be outed or discovered, national anti-discrimination protections and police, court and equality-body recourse apply, and the capital's police are described as well-resourced and accustomed to diverse presentations, with no documented pattern of police or official targeting of trans visitors or hostile local directives; the residual exposures are administrative friction or passport/presentation mismatches at airports, hotels or medical appointments, isolated social discomfort, and national-level gaps including long waits for gender-affirming care, restrictive clinical guidance for minors, and a conversion-practices ban still pending.

regions.name: Åland Islands
regions.merged_summary:
The Åland Islands are an autonomous, demilitarised, Swedish-speaking archipelago of Finland with Mariehamn as its tourist centre, and its autonomy does not alter the Finnish legal framework that applies to visitors: trans identity and expression and same-sex conduct are not criminalised, discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression has been a criminal offence since 2005, equality protections cover goods and services, legal gender recognition has been available since 2023 without prior sterilisation or diagnosis requirements, same-sex marriage is legal, and police and courts function and record hate motives. Police-recorded hate incidents, including those involving gender identity or expression, have risen but remain modest, and there is no statutory hate-crime aggravation. No Åland-specific restriction on documents, facilities, healthcare access or public presence, and no documented pattern of police targeting, entry refusal, facility exclusion or visitor-facing hostility, is known; border, facility, custody and emergency-care practice is simply not documented locally, and knowledge of region-specific enforcement is limited, so that uncertainty should not be read as evidence of safety. Daily life is tourism-oriented, accustomed to foreign visitors, and generally tolerant under Nordic social norms, with Finnish remedies and emergency care available through the national system.

The main local differences are scale and language: Åland is a small, close-knit society of roughly 30,000 with a Swedish-language environment, a tourism-dependent economy and fewer services than the mainland, so a visibly trans visitor is more conspicuous, anonymity is thinner than in Helsinki, and word travels quickly. Rural social attitudes tend to be more conventional than in the capital, raising the likelihood of staring, awkward misgendering, gossip or local officials knowing one Health and education are administered by Åland's own authorities, and specialist gender-affirming care is obtained through mainland Finland, involving referral and waiting times — a practical rather than legal concern. For a transgender visitor who is out or discovered, these tight-community visibility effects combine with Finland's protective equality and non-criminalising regime: consequences remain generally mild, with the discomfort being social rather than a state or street-level threat, and no trans-specific incidents or facility disputes are recorded. One assessment notes that Finland's residual concerns — rising hate-crime reporting, the absence of statutory aggravation and care-access friction — are not aggravated locally and do not plausibly reach imprisonment or severe outcomes for a visitor.

regions.name: Central
regions.merged_summary:
Central Division, anchored by Suva — Fiji's capital, largest city, most urbanised and internationally connected region, and seat of government and most public-sector and police institutions — inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct lawful since 2010, constitutional protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, but no legal gender-recognition or gender-marker-change route, no legal status for traditional third-gender identities, and a non-discrimination guarantee not operationalised for gender markers, so a visitor's foreign documents remain the exposure point. Locally, Suva's international visitor presence, expatriate community, LGBTQ+ advocacy and health services, visible Pride and vaka sa lewa lewa organising, diverse hospitality sector and comparatively plural public life offer more anonymity, community and practical support than rural divisions, and gender-nonconforming presentation is comparatively familiar in urban, government and university settings — softening everyday outing consequences modestly above the national picture. Urban administration and courts also make complaint routes more accessible than in remote divisions. No Central-specific criminalisation, facility ban, border practice or additional legal protection distinct from national law is documented, and there is no evidence of organised state targeting or a documented pattern of trans-specific violence beyond the national picture; nor is there reliable evidence of effective local enforcement of protections.

Offsetting this, conservative Methodist, Catholic and Muslim norms remain influential across the division's towns and peri-urban areas; discrimination, bullying and longstanding distrust of police — documented in Suva itself — complicate reporting anti-LGBTQ harm, while the concentration of churches, police checkpoints and bureaucratic offices can make scrutiny and conservative disapproval more visible. The division includes the site of the documented May 2018 murder of a young transgender woman in Suva, the most recent such killing on record, with no documented anti-trans killing since in the sources reviewed — a serious local signal that one case does not by itself establish as a rate or pattern, and Suva's greater visibility thus cuts both ways: more familiarity and community, but also documented local violence. Conditional on discovery, formal protections are real but thin and uneven: document mismatches, hospital or service enquiries and police stops can out a traveller, and discovery by police, in custody, or outside central neighbourhoods carries harassment and, in custody, misplacement risk. The likely outcomes are social hostility, service friction, harassment or denial of services with delayed or uneven recourse rather than state punishment, imprisonment or lethal state action.

regions.name: Western
regions.merged_summary:
The Western Division — Nadi (including the international gateway and Denarau resort zone), Lautoka, Ba, the Coral Coast and the Mamanuca/Yasawa resorts — is Fiji's principal tourism and commercial hub, with international flights, resorts, a large expatriate and Indo-Fijian presence, and routine contact with foreign visitors. It inherits the national position: consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since 2010, there is no trans-specific criminal offence, and the 2013 Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender identity and expression, though there is no legal gender recognition or gender-marker change route and that protection has little documented operative implementation. The traditional vaka sa lewa lewa third-gender presence is accepted in Fijian society but carries no legal status. No local statute restricts transgender visitors, no Western-specific hostile law, targeting pattern, rejection of foreign documents, facility restriction or adverse enforcement practice is known, and no region-specific criminalisation, detention pattern or violence against trans travellers is evident; the documented 2018 murder of a transgender woman occurred in Suva, outside this division, and is a single dated case. The tourism-facing economy means hospitality staff and police are accustomed to foreign guests and documents, dress and gender diversity is less conspicuous in towns and hotel areas than in rural villages, and ordinary hospitality toward visitors is the norm, a modest practical distinction that may reduce routine friction but is not evidence of trans-specific protection.

Because no local remedy offsets the national gaps, discovery or being outed exposes a visitor to the country's regime overall: conservative religious social currents are widespread, with Methodist, Catholic, Hindu, Muslim and conservative village communities — particularly in the Lautoka and Ba sugar-belt areas, and rural Rakiraki and the interior — viewing cross-dressing as sinful and potentially sustaining misgendering, social pressure and service friction outside tourist zones. Bullying and discrimination are documented nationally, trust in police is limited and reporting of anti-LGBTQ violence is discouraged, making police recourse after harassment unreliable and the effectiveness of remedies uncertain; as Nadi is the main international gateway, a mismatch between a passport and presentation can prompt border questioning, though no systematic targeting of trans visitors is documented, and no local protective or enforcement difference from the national picture is known.

regions.name: Centre-Val de Loire
regions.merged_summary:
Centre-Val de Loire has no trans-specific legislation, ban or protection of its own: gender identity, facilities and discrimination law are national, police and courts operate on the national system, and no local sweeps, border practices or facility bans differ from the French pattern. The region is largely rural and small-to-mid-sized — Orléans, Tours, Blois, Chartres and Bourges, with château and Loire Valley tourism — and is less cosmopolitan and more socially centre-right than Paris and Île-de-France, with trans community infrastructure and trans-affirming clinicians thin outside Tours; Orléans and Tours do provide institutional recourse and visibility. A visibly trans visitor in small towns or rural château country should expect staring, curiosity and ordinary day-to-day friction, along with more misgendering and administrative scrutiny where specialist services are scarce, rather than organised hostility, and tourist-facing hospitality in the Loire Valley marginally softens that picture; compared with France's lower-acceptance overseas departments, the region offers a more urban, tourist-oriented rule-of-law setting. Overall practical exposure therefore remains close to the national picture.

If discovery or being outing occurs, national conditions apply unchanged: gender expression is not criminalised, transphobia has been a statutory aggravating factor since 2017, conversion therapy is banned, and anti-discrimination and hate-speech law sit alongside a functioning rights ombudsman and prosecutorial machinery. Against these protections stand documented exposures — documents are checked at entry and in everyday services, with border-police document friction; in custody, placement follows the gender or birth sex recorded on identity papers, with isolation, improvised units and strip-search exposure reported by custodial oversight as unremedied since 2010; and discrimination persists in services and healthcare, with a 2023 EU survey recording 64% reporting identity-related discrimination.

regions.name: Grand Est
regions.merged_summary:
Grand Est applies France's national framework unchanged: trans identity is not criminalised, there is no trans-specific entry ban, transphobia has been a statutory aggravating factor since 2017, and equality and anti-discrimination protections are in force. The national exposures remain: border officers may publicly question a mismatch between a traveller's documents and presentation, with a documented case of a trans traveller questioned at an airport; periodic security and immigration controls at the Schengen crossings — Mulhouse-Basel and the German, Belgian and Luxembourg borders — apply the same French document checks and can raise routine scrutiny; and in custody, placement follows either the sex shown on identity documents or birth sex (accounts differ), with isolation and, as reported by inspectors, strip-search exposure. Ombudsman findings record persistent discrimination in services and accommodation.

Within the region, Strasbourg — home to the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights — along with Metz, Nancy and Reims have larger LGBTQ communities, visible Pride events, LGBT associations, university hospitals and cosmopolitan settings, and cross-border traffic with Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland makes official and service-provider encounters there comparatively routine; the visitor-facing tourism economy of Alsace Christmas markets, Reims and Colmar is habituated to outsiders. Rural and small-town areas — the Vosges, Ardennes, parts of Champagne, former industrial areas, and Alsace-Moselle with its retained local law and practising Catholic milieu — are more socially conservative, with thinner recourse in practice. No region-specific punitive measures, hostile legislation, enforcement pattern, protective regime or documented exception to national border, facility or custody practice is known here; the difference from the national picture is one of degree rather than kind.

regions.name: Chuuk
regions.merged_summary: Chuuk follows the Federated States of Micronesia national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and a 2018 constitutional equality guarantee applies on grounds of sexual orientation, though protection for gender identity is not established. No trans-specific criminal rule, police targeting of trans people, border restriction, document-marker or visitor-facing document requirement, facility ban, gender-recognition machinery, or care regime targeting trans visitors is documented; visitors' home-issued documents govern, and no local visitor remedy is documented. The region differs from the national picture chiefly in its social and practical conditions: a predominantly Christian, church-centred and socially conservative setting with traditional family norms, where stigma toward gender-nonconforming people is more likely than in the federal capital, alongside a small, tightly-knit island community with little anonymity and little tourism, so visitors are few and conspicuous. Police and court capacity is limited outside Weno and formal complaint recourse is thin on the outer islands, leaving a thin service and protection infrastructure overall and no meaningful local recourse. No region-specific documented incidents, prosecutions, trans-specific police targeting, custody abuse, organised violence, regional pattern of violence, or facility rules are identified, and that absence is not evidence of safety. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, the exposure is curiosity, possible disapproval, stigma and family or community scrutiny — creating everyday friction, particularly for a traveller accompanied by a minor — rather than institutional enforcement or severe punishment, though the lack of documented, working protections leaves conditions somewhat below the national baseline.

regions.name: Kosrae
regions.merged_summary:
Kosrae is the smallest and easternmost of Micronesia's four states: a remote island of roughly seven thousand people with very low anonymity, a small, close-knit, devoutly church-centred community described as the most socially and religiously conservative of the four states, with strong church influence and conservative dress and gender norms, and with limited tourism, medical and legal infrastructure. The island inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised and the 2018 constitutional equality reform bars discrimination on sexual orientation, but there is no legal gender-recognition procedure, no trans-specific statutory protection, and no document-marker mechanism for visitors — documents must match the passport used for entry. No trans-specific criminal provision, police targeting, official harassment, facility ban, border practice, or violence against trans visitors is recorded on Kosrae, though such gaps are unverified rather than evidence of safety, and no Kosrae-specific policy differs from the national picture beyond this general conservatism; some of the underlying national information is not recent.

Because in such a small community nearly everyone is known to everyone, a transgender visitor's identity is likely to become common knowledge quickly, and the nationally documented stigma toward transgender people carries added visibility here. Realistic exposure is therefore social rather than state: curiosity, disapproval, misgendering, intrusive questioning, service refusal or friction, and informal social pressure, together with official discretion at borders or in emergencies. Practical recourse is thin — there is no local trans community infrastructure, specialist healthcare, or trans-specific police or facility policy; officials and service providers may have limited training; and specialist care, onward travel and practical help are constrained by limited hospital capacity and distance from Pohnpei and Chuuk. Consequences may be moderated by hospitality and tourism.

regions.name: Pohnpei
regions.merged_summary: Pohnpei hosts the national capital Palikir, the state government and town of Kolonia, the College of Micronesia, the main international airport and gateway, and the largest expatriate, diplomatic, aid and church presence, making it the federation's most urbanised, populous and externally connected state; foreign visitors and unfamiliar presentations are routine there rather than novel, and foreign documents are processed without documented gender-specific challenge. It inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, a 2018 constitutional reform made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation unlawful (though explicit transgender coverage is not established), no trans-specific statute, border practice or facility rule is documented, and no legal gender-recognition or document-alignment mechanism exists, so visitors should carry documents matching the passport used for entry. No Pohnpei-specific law or enforcement practice distinguishes it from the national picture: no trans-targeted policing, arrests, prosecutions, violence, facility exclusion or state-directed hostility is recorded locally or nationally, and one assessment notes no current Pohnpei-specific data on trans visitors beyond a 2015 report of societal stigma, so conditions should not be presumed either more protective or more hostile. On the social side, Christian church influence, traditional chiefly authority and close-knit communities mean a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is quickly noticed and draws staring, gossip, misgendering, uncomfortable reactions and possible service friction; the small police and courts offer little proactive formal recourse, so a visitor outed or discovered locally would rely mainly on informal tolerance and hospitality, though cosmopolitan exposure in Pohnpei modestly improves on the wider national picture and police and service encounters are generally low-key.

regions.name: Yap
regions.merged_summary:
Yap inherits the Federated States of Micronesia national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2018 constitutional equality reform made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation unlawful, though it protects orientation rather than gender identity specifically. No trans-specific criminal offence, document-marker rule or legal gender recognition procedure is recorded for a visitor, and no local Yap law or official practice is documented that departs from that national picture. Visitors should carry documents matching the name and marker on the entry passport. The national record includes societal stigma toward LGBT people in State Department reporting, though that reporting is dated and lacks trans-specific detail, leaving current consequences uncertain; legal discrimination has not been recorded, and remedies are thin as in the nation generally.

Yap is among the most socially conservative and traditionally governed FSM states, with customary chiefly and caste hierarchy, strong Catholic and Protestant church influence, village structure, and a population of roughly eleven thousand, so a visibly gender-nonconforming foreign visitor is conspicuous, anonymity is essentially unavailable, and gossip travels quickly through families, hosts and local institutions. Exposure is therefore mainly social rather than legal or institutional: discovery risks stigma, awkward misgendering, possible service friction, community scrutiny and informal pressure, with ordinary daily life in an informal small-island setting also relatively low-scrutiny. There is no documented record of anti-trans violence, police targeting, service refusal or facility restrictions in Yap, and courts and police function under FSM and US-compact arrangements, so there is no documented custody or state-hostile pathway; the absence of documented local incidents should not be read as proof of safety. Health, lodging and facilities are limited, with no trans-specific support infrastructure.

regions.name: Estuaire
regions.merged_summary: Estuaire is Gabon's most urban province, centred on the capital Libreville and its international airport and port — the country's busiest border and airport screening points and the main entry point for visitors — and it operates under the national framework. Same-sex conduct is lawful following the 2020 repeal of the 2019 offence, no later prosecution is documented, and the 2024 constitution declined re-criminalisation while adding privacy protections and defining marriage as opposite-sex only; gender identity itself is not criminalised and there is no trans-specific criminal offence. However, there is no legal gender recognition, no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination, and no hate-crime recourse, and facilities, custody and care follow birth sex with no documented remedy. Police have occasionally — reported as not widespread or systematic rather than as a local campaign — applied neutral 'breaches of modesty' or decency provisions against gender-nonconforming presentation, while state-sponsored harassment is absent and harassment by individuals is described as common. No local protection, ordinance, or pattern of local hostility distinguishing Estuaire from the national picture is documented, and the absence of reported Estuaire cases does not establish safety. Libreville's larger, more cosmopolitan population, expatriate and diplomatic presence, nightlife and business and tourist activity offer greater anonymity, more services and somewhat more room to move without attention than rural provinces, but routine police checkpoints and document checks in the capital raise the chance of presentation or document mismatches being flagged, and police retain discretion to apply public-order provisions. If discovered or outed, a visitor may face humiliation, official friction, invasive questioning, refusal of service or detention-based embarrassment, with recourse remaining informal and uncertain; imprisonment on the basis of gender identity alone is not documented, and social conservatism can mean harassment or bureaucratic delay.

regions.name: Haut-Ogooué
regions.merged_summary:
Haut-Ogooué, Gabon's mining province centred on Franceville and Moanda, is the Bongo family's home region: it is more urbanised and exposed to expatriate mining communities than much of the country, yet its smaller communities and provincial small-town social cohesion make a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor far more conspicuous than in Libreville, with limited anonymity, strong customary and religious authority, and no local LGBTQ+ organisation, dedicated legal aid or advocacy network to turn to — consular or NGO assistance is distant. The mining towns are socially conservative with thinner institutional oversight than the capital, and remote border crossings involve more discretionary document checks. No region-specific record documents police targeting, arrests or violence against transgender visitors there, and no documented local enforcement, tolerance or facility rules specific to the province were found, so the absence of local evidence leaves conditions uncertain rather than showing visitors are safer there.

Gabon's national regime applies unchanged: same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2019 offence was repealed in 2020, the 2024 constitution rejected recriminalisation and defines marriage as opposite-sex only, gender identity and expression are not criminal offences, no trans-specific offence exists, there is no organised state campaign against LGBTQ+ people, and no later prosecution is documented. However, there is no legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination for a visitor to invoke; police have occasionally used neutral 'breaches of modesty' or indecency provisions against non-gender-conforming presentation — reported as not widespread, with the last documented enforcement predating the repeal — and harassment by individuals is described as common. Constitutional privacy protections and sensitive-data rules offer only limited indirect safeguards, and no working local recourse is documented. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, the added exposure comes from visibility, isolation and policing discretion rather than distinct provincial law: remedies exist in principle but are weaker outside the capital, and the usual risks are stigma, staring, questioning, refusal of services, an arbitrary police stop, bribery demands and service humiliation rather than severe legal punishment or custody campaigns.

regions.name: Moyen-Ogooué
regions.merged_summary:
Moyen-Ogooué has no documented laws, enforcement patterns or incidents specific to transgender visitors, so Gabon's national framework governs. Same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2019 offence was repealed in 2020 and there is no trans-specific criminal offence; the 2024 constitution rejected re-criminalisation, added privacy protections and defines marriage as opposite-sex only. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection against gender-identity discrimination, while police have occasionally used neutral "breaches of modesty" or public-decency provisions against gender-nonconforming presentation and same-sex couples (one 2019 arrest was resolved by bribery), and harassment by individuals is common without documented state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group. The national picture offers limited assurance about how a visitor would be treated if questioned or outed, and no region-specific border, facility, custody or service practices are documented here, leaving those risks undocumented rather than established as absent.

Moyen-Ogooué is a small, largely rural interior province centred on Lambaréné, a low-rise river town on the Ogooué with a hospital, a port and logging traffic, without the anonymity of Libreville or Port-Gentil and with no significant tourist economy. Its comparatively conservative social setting, thinner institutional and community infrastructure, fewer and less-trained police, medical and hospitality staff, and reliance on Libreville-based remedies mean a visibly transgender or non-conforming foreigner is conspicuous and word travels quickly; a mismatched passport or non-conforming presentation invites routine outing risk. Discovery therefore tends to mean gossip, staring, invasive questioning, refusals and uneven local official discretion through hotels, clinics and police contact, with possible discretionary charges, police leverage and extortion, and fewer established avenues for redress. There is no documented local hostility, trans-specific violence or targeting pattern beyond the national picture, no documented pattern of imprisonment for being transgender, and no credible custody or lethal pathway.

regions.name: Ngounié
regions.merged_summary:
Ngounié is a largely rural interior province centred on Mouila, and no region-specific laws, incidents, or official practices distinguishing transgender visitors from Gabon's national picture are documented — there is no known local exception, protective or hostile. The national framework applies: same-sex conduct is lawful following repeal of a short-lived 2019 offence in 2020, and no prosecution has been documented since 2019; the 2024 constitution rejected re-criminalisation, added privacy protections, and defines marriage as opposite-sex only, but there is no legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against discrimination based on gender identity. Police occasionally use neutral 'breaches of modesty' provisions against gender-nonconforming presentation, though such use is not described as widespread, and state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ people as a group is reported absent; individual harassment, by contrast, is described as common. No organised anti-trans activity or patterned provincial violence is documented, but the absence of province-specific evidence does not establish safety.

For a visitor who is discovered to be trans or is outed, these conditions combine with the province's rural, small and tight-knit setting: a visibly gender-nonconforming foreign visitor draws immediate attention and cannot rely on urban anonymity, and social disapproval and gossip are reportedly more pronounced than in Libreville. Local police, health staff and lodging operators are less resourced and less accustomed to diversity, so responses to disclosure depend heavily on individual discretion, and specialist support and advocacy infrastructure is absent. The military government in place since the 2023 coup, along with thinner institutional presence in the province, provides limited dependable recourse — a point about rural settings generally rather than documented local evidence. The likely harms are individual harassment, suspicion, possible questioning or extortion under vague public-decency norms, refusal of services, and difficulty obtaining respectful health or lodging support, rather than prosecution or severe custody risk; the constitution's opposite-sex marriage definition and the absence of gender-identity protections offer no direct visitor remedy, and police, medical or other recourse after harassment or service refusal is thin.

regions.name: Nyanga
regions.merged_summary:
Nyanga is Gabon's southern Atlantic province centred on Tchibanga, sparsely populated, forested and rural, with limited tourist, medical and legal-aid infrastructure compared with Libreville; in its small towns anonymity is low and departure options are limited. No Nyanga-specific law, enforcement pattern, court practice or protective mechanism is documented, so the province sits under Gabon's national picture. Same-sex conduct between consenting adults has not been criminal since 2020, trans identity or gender expression is not itself an offence, and the 2024 constitution rejected re-criminalisation while defining marriage as opposite-sex. There is no legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination in public services.

For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, the reported risks are bureaucratic document mismatches, possible police questioning or extortion under modesty or public-order provisions — charges police have occasionally, though not widely, used against gender-nonconforming presentations — and harassment by private individuals or accommodation providers, which is described as common and may be sharper where social attitudes are conservative. State-sponsored group harassment is not reported, and no documented prosecution of a trans visitor, custodial placement rule or facility restriction appears in the record; likely outcomes are humiliation, discretionary police attention or service friction rather than imprisonment. Formal recourse is thin, and local treatment of an outed visitor and the effectiveness of any remedy in Nyanga remain uncertain.

regions.name: Ogooué-Ivindo
regions.merged_summary:
Ogooué-Ivindo is a sparsely populated, heavily forested northeastern province centred on Makokou, with small, tightly knit communities, limited state administrative and security presence, little cosmopolitan exposure, no known trans community infrastructure or protective local practice, and few foreign visitors. No province-specific evidence documents anti-trans legislation, local hostility, arrests, violence or organised targeting there, nor any tolerance exceeding the national picture, and local enforcement, social attitudes and effective recourse remain uncertain. Its rural, small-town character means a transgender visitor — especially one travelling with a minor — is more conspicuous than in Libreville or Port-Gentil; anonymity is scarce, word travels quickly through small towns, and local social attitudes are conservative, with strong reliance on community, family and customary norms.

Under Gabon's national framework, same-sex conduct between consenting adults has been lawful since the 2020 repeal of the 2019 offence, and the 2024 constitution added privacy protections and declined to re-criminalise it while defining marriage as between people of opposite sexes; however, there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity, and police are documented occasionally using neutral 'breaches of modesty' or public-order provisions against people with non-gender-conforming presentations, with bribe-for-release episodes recorded. Harassment by individuals is described as common, while state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is not reported as widespread. A home-country gender marker on documents may draw scrutiny, although the absence of legal recognition does not itself create a visitor-facing document restriction. If discovered or outed, a visitor in this province faces persistent stigma, informal pressure on families, harassment, opportunistic extortion or solicitation at checkpoints, and possible police misuse of modesty or public-order provisions, with any detention occurring far from consular and legal support; police and healthcare recourse are thin and weaker than in larger cities, and rural officers exercise wide discretion. Everyday harm is expected mainly from social hostility and opportunistic extortion rather than formal criminalisation, with expected consequences on discovery being harassment, extortion or possible short detention rather than systematic detention or threats to life. Overall, the province's conditions sit somewhat below the national picture.

regions.name: Ogooué-Lolo
regions.merged_summary: Ogooué-Lolo is a sparsely populated, largely rural forest province in Gabon (described in some accounts as southeastern and in others as east-central), centred on its largest town and capital Koulamoutou, with towns along the railway serving as administrative and logging centres. It has little tourist traffic and visitor infrastructure, no major urban centre, no trans-specific community infrastructure or advocacy presence, and no documented local law, official practice or province-specific pattern of trans-targeted police action, violence or effective protective services — an absence that is not proof of safety. Local conditions differ from the national picture mainly in degree: rural conservative communities, weak oversight of local officials, weaker police and judicial infrastructure, fewer alternative services or complaint mechanisms, and thin NGO or community support. In small, tight-knit provincial towns a visibly trans foreigner attracts sustained attention and word travels through employers, guesthouses and clinics, while health and lodging staff have little familiarity with foreign documents or transition-related care, making disclosure at clinics and hotels more likely; the nearest specialist services, consular access and legal assistance are in Libreville or Franceville. Local enforcement and social attitudes are otherwise undocumented in the province. The national framework applies in full: same-sex conduct between consenting adults has been lawful since the 2020 repeal of a short-lived 2019 offence, and the 2024 constitution retained decriminalisation and added privacy protection while defining marriage as between people of opposite sex; there is no legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination. Police have occasionally used neutral 'breach of modesty' provisions against visibly gender-nonconforming people (one 2019 arrest was resolved by bribery), police extortion patterns reported nationally would apply, harassment by individuals is described as common, and state-sponsored harassment of the group as a whole is not documented. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered here, these conditions mean greater social visibility, community scrutiny and social intimidation, a heightened chance of arbitrary police questioning or detention, and less practical recourse and fewer discreet services than in Gabon's cities — making discovery riskier than the national baseline, though harsher punishment than the national framework provides is not the expected outcome.

regions.name: Ogooué-Maritime
regions.merged_summary:
Ogooué-Maritime, centred on the coastal oil port of Port-Gentil, follows Gabon's national framework: same-sex conduct between consenting adults is lawful after the 2019 offence was repealed in 2020, with no recent prosecutions documented, while the 2024 constitution provides privacy protections but reserves marriage to opposite-sex couples. There is no legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination. Police have occasionally applied breaches-of-modesty or public-decency provisions to gender-nonconforming presentation, a practice described as not widespread, while individual harassment is described as common; state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ people is not documented, and no organised anti-trans campaign or region-specific trans protection is known.

Locally, Port-Gentil's oil-driven, internationally staffed economy — an urban, transactional environment where outsider status and transient traffic are routine — and the regularly visited coastal tourism belt around Loango, Mayumba and Pongara offer visitors anonymity, with no record of local authorities targeting gender-nonconforming travellers; outside expatriate and tourist settings, social conservatism and misgendering friction remain plausible, and the province's fishing villages and remote park areas provide less urban cover, where small-community scrutiny and limited access to advocacy or legal support raise the consequences of being outed. Airport and port entry, hotel checks and police stops can still surface document or presentation mismatches, and corruption can bring informal payments or misuse of public-order offences, with weak oversight and no reliable complaint mechanism. Where a visitor is discovered or outed, exposure centres on humiliation, extortion and discretionary stops rather than prosecution — documented abuse, including extortion and bribery, dates from 2019 enforcement of the since-repealed offence — with no custody campaign or lethal pathway documented, thin recourse, and real social hostility toward visible non-conformity.

regions.name: Woleu-Ntem
regions.merged_summary: Woleu-Ntem is Gabon's sparsely populated northern province, centred on Oyem (also referenced as Camayou), with long rural stretches, a predominantly Fang population, few foreign visitors, limited hospitality and health facilities, and active land borders with Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. No region-specific law, enforcement campaign, protective practice or documented violent incident concerning transgender visitors is known for the province — including no local trans or legal-aid infrastructure and no documented differences in facility, border, custody, care or protection practices, or in how travelling families and minors are affected — so the province largely inherits the national framework: same-sex conduct is lawful following the 2020 repeal of the offence briefly enacted in 2019 (which was enforced at the time, with bribe-based detentions and police bribery documented in those earlier arrests, and no later prosecution is documented), there is no trans-specific criminal offence and no organised state or local targeting, but there is likewise no legal gender recognition and no protection against gender-identity discrimination, and the constitution defines marriage as opposite-sex. Police have occasionally — though not widely — used neutral 'breaches of modesty' or public-decency provisions against gender-nonconforming presentation, while harassment by individuals is described as common; sensitive-data handling for orientation is also reported. Province-specific conditions compound these: conservative, close-knit rural communities and small-town scrutiny make a transgender visitor conspicuous, and police and gendarmerie checkpoints with routine document checks are common, so identity papers or presentation may be scrutinised in everyday stops; because Equatorial Guinea criminalises same-sex conduct, crossings may carry added sensitivity. Combined with limited practical recourse outside the capital, this means individual harassment is more likely to be witnessed and less likely to be remedied, and discovery or being outed would most plausibly bring staring, refusal or awkwardness in services and accommodation, pressure to conform, extortion, humiliating or arbitrary questioning and modesty-related harassment rather than a known formal penalty — falling well short of systematic arrest or custodial punishment, with no documented region-specific hostility.

regions.name: Adjara
regions.merged_summary:
Adjara is Georgia's autonomous Black Sea region centred on Batumi, a resort and tourism hub where foreign visitors are a routine part of daily life, service refusal by commercial staff is less likely than inland, and nightlife is more cosmopolitan than in rural areas, so everyday street hostility and scrutiny may be less overt than elsewhere in Georgia. However, the surrounding mixed Orthodox and Muslim communities are socially conservative, with religiously influenced rural highland villages, clerical influence, and sparse trans community infrastructure making visible gender nonconformity riskier outside resort settings. No separate Adjara protective law, policing exception, civic infrastructure, or documented local enforcement practice distinguishing the region from the national picture has been established, and the absence of recorded Adjara-specific enforcement against transgender visitors is not evidence of safety.

The national regime applies throughout: since 2024 gender-reassignment medical care is prohibited at all ages (including for a minor in a travelling family), a gender marker differing from one's own cannot be entered on identity documents and no recognition procedure is available, public promotion of gender diversity, rainbow displays, and pride events or related gatherings are restricted or banned, and hate-crime protection covering gender identity exists on paper but is weakly enforced, with LGBTI assemblies elsewhere in Georgia violently disrupted by counter-protests and police failing to protect participants. A visitor's foreign-issued documents are not altered, so any mismatch can draw scrutiny; against the conservative local environment, police discretion limited accountability, and the absence of reliable remedies, discovery or being outed exposes a trans traveller to social hostility, detention, outing, refusal of services, violence, or forced disclosure, with little reliable recourse. Local differences modestly affect daily exposure rather than transforming the underlying risk.

regions.name: Imereti
regions.merged_summary:
Imereti operates under Georgia's 2024 family-values package, which bans gender-reassignment surgery and medical intervention at any age (including for minors, with the wider package also affecting travelling families), bars registering a gender different from that on state documents, prohibits public promotion of a different gender and pride events, and undercuts labour rules framed around biological sex; a companion foreign-agents law has sharply reduced LGBTI services. A visitor's own passport remains the only recognition available — the law sets out no documented procedure for handling foreign-issued documents, so any mismatch between papers and presentation invites scrutiny — while hate-crime and anti-discrimination provisions covering gender identity exist on paper but are documented as unenforced, with police homophobia, withdrawn complaints, and slow or absent protection as public LGBTI assembly has repeatedly been violently suppressed nationwide amid attacks on public events and anti-trans rhetoric.

Locally, Imereti is a largely rural, strongly Orthodox and socially conservative western region centred on Kutaisi, with less international and NGO presence, no visible trans community, few LGBTI-friendly services, little local advocacy capacity and limited anonymity; outside tourist routes around Kutaisi, its airport and cave sites the environment is markedly more traditional and church-influenced than in Tbilisi. Kutaisi saw far-right violence against an LGBT-linked venue in 2023, while documented assaults, police hostility and pride-event violence concentrate in Tbilisi, and no comparable incidents, region-specific raids or lethal enforcement are documented locally. A visitor discovered in a hotel, clinic or police stop may face gossip, service refusal or hostility, with bureaucratic checks or emergency care more likely to expose them and with police accountability, victim support and recourse all thinner than in the capital and local enforcement unaccountable if they are outed; foreign visitors are not singled out and there is no evidence of region-specific organised targeting, though accounts differ on whether local friction sits at or slightly below the already restrictive national baseline or, given the absence of safe infrastructure, leaves a visitor more exposed than in Tbilisi.

regions.name: Ashanti Region
regions.merged_summary: Ashanti Region operates entirely under Ghana's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminal under colonial-era provisions, there is no trans-specific offence, no legal gender recognition and no trans-specific protection, and the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill — passed by parliament in May 2026 and awaiting presidential assent, with one account noting that an earlier passage was sharply expanded in 2024 — would sharply raise penalties and criminalise advocacy; the Supreme Court has declined to block or has deferred review of the bill before assent, while religious and political leaders actively press for enactment. A transgender visitor who is outed or discovered therefore faces likely police harassment, extortion, detention under public-order or morality provisions, public humiliation, social rejection and community confrontation, with thin recourse; police and courts function, but complaints touching gender nonconformity are read through a morality lens and rarely protect the person who is outed, and documentation of hostility toward visibly gender-nonconforming people is established at the national level. Region-specific enforcement records are sparse, and the extent of trans-specific police targeting locally is uncertain — which is not evidence of safety. Ashanti adds a distinctly conservative local layer: Kumasi and its hinterland are a heartland of traditional chieftaincy and the Asantehene's authority alongside assertive Pentecostal, evangelical, Christian and Muslim moral influence, with active anti-LGBT campaigning, dense community surveillance, and anti-LGBT sentiment broadly socially licensed rather than confined to officials. There is no documented local protection regime or enforcement exception. Discovery in hotels, transport or through vigilant community reporting can escalate quickly: risks include denial of rooms, transport scrutiny, hostile treatment in hospitals, eviction, and denunciation or possible mob confrontation in a market, lorry station or Zongo neighbourhood. Kumasi's larger urban, commercial and tourism character offers some anonymity compared with rural areas, foreignness buys some eccentricity allowance in hotels and transport, and a historical Asante tradition of feminine-identified men exists, but none of these offsets police discretion, arrest, extortion or hostile public confrontation once a trans visitor is identified; the region has less visible support infrastructure and less cosmopolitan tolerance than Accra, and is among Ghana's most socially and religiously conservative areas.

regions.name: Central Region
regions.merged_summary: The Central Region — centred on Cape Coast and spanning coastal and interior districts including Elmina, Winneba and Kasoa — is governed by the same police service, criminal law and pending legislation as the rest of Ghana, with no documented region-specific enforcement pattern, exemption, protective practice or regional protection for transgender visitors. Colonial-era provisions criminalising same-sex conduct remain on the books, and parliament passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill on 29 May 2026, awaiting presidential assent, with Supreme Court review deferred or dismissed pending assent; an earlier version lapsed unsigned in 2024. The bill would sharply increase penalties and criminalise advocacy, though its present legal force is uncertain, and the campaign around it contributes to a hostile climate. Legal gender recognition does not exist, foreign documents are not recognised, police recourse for transgender complainants is unreliable, unenforced common-law morality offences remain available as a police lever, and there is no documented effective remedy amid strong public and religious opposition to gender diversity. Locally, Cape Coast and Elmina form a visitor-facing heritage-tourism and university corridor where foreign visitors are routine and a traveller can move with relative anonymity, and hotel and heritage-site staff may try to avoid public disputes with foreigners; however, the surrounding fishing districts and smaller towns are more socially conservative and tightly networked, and conservative churches, customary authorities and under-resourced municipal police create more discretionary, reputation-sensitive encounters. This local mix offers no documented legal protection, and no local facility bans, organised morality-police sweeps or documented pattern of trans-specific violence are known. If discovered or outed, a transgender visitor would face social hostility, service refusal, document challenges, bribes or extortion, possible police detention, humiliation, misgendered custody and violence, with hostility amplified by religious pressure and no effective remedy.

regions.name: Gibraltar
regions.merged_summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory, so its own statutes, legislature and British-style courts and policing govern a visit rather than any separate regional regime: it is a very small, English-speaking, tourism-dependent territory where visitors are routine, openly LGBT people are visible including an annual Pride, violent crime is low and a small local trans presence is integrated, and courts function with a record of rights-protecting rulings. Statutory protections include the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 barring gender-reassignment discrimination in employment and in goods and services (with such protection applying since 2007), hate-crime coverage extended to transgender identity in July 2026, and a 2026 conversion-therapy offence; same-sex marriage, equal age of consent and same-sex adoption also apply, though the Equality Act does not apply without an Order in Council. There is no criminalisation of gender expression, same-sex conduct or public presence, no documented trans-specific criminal offence, bathroom or facility restriction, visitor-specific police targeting, detention, service denial or violence, but protection may be narrower for someone not undergoing a reassignment process, and the frontier with Spain is operated under Spanish procedures outside Gibraltar's control. One assessment notes that how officials handle document discrepancies, how these protections operate in practice and current social attitudes toward trans visitors are not established, and that this uncertainty is not evidence of safety.

Conditional on being outed or discovered, the main exposure is documentary: no local route to change a legal gender marker exists, so a visitor travels on a home passport and is read at the border and in public under that marker, with no local document remedy, creating friction at border and hotel checks. Because the territory is a dense, close-knit and partly socially conservative small town where anonymity is scarce and a visitor is highly visible, discretion in hotels, clinics and police contact depends on individuals; the expected consequences are friction, stares and occasional service issues rather than custody, with no evidence that identity questioning escalates to detention, service denial or violence.

regions.name: Labe
regions.merged_summary:
Labé, Guinea's second-largest city in the Fouta Djallon highlands, is a predominantly Fulani and conservative Muslim centre where religious and family norms are stricter than in Conakry and visible gender nonconformity draws close scrutiny. The national regime applies in full: Article 274 of the Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with imprisonment of six months to three years and fines, and police have arrested people on the basis of clothing or appearance, used the law for extortion, held people for five days beyond the legal limit before releasing them against bribes, and placed transgender women in male prisons where sexual violence is reported. Guinea provides no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection in health, housing, education or employment, and no operative hate-crime recourse; surveys show widespread hostility to gay neighbours, and most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly because of threats of violence and stigma.

In Labé itself, anonymity is harder to maintain in a mid-size highland city with limited tourist infrastructure, which makes a visibly transgender visitor more identifiable, and there are fewer LGBTQ organisations, legal-aid options, anonymous urban spaces, independent services and functioning complaint mechanisms than in Conakry; no local protection, sanctuary or LGBTQ infrastructure is documented. Stronger family and community monitoring means discovery could quickly involve relatives, local religious authorities or police, and local practice appears more likely to escalate disclosure into moral or security enforcement with limited recourse, so an outed transgender visitor faces conditions somewhat below the national picture. Region-specific police practices, border treatment and incidents involving transgender visitors are not documented, and that uncertainty is not evidence of safety; no execution pathway is documented.

regions.name: Banjul
regions.merged_summary: Banjul is Gambia's small administrative capital and seat of government, police headquarters and main port: a compact, devoutly Muslim city with a concentrated police and immigration presence, identity checks around the airport, port and ferry terminal, and limited anonymity, in a society where LGBT identity carries strong taboo and media and religious hostility toward gender nonconformity is documented. A visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is conspicuous, discovery can come through passports, hotel registration, checkpoints or hospitals, and reporting of enforcement is sparse while official discretion is high; police have conducted sweeps of venues and couples in the 2014–2015 era, and there is no Banjul-specific tolerance, protective machinery, trans community infrastructure or documented relief for people targeted by police. Its tourism role is described differently: it is presented both as a main tourism hub with greater foreign visibility and some commercial caution in guest-oriented areas, and as separate from the tourist economy, which sits across the ferry in Kanifing and along the coast, with the capital's cosmopolitan buffer and tourism infrastructure limited by comparison. Partial offsets are that the city offers more urban anonymity and tourist-facing services than rural areas, enforcement against tourists is sporadic rather than systematic, civil-society organisations operate locally, and its concentration of embassies may improve consular access after detention — none of which alters the national picture. Under the national regime, same-sex conduct remains criminalised by the 2025 Criminal Code, which sets a mandatory five-year minimum for unnatural offences and three years for gross indecency, with gross-indecency provisions covering private acts and the 2014 aggravated-homosexuality provisions now removed; there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, and trans identity or gender expression is not itself a separate offence, though the sexuality law can raise scrutiny and hostility toward a gender-nonconforming visitor. If outed or discovered, a visitor faces intrusive questioning, humiliation, extortion, arbitrary detention and arrest, with prosecution risk under broad indecency or unnatural-offence framing and severity increasing if police or community actors treat gender nonconformity as sexual immorality or public nuisance, and with no reliable local remedy. Lethal punishment is not credibly expected: former president Jammeh's era of explicit extermination rhetoric ended in 2017 and no executions for gender or sexuality offences are credibly documented since. Patterns of targeting trans visitors specifically, document or border problems, facility rules and effective remedies in the city are not established.

regions.name: Basse
regions.merged_summary:
Basse (Basse Santa Su), the main market and transport town of Gambia's Upper River Region in the east, sits on the Senegalese border as a small, predominantly rural and conservative Muslim-majority community with close-knit family, market and mosque networks through which news spreads within days, giving religious and traditional authorities more practical weight than distant institutions in the capital. It inherits Gambia's national framework, under which same-sex conduct is criminalised as unnatural offences (with a five-year minimum) and gross indecency (three years) under the current Criminal Code, with no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection based on gender identity, no trans-specific offence of identity or expression, and no documented police or court protection for transgender visitors; morality and public-order provisions remain available to police. Basse itself offers little tourism infrastructure, no trans or LGBT organisation, no specialist legal aid, few health and lodging providers, distant courts and advocacy groups, and fewer independent oversight bodies than larger cities; the nearby border crossing adds document scrutiny, and a foreigner is conspicuous in a town where anonymity is limited. No documented local legal exception, sanctuary policy, tolerance or trans-aware enforcement practice offsets the national regime.

For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the national regime: national provisions can operate in a more discretionary local setting, raising the practical likelihood of police suspicion, morality-law application, extortion, public shaming, service refusal, informal mediation or detention rather than formal protection, alongside community hostility and weak recourse if detained or mistreated, including limited medical continuity options and remedies. Remote geography and weaker accountability increase exposure compared with national averages, while imprisonment or mob violence remain possible but not certain. No Basse-specific pattern of police targeting or violence against transgender visitors is established and such evidence is limited, a gap that is not evidence of safety, and the precise treatment by local officials remains uncertain.

regions.name: Brikama
regions.merged_summary: Brikama is a large, densely settled market town in Gambia's West Coast Region, built around markets, mosques, schools and local administration, with less tourism-oriented infrastructure than the Banjul and Senegambia coastal areas and sitting inland from the more international Senegambia strip, though it lies near the coastal tourist strip where some familiarity with foreigners can offer limited anonymity and privacy around resort lodging. It is a conservative, Mandinka-majority, Muslim-majority community with strong social and religious conservatism and less accustomed to foreign gender-nonconforming visitors. No separate local ordinance, police practice, protective mechanism or documented pattern of local hostility is known: no local support, health or legal services for transgender people, no local practice protecting visitors, and no localised violence or enforcement record. Gambian law criminalises same-sex conduct, with the 2025 Criminal Code prescribing a five-year minimum for unnatural offences and three years for gross indecency alongside mandatory imprisonment, and broad public-order and indecency provisions that police use against visibly gender-nonconforming people; these offences do not expressly criminalise transgender identity or presentation but may create exposure if a visitor is perceived as engaging in prohibited conduct. There is no legal gender recognition or gender-marker change available to visitors, no national anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage of gender identity, no documented prosecutions, violence patterns or official protections specific to transgender travellers, and detention conditions are poor. A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed faces the national criminal exposure with less anonymity and less likely assistance in this local setting: document-mismatch scrutiny at checks, police questioning or service refusal, stop-and-question by police, hotel staff or bystanders, and extortion are all plausible, with imprisonment under the indecency and sodomy provisions a real possibility as social licence, discretionary reporting or arrest under criminal provisions and detention procedures, alongside family, community and service-sector stigma, and no reliable remedy or practical recourse documented.

regions.name: Janjanbureh
regions.merged_summary:
Janjanbureh is a small, comparatively remote riverain town on MacCarthy Island in the Central River Region of the Gambia River, with tight social networks, strong conservative religious authority in a Muslim-majority community, limited tourism infrastructure, and far less internationally oriented visitor environment than Banjul. It has no documented local exception, protective regime, tolerance practice, trans-specific facility protocols or reliable complaint mechanisms, and it has fewer concentrated legal-aid and advocacy services than the greater Banjul coastal area. No region-specific reports of targeting or official pattern of targeting have been documented, but the small size of the community means discovery would spread quickly through family, community leaders and police networks, and the absence of reported incidents is not evidence of safety. A visibly transgender visitor would attract attention quickly, with local police and officials unlikely to offer protection and no evidence of local recourse.

The town inherits Gambia's national criminal regime, under which the 2025 Criminal Code sets a five-year minimum for unnatural offences, defined to include any homosexual act, and three years for gross indecency, while the 2014 aggravated-homosexuality framework signals sustained legislative hostility toward gender and sexual nonconformity; these provisions target conduct rather than transgender identity itself, though visible gender nonconformity could be misread or draw attention in a hostile climate, and gender-expression or trans-specific enforcement is not documented nationally. No trans-specific legal recognition, document protection or hate-crime recourse is documented.
