Portland, a small rural eastern parish centred on Port Antonio, Boston Bay and Frenchman's Cove, inherits Jamaica's national regime in full: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act's buggery provision, which carries hard labour, there is no legal gender recognition so foreign documents may not match a visitor's presentation, no statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no recognised partnership status. The criminal law is not itself a trans-identity offence, but it sits within a documented pattern of police leaks, failure to investigate or intervene in anti-LGBT violence, and weak state protection, alongside consistently hostile recorded public opinion, mob violence including an unsolved mob killing of a gender-nonconforming teenager, family violence and extortion by non-reporting, and identity-targeted abuse in detention, including in prison and hospital settings. Portland's tourism economy along the coast — Port Antonio's small eco-tourism, Boston Bay and Frenchman's Cove — is used to foreigners, and its relatively lower level of violent crime and laid-back, visitor-oriented character, plus welcoming statements from tourism officials, may soften everyday friction in hospitality settings; these do not displace national law, provide recourse, or establish safety, and the absence of known Portland-specific incidents does not establish safety.

Conditional on being outed or discovered, the parish's character works against the visitor in other ways: it is tight-knit and church-dominated, small enough that an outed or outable visitor becomes known quickly, and attitudes can be more conservative than in tourist-centric areas, while constrained health, policing and legal services and smaller communities reduce anonymity and recourse. There is no LGBT venue, advocacy office or crisis support in the parish to call on, no documented local protective exception or enforcement reform, and no tolerant institution or trans community infrastructure distinguishing it — meaning discovery offers thinner recourse even than Kingston's sparse services. Detention would fall to rural lockups and, on transfer, to Kingston facilities where identity-targeted violence is documented, leaving the visitor facing the national exposure set — hostile public, unreliable police, and identity-targeted violence in custody — with no local offset.

regions.name: Saint Catherine
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Catherine — taking in Spanish Town, Portmore, Old Harbour and Linstead, as well as Port Royal, and forming part of the greater Kingston/Portmore metropolitan area — is a densely populated residential, suburban, semi-rural and industrial corridor rather than a tourist-resort parish, so the limited hospitality-sector shielding that tourism officials sometimes assert in coastal areas does not apply here. Parts of the parish have high violent crime and gang violence, police capacity and responsiveness are weak, conservative church influence is strong, and social attitudes are consistent with, and in some settings less moderated than, the Kingston and Montego Bay tourist corridors where officials have issued welcome statements. No parish-specific trans protection, ordinance, sanctuary practice, police protocol or visible trans advocacy infrastructure is documented, and the parish's main detention facility, the St Catherine Adult Correctional Centre, falls under the national prison regime.

The regime inherited from Jamaica criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, punishable by up to ten years' hard labour, offers no legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination, and the constitution bars recognition of same-sex unions. Police are documented to leak details of LGBT people, fail to investigate violence against them and not intervene during attacks, and discriminatory police and health-care practices persist. Detention follows birth-sex placement with no protection: facilities are overcrowded, with severe prisoner-on-prisoner violence targeting perceived LGBT identity and no specialised housing. Public hostility, mob violence and impunity are documented nationally, including the unsolved 2013 St James mob killing of gender-nonconforming Dwayne Jones and a 2019 Montego Bay episode in which local officials refused venues and police declined protection during heightened hostility. A trans visitor who is discovered orouted here therefore faces the national pattern of societal hostility with effectively no recourse — risks including harassment, exploitation, service denial and unsafe custody — while local conditions offer no offset and some high-crime areas add further risk.

regions.name: Saint James
regions.merged_summary:
Saint James parish, home to Montego Bay and Jamaica's main tourist corridor, inherits the national regime: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act with penalties up to ten years' hard labour, there is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity and no hate-crime or other legal recourse, and no legal gender recognition exists. Police are documented to leak reports, fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence and not intervene during attacks, while detainees are housed by birth sex in overcrowded, violent facilities with no protective housing and no gender-recognition framework guiding accommodation, where inmates perceived as LGBTQ face severe targeted violence.

Local conditions are negative rather than mitigating: in 2019 Montego Bay's mayor and councillor blocked the parish LGBT group's use of the local cultural centre, other venues cancelled Pride bookings amid backlash, and police stated they could not provide protection; the 2013 mob killing of gender-nonconforming 16-year-old Dwayne Jones in the parish remained unsolved, with no arrests reported as of 2022 and lasting impunity. Tourism-dependent officials and tourist-board messaging publicly welcome gay visitors, and the resort enclave gives foreign guests a measure of insulation, but that goodwill is discretionary and undocumented, with no record of it extending to visibly gender-nonconforming visitors once hostility surfaces. No distinct local protection is documented, and the killing does not establish a local violence rate; for a trans visitor discovered or outed outside the resort perimeter, effectively no remedy or reliable protection remains.

regions.name: Westmoreland
regions.merged_summary: Westmoreland, Jamaica's rural southwestern parish (capital Savanna-la-Mar, also including Bluefields), inherits the national regime in full: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised, no statute protects against gender-identity discrimination or hate-motivated violence, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and no same-sex partnership status exists. No parish-level law, trans organisation, venue or advocacy presence modifies those rules, and no region-specific protective enforcement or recourse is documented. Local conditions include deep social conservatism, high general violence, weak state presence, and church-centred small towns where strangers are noticed and gender-nonconforming presentation is read as a moral offence; mob violence against gender-nonconforming people in the western parishes has gone unsolved, with the nearest documented comparable case being the 2013 mob killing of Dwayne Jones in adjoining St James. The parish's partly tourist-facing economy around Negril — the resort strip on the western end and the cliffs and Whitehouse coast, where hospitality staff have a commercial incentive to be discreet toward foreign visitors — may modestly ease everyday hotel and street encounters and offers some anonymity and a few gay-friendly venues, but this buffer is narrow, uneven across the parish, and is a zone of reduced scrutiny rather than documented protection; rural conditions are generally harsher than the national picture, and the absence of documented parish-specific incidents is not evidence of safety. Discovery or being outed anywhere in the parish would route a transgender visitor into the same police, hospital and custody system documented nationally as indifferent or hostile: local authorities are unlikely to intervene effectively, exposing the visitor to harassment, extortion, refusal of services, assault or arrest, with identity leaks and failures to investigate or interrupt attacks documented, custody following national birth-sex placement practice amid prisoner-on-prisoner violence, and public opinion across the island remaining strongly hostile.

regions.name: Balqa
regions.merged_summary:
Balqa governorate — taking in Salt, Mahis, Fuheis, the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea corridor — is a predominantly rural, tribal and small-city area west of Amman, with tighter community ties and far less anonymity than the capital, and its settings vary. The country's documented tolerant spaces, including its gay-friendly cafés, are concentrated in Amman and nothing comparable is recorded in Balqa; there are no known local transgender organisations, tolerant venues or official protections, though the governorate has some historic-town tourism and visitor-oriented Dead Sea facilities, which do not establish protection for trans visitors. No Balqa-specific trans-exclusion order, border practice or police sweep beyond the national pattern is documented, and no organised campaign or lethal pathway targeting trans visitors is known locally, though no region-specific protective practice is recorded either; travel to Amman or Fuheis may be somewhat less exposed, and greater caution is warranted outside visitor-oriented settings.

Within Balqa, Jordan's national regime applies in full: same-sex conduct and gender expression are not expressly criminalised, but vague public-morality and debauchery provisions and the 2023 cybercrime law have been used by security forces to harass LGBT people and to chill digital expression of gender diversity; gender-affirming surgery for transgender people is criminalised under Article 8 of Law 25 of 2018 with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment; no clear legal gender recognition pathway exists; security forces have intimidated LGBT activists and pressured community spaces to close, and a 2023 crackdown targeted queer organising; a 2019 Arab Barometer survey found 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality. In Balqa's close-knit small towns, family and community scrutiny is intense, services can refuse, and local police in Salt and surrounding towns draw on the same morality provisions with fewer moderating urban influences than the capital. Conditional on discovery or being outing, a trans visitor could face discretionary police stops, morality or cybercrime questioning, extortion or intimidation, detention or custody/facility placement by birth sex under vague charges, heightened community discomfort or reporting risk, and thin or absent practical recourse — the national pattern operating in a less anonymous, more conservative setting where overall conditions are harsher for a trans visitor than the country as a whole.

regions.name: Aichi Prefecture
regions.merged_summary: Aichi Prefecture, centred on Nagoya, operates under Japan's national framework with no prefectural rule restricting gender expression, no prefecture-level anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on the basis of gender identity, no documented prefectural or municipal hostile measure, and no local protective ordinance actually operating for visitors. Nationally there is no trans-specific criminal law and no statute guaranteeing protection from discrimination or violence based on gender identity; the 2023 promotion law was narrowed in debate, while favourable Supreme Court rulings address bathroom access and the surgical requirements for changing documents. Gender-segregated facilities including onsen, sento and toilets remain the norm, documents and custody or family-register placement follow registered sex, and foreign nationals face bureaucratic and conflict-of-laws friction where home records diverge from presentation; the practical application of custody practices to visitors in Aichi is uncertain. Regionally, Nagoya is a large, largely anonymous metropolitan and tourist centre where a foreign visitor is unlikely to be singled out, with an established LGBTQ scene, regular pride events, a municipal partnership-certificate scheme, nightlife and LGBTQ-friendly venues in areas such as Sakae, and Centrair airport as an international entry point with routine tourist-facing services — conditions that lower everyday social friction and offer practical workarounds such as alternative private-bath options — though elsewhere in the Chubu region social attitudes are comparatively conservative. Outside the metropolitan core, local tolerance is less documented, and rural districts and traditional onsen or sento carry more friction, such as staring, misgendering and service hesitation. If a transgender visitor is outed, ordinary contact generally stays reserved rather than confrontational and friction remains bureaucratic, institutional and spatial rather than violent or criminal, with local enforcement rule-bound and no documented pattern of police or official targeting — but the absence of any visitor-targeting practice or operative local protection should not be read as proof of safety, since no local protective regime alters the national institutional gaps.

regions.name: Chiba
regions.merged_summary:
Chiba has no local ordinance, enforcement pattern, or documented hostility toward transgender visitors, and no local protective measure, so the prefecture inherits Japan's national framework: no statute guarantees protection from discrimination or violence based on gender identity, while the 2023 promotion law is narrow and carries no anti-discrimination guarantee (recent Supreme Court decisions on workplace facilities and document requirements offer only limited recourse). Gender-segregated toilets, onsen, sento and other bathing venues remain strongly gendered, and document-handling procedures follow the registered gender on a visitor's home-country records — foreign gender-marker changes require action in the country of nationality, and there is a documented case of a foreign national whose gender change was refused recognition by Tokyo ward offices. Custody, ward placement, and detention or medical placement follow family-register records rather than presentation, and escalation depends on police, hospital, border, or correctional discretion rather than clear local protections; ordinary encounters are generally reserved and low-confrontation rather than overtly hostile, with little documented police targeting, though local services may be less familiar with foreign documents or trans needs. The exposure is therefore mostly social reserve plus facility and document friction, not criminalisation, and visitor-facing remedies and trans-specific violence patterns are not documented.

Narita International Airport sits in Chiba as the country's principal international gateway, so national border and document practice applies directly to arrivals: passport and presentation mismatches can trigger secondary inspection, though Chiba-specific discriminatory treatment of trans travelers at the airport is not documented — which is not evidence that mismatches will never cause difficulty. Chiba's major visitor destinations, including Tokyo Disney Resort, the Urayasu and Makuhari areas, and Tokyo's commuter belt, are urban and accustomed to foreign tourists; metropolitan-fringe areas offer more LGBTQ-friendly venues and private-bath or customer-service alternatives than rural parts of the prefecture, and suburban and rural areas are more socially conservative. The tourist-facing economy and proximity to Tokyo argue for marginally lower everyday friction than the national picture overall, and there is no documented local trans-specific enforcement beyond national practice.

regions.name: Ehime Prefecture
regions.merged_summary: Ehime Prefecture has no trans-specific criminal offence and no region-specific hostile law, arrest pattern or documented incident; no prefectural protection exists, so the national position applies in full. In Japan there is no enforceable guarantee against discrimination or violence based on gender identity, the 2023 understanding-promotion law contains no enforceable protections, custody follows the family register rather than identity, and document handling at ward offices has been cumbersome for foreign nationals whose registered gender is not recognised, alongside national detention and prison-placement cases. Ehime is a largely rural, ageing prefecture centred on Matsuyama where its main draw, the Dogo Onsen area and other sento, makes gender-segregated communal bathing central to the visit, with no documented rule permitting or barring trans access; no Ehime-specific policy or enforcement pattern is known that would change these exposures. Its LGBTQ venues, support organisations, private-bath and co-ed alternatives, and specialist legal help are thinner than in Tokyo or Osaka and sparse outside Matsuyama, and local facility access, police treatment and protections for visiting families or minors are not documented. Against this, the prefecture is politically conservative and reserved in small communities, and its small foreign population can make an outed visitor conspicuous; however, tourism hospitality may lead travellers to be treated as visitors rather than social threats, violent crime is low, and police and courts function. If discovery or being outed occurs, the combination of sparse recourse and alternatives with national bureaucratic friction makes awkwardness, misgendering, service hesitation, scrutiny or facility-related friction more likely than organised or officially directed danger, with private and family baths offering a possible alternative to open onsen, though such options are unevenly available.

regions.name: Fukuoka Prefecture
regions.merged_summary: Fukuoka Prefecture operates under Japan's national framework: no statute guaranteeing protection from gender-identity discrimination (the 2023 public-understanding law is symbolic only), gender-segregated onsen, sento and other bathing facilities, document friction where IDs do not match, custody and prison or detention placement following the family register rather than gender identity, and no national recognition of gender marker changes or partnership for foreign couples, though Supreme Court rulings on bathroom access and surgery requirements have been favourable and courts and police generally function. Local conditions differentiate the prefecture mainly in an upward direction: Fukuoka City (including Hakata and Nakasu) and Kitakyushu are large, internationally oriented, tourist-facing centres with visible LGBTQ venues, an annual Pride/rainbow event, a municipal partnership certification or declaration system and municipal diversity guidance, and staff in hospitality districts are accustomed to foreign visitors, so ordinary contact tends to be reserved and non-confrontational rather than hostile, with foreign visitors often afforded latitude. Some onsen areas offer private-bath or gender-neutral options, though onsen and sento remain sex-segregated with limited alternatives, and Kyushu as a whole is considered more socially conservative than Tokyo, with rural onsen areas retaining the same segregation. No prefectural rule overrides national facility, document or detention practices, no Fukuoka-specific protection addresses trans visitors, and no local hostile ordinances, local targeting or documented pattern of anti-trans policing or facility bans is known — an absence that is not itself a guarantee of access. If discovered or outed, these conditions combine so that consequences fall mainly under national procedures: document checks at hotels or by police can expose a traveller, hospital or custody placement can follow registered sex rather than identity, and bureaucracy can produce disclosure, misplacement or denial of service, while everyday outcomes are more typically exclusion, humiliation and service friction than arrest. Residual friction — bathhouse access, mismatched documents and reserved attitudes — therefore persists, and records of local enforcement against trans visitors are limited.

regions.name: Hiroshima
regions.merged_summary:
Hiroshima — a large, internationally oriented city on the Seto Inland Sea and gateway to Miyajima, drawing heavy peace-tourism and conference traffic — shows no local statute, facility rule or enforcement practice that differs from Japan's national picture: no law guarantees protection from discrimination or violence based on gender identity, no local protective ordinance covering transgender visitors is documented, and there is no record of anti-trans violence, police hostility toward transgender visitors or hostile local legislation in the prefecture. Policing and courts operate routinely and professionally, while municipal partnership-oath schemes, an annual pride march, the Nagarekawa entertainment district and a visible market of friendly venues give the city a small but visible LGBTQ presence, so visitors are neither unusual nor conspicuously targeted. Everyday contact is generally reserved rather than hostile, and visitor-facing onsen and accommodation options include private facilities; the rural northern and island districts and the wider Chugoku countryside are less accustomed to foreign or visibly gender-nonconforming visitors, producing milder social friction rather than threat.

If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed, those local conditions combine with the national regime: gender-segregated onsen, sento, changing rooms, hospital wards and service norms — including baths on Miyajima — remain the likeliest point of friction, and ward-office document handling can expose a mismatched foreign visitor, since gender changes for foreign nationals depend on coordination between the country of nationality and Japanese local offices that can break down, while custody follows the family register rather than gender identity. In an official encounter, ordinary contact is most likely to bring curiosity, misgendering or staff uncertainty rather than organized hostility or state targeting, but there is no binding anti-discrimination protection to rely on, no trans-specific criminal prohibition, and no documented local remedy, visitor rule or facility exclusion — a gap that does not establish safety, and absence of evidence does not secure emergency care, custody placement, onsen or sento access, or correct marker handling for families or minors. National courts have also ruled for transgender claimants, including a 2023 Supreme Court decision protecting workplace toilet use and a ruling against compulsory sterilisation for document changes, though how often document problems affect visitors in Hiroshima is uncertain.

regions.name: Hokkaido
regions.merged_summary:
Hokkaido follows Japan's national framework: there is no statute guaranteeing protection against gender-identity discrimination or violence, and the 2023 understanding-promotion law is hortatory and was passed in narrowed form. Gender-segregated facilities — onsen, sento, prisons and many others — are assigned by registered sex, custody is governed by family-register rules, and foreign visitors' registered gender and residence cards are handled through a conflict-of-laws process that can break down at local offices, causing document mismatch and bureaucratic friction. There is no criminalisation of gender expression, and although courts have recently upheld a trans woman's workplace bathroom access and struck the surgery requirement for gender-marker changes, these do not amount to a general legal guarantee, nor is there national recognition of same-sex partnership. Outside Sapporo, no Hokkaido-specific law or enforcement practice, bathhouse access rule, or region-wide visitor restriction or protection is documented, and no pattern of anti-trans violence, police targeting or official hostility specific to the prefecture is known.

Locally, Sapporo holds the main concentration of hotels, clinics and community support, runs a municipal partnership certificate (oath) system introduced early among Japanese cities, hosts one of Japan's longest-running Pride events and a cluster of queer venues around Susukino, and has visible LGBT community organisations and generally courteous, internationally minded hospitality; such partnership arrangements are local climate signals rather than protections that guarantee facility access or redress. The tourism economy in Sapporo, Niseko and Noboribetsu is accustomed to foreign visitors and less demandingly conformist than the family-register culture of provincial mainland, and Hokkaido's onsen culture includes established mixed-gender bathing options. Violent crime is low and police and courts function, so for a trans visitor who is out or discovered the likely outcome is curiosity, misgendering, service awkwardness and bureaucratic or facility friction rather than arrest or violence. Beyond the capital, towns and hot-spring resorts are small, thinly foreign-populated and unfamiliar, with thinner foreign tourism, English-speaking services and LGBTQ-friendly venues, more reserved and conventional gendered norms, and less infrastructure, and rural conditions are less certain; routine or emergency care far from Sapporo may mean delay and disclosure. Public onsen, sento and hotel baths are especially central to travel, venue rules vary, no Hokkaido-specific bathhouse access rule is documented, and private-bath arrangements usually must be booked in advance. These local differences are real but modest and do not alter the national framework.

regions.name: Hyogo Prefecture
regions.merged_summary:
Hyogo Prefecture has no trans-specific rules of its own: it applies Japan's national framework, under which gender identity and expression are not criminalised but no statute guarantees protection from gender-identity discrimination, the 2023 understanding-promotion law being diluted and lacking a binding non-discrimination mandate. Courts and police function, so gender expression does not invite routine arrest or imprisonment and there is no credible custodial or lethal escalation, but prefectural anti-discrimination enforcement and hate-crime recourse for gender identity are not documented, and no age-specific restriction on travelling minors is known. The practical exposures for a visitor who is outed or discovered are bureaucratic and spatial rather than penal: gender-segregated onsen and sento, hotel check-in with mismatched documents, municipal document procedures, and police identity checks that may compel disclosure. Detention, custody and medical settings follow family-register sex rather than lived gender, so a detained visitor may be placed accordingly, while a Supreme Court decision does protect access to a women's workplace restroom on government premises. Foreign visitors' registered gender is handled through the home-country conflict-of-laws process and updates to foreign documents may meet administrative friction; urban, visitor-facing friction is largely service discretion and administrative confusion, while rural onsen access can still produce outing, refusal or a segregated alternative — leaving thin recourse and protection far short of a reliably enforced equality regime.

Local conditions are mixed. Kobe — a major international port and tourist city, Osaka-linked and highly exposed to foreign visitors — has one of the Kansai region's more visible LGBTQ communities, with Pride events, community organisations and a municipal partnership certification scheme that confers no national legal effect; its urban, tourist-facing character makes everyday encounters generally reserved but non-confrontational and less hostile than might be feared. Himeji's tourism economy and established ryokan and onsen districts such as Kinosaki, along with Arima, give relatively high exposure to private-bath and foreign-guest alternatives, though private-bath options are left to individual venues and smaller towns and traditional facilities can remain reserved and discretionary. Northern and rural Tajima and other rural parts of the prefecture are more conservative, yet no local ordinance restricting transgender visitors is known. No region-specific bathhouse rule, local exclusion statute, hostile immigration practice, enforcement campaign, targeted pattern of anti-trans violence by officials, or documented local hostility, targeting or custody exposure is known to distinguish Hyogo adversely from the national baseline, and local venue practices remain uncertain.

regions.name: Ibaraki
regions.merged_summary: Ibaraki is a largely suburban and agricultural prefecture centred on Mito, with an academic and research community around Tsukuba and coastal tourist areas such as Hitachi and Oarai, and a comparatively small foreign population. It adds no known prefectural law, enforcement practice, or documented incident that separates it from Japan's national picture: there is no local criminalisation of gender expression, no prefectural protection beyond national law (the 2023 promotion act carries no gender-identity anti-discrimination guarantee), and no record of police targeting, venue exclusion, or hostile official action against transgender visitors; police and courts function routinely, and everyday contact in towns and tourist areas is usually neutral. What differs here is scale and visibility — fewer LGBTQ-friendly venues, clinics, community services and English-language guidance than Tokyo or other major hubs, thin LGBTQ visibility outside Tsukuba's international community, and generally reserved, politically conservative attitudes that can raise the odds of stares, intrusive questions and document-check friction. Onsen and sento-style gender-segregated bathing are customary, and local offices and facilities may rely on document sex, so practical friction around facilities is greater than in the main tourist corridors. For a visitor who is outed or discovered, these conditions combine with the national regime: gender-segregated baths with uncertain access, document handling tied to the family register and foreign-passport gender markers, and possible hesitation over pronouns, bathrooms or records across transport, hotels, municipal offices and emergency care, alongside family-register-based custody placement. National law provides no gender-identity anti-discrimination guarantee, and court rulings and the public-understanding law offer limited protection without establishing visitor-wide facility access or a reliable remedy; the resulting exposure is social friction, discretion and service hesitancy rather than organised hostility, well short of arrest or custodial abuse, and it varies with a visitor's discretion and with rural or urban setting.

regions.name: Kagawa Prefecture
regions.merged_summary: Kagawa Prefecture, a small, low-crime region on Shikoku centred on Takamatsu with rural and island communities and art-island tourism at Naoshima, follows Japan's national framework: gender identity and presentation are not criminalised, there is no death penalty or imprisonment for being transgender, and there is little direct police targeting, but no statute guarantees protection from discrimination or violence on the basis of gender identity. The 2023 diversity-promotion law has been narrowed by culture-war debate, and court rulings on workplace facilities and legal gender markers have offered only limited protections in particular cases without establishing a general remedy for visitors. Gender-segregated toilets, baths, changing facilities and custody apply, with no documented rule governing trans access to onsen, sento or super-sento; private-bath and co-ed options are visitor guidance rather than law. Administrative handling can break down where a residence card's gender conflicts with foreign-issued documents, and custody follows the family register rather than lived gender. Kagawa adds no prefectural ordinance offering extra visitor-facing protection and no local rule harsher than the national picture, but it is quieter and less English-accessible than Tokyo, with a small visible LGBTQ community, fewer LGBTQ-friendly businesses, documented services and specialist capacity than larger cities, and reserved, socially conservative local norms; everyday attitudes in Takamatsu and the art-island tourism economy are more accustomed to visitors, while rural areas and traditional guesthouses and onsen are more reserved. General crime is very low and neither anti-trans violence nor police targeting is documented as a local pattern; day-to-day reaction is reserved rather than hostile. Should a transgender visitor be outed, the tight-knit prefecture means word is more likely to spread across a limited social circle, combining with Japan-wide institutional constraints, bureaucratic and facility barriers, curiosity, misgendering and social awkwardness, with the operative difficulty being social exposure and friction in gendered spaces rather than arrest or state hostility. Kagawa-specific enforcement, service access and trans-targeted violence are not documented, which reflects uncertainty rather than evidence of safety.

regions.name: Kanagawa
regions.merged_summary: Kanagawa — taking in Yokohama, Kawasaki, Kamakura, Shonan, Hakone and the wider metropolitan coast — inherits Japan's national framework in full: no criminalisation of transgender identity, but no statute guaranteeing protection against discrimination or violence based on gender identity, a narrowed 2023 LGBTQ promotion law carrying no anti-discrimination guarantee, favourable Supreme Court rulings including a 2023 workplace bathroom decision, gender-segregated bathrooms, baths, changing rooms and some transport spaces, residence and family-register procedures that can expose mismatched documents, custody assigned by the family register, and national rules on detention, prison placement and legal gender recognition that local policy has not changed. No region-specific hostile legislation, police targeting, documented anti-trans incidents or known pattern of trans visitors being targeted or denied entry distinguish Kanagawa from that national picture — such records are missing information rather than evidence that such risks are absent — and no distinct local rule for visiting minors is known. What does set the prefecture apart is its large, urban and tourist-facing setting: a substantial foreign-resident population, universities, comparatively liberal secular social norms, pride visibility and public familiarity with LGBTQ people somewhat above the national norm, and long-running same-sex partnership certification plus diversity and human-rights ordinances at both prefectural and municipal level covering sexual orientation and gender identity. These signal comparatively trans-aware municipal services and police conduct and may reduce everyday hostility and street-level friction, more so than in more conservative rural areas, and improve informal customer-service handling, but they are cultural and service-level accommodations rather than a legal safeguard, they do not extend partnership recognition to a visitor travelling with a same-sex partner, and greater familiarity with LGBTQ people is not reliable visitor protection. Document handling at hotels and ward offices is bureaucratic rather than hostile, though conflict-of-laws friction at ward offices still applies to visitors. The density of ryokan and onsen towns in Hakone, Atami, Yugawara and Isehara concentrates the gender-segregated bathing difficulty: private-bath bookings, inclusive or co-ed alternatives are offered as guidance rather than a legal right, and Hakone's traditional onsen culture remains a practical difficulty. Where a trans visitor is out or is discovered, the likely results are awkward questioning, refusal at gender-segregated facilities, hotel or local-office friction, and delay or outing through administrative document practices; in serious encounters this can extend to detention or placement mismatches, but not to criminal punishment or lethal consequences.

regions.name: Miyagi
regions.merged_summary:
Miyagi, centred on Sendai, operates under Japan's national framework with no known local exception: there is no nationwide statute prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity, the 2023 promotion law is weak, transgender identity is not criminalised, and official documents, residence-card handling and custody decisions follow registered sex and the family register rather than gender identity, though courts have recognised limited protections. Gender-segregated facilities — baths, onsen and sento, restrooms, hospitals and ryokan shared areas — plus hotel, ward-office and other paperwork can produce document mismatch or forced outing, and families or minors face birth-marker paperwork and facility placement in schools, clinics and baths. There is no documented Miyagi-specific law restricting transgender visitors, nor a known local pattern of police targeting, anti-trans violence or detention beyond national patterns, and no prefectural or municipal protection providing a short-term visitor with an enforceable remedy; local enforcement and treatment in particular facilities remain uncertain. The principal exposure is institutional discretion over documents, facilities and health care rather than imprisonment or lethal punishment.

Sendai, as the prefectural capital, Tohoku's largest city and a major university and tourist destination with low general crime and well-trafficked transport hubs, has a visible LGBTQ community, municipal partnership recognition and ordinary urban hospitality, though everyday contact is reserved rather than hostile and the partnership system is resident-facing, amounting to a climate signal rather than a visitor protection. Outside the city, Tohoku is socially more reserved than Tokyo: smaller towns, coastal areas and hot-spring resorts such as Zao and Naruko are more conservative, tourist infrastructure is thinner, and there are fewer explicit alternatives to gendered facilities, raising the chance of staring, misgendering or refusal at a bathhouse — though private-bath alternatives exist. Overall the position stays close to the national picture, with urban Sendai somewhat easier than rural onsen areas.

regions.name: Osaka Prefecture
regions.merged_summary:
Osaka Prefecture inherits Japan's national framework: no statute guaranteeing protection from discrimination or violence based on gender identity, a 2023 promotion act that is non-binding and was watered down amid debate, gender-segregated onsen, sento and other facilities whose guidance is documented rather than codified, custody and detention or emergency-care placement based on registered family status, and document-based bureaucracy at ward offices — including a documented residence-card refusal for a trans person. Court-recognised bathroom access remains contested policy rather than settled practice, though courts have ruled for trans people. For a visitor who is outed or discovered, the resulting exposure is institutional and spatial: friction or refusal at bathhouses, hotels and offices where presentation and documents differ, awkwardness or denial in gendered facilities, misread documents and possible invasive secondary screening, and limited remedies — with family-register rules applying in detention or emergency care.

Local conditions differ modestly from rural Japan: Osaka is a large, tourism-facing metropolitan prefecture with an outgoing public culture, a visible LGBTQ district around Namba and Horie and the Doyamacho commercial district in Osaka city, established queer venues, municipal partnership certificates since 2016, and hospitality-sector familiarity with visible difference. Everyday encounters in major tourist and nightlife districts such as Namba and Shinsaibashi are generally reserved and non-confrontational rather than hostile, and more LGBTQ and private-bath options exist than in smaller cities. However, no Osaka-specific rule changes the national institutional picture, partnership measures are not visitor protections, visibility is not a legal safeguard, and regional documentation of local enforcement hostility or police targeting of trans visitors is limited — an absence that does not itself establish safety.

regions.name: Saitama
regions.merged_summary:
Saitama is a densely urbanised prefecture in the Greater Tokyo commuter belt, largely residential and suburban, with heavy day-trip and commuter traffic but limited standalone tourism compared with central Tokyo. No prefecture-level rule, facility practice or enforcement pattern specific to transgender visitors was identified, so conditions track Japan's national framework: no trans-specific criminal offence but also no binding guarantee against discrimination or violence on grounds of gender identity (the 2023 promotion statute contains none), gender-segregated baths, sento and toilets as the main everyday friction, and document handling that can expose a mismatched foreign passport or family-register discrepancy at hotels, ward and municipal offices. Some municipal same-sex partnership schemes and local human-rights ordinances acknowledging sexual orientation and gender identity are recorded in Omiya, Kawaguchi and Saitama City, though no prefecture-level protective machinery exists, and the more rural western and northern areas are less LGBTQ-facing. Favourable court rulings — including the 2023 Supreme Court bathroom decision, the ruling against the surgery requirement and the workplace ruling — are recorded but concern domestic residents rather than visitors. Street-level attitudes are generally reserved rather than hostile, though Saitama's family-oriented social climate offers less anonymity and less international-service familiarity than central Tokyo, and LGBTQ-specific infrastructure is limited, with private LGBTQ-friendly venue guides available as an alternative.

Conditional on being outed or discovered, a transgender visitor should expect social and bureaucratic friction rather than organised targeting: staring, misgendering, invasive or awkward questioning, occasional outing, refusal or denial of entry at some bathing and accommodation venues, and possible exposure of a document or gender-marker mismatch at offices and in detention or emergency care, where custody practice follows legal records rather than identity. Bathhouse access and treatment of foreign identity documents remain uncertain, and no Saitama-specific rule affecting travelling minors is documented, so the national institutional exposures still apply. There is no documented pattern of police targeting, organised hostility or custody arising from being transgender in the prefecture, and no local rule removes these inherited exposures; the likely consequence is social friction and service exclusion rather than arrest.

regions.name: Shiga
regions.merged_summary:
Shiga Prefecture follows Japan's national framework: transgender identity and expression are not criminalised, but no statute guarantees protection against discrimination or violence based on gender identity, and the 2023 law promoting public understanding of sexual orientation and gender identity is aspirational and non-binding. Gender-segregated spaces — onsen, sento and other bathing venues — are organised by sex, with private-bath options at some venues, while official document handling and custody placement follow the family register rather than identity; nationally, custody and prison placement by registered sex has produced documented misgendered treatment, including the Kasamatsu Prison case, and foreign visitors' papers are handled through their home country's conflict-of-laws arrangement, which can break down at local offices. Locally, Shiga is a quiet, low-crime, largely residential and semi-rural prefecture centred on Otsu, Lake Biwa, shrines and resort areas, with modest and largely domestic lakeside tourism. No Shiga-specific rule, local ordinance, enforcement pattern, documented anti-trans incident, raid, organised violence or police targeting is known, and the region shows neither stricter enforcement nor added protection relative to Japan generally; courts and police operate under stable national rule of law, and the prefecture lacks the nightlife scrutiny zones of major metros. It is also not a major international hub, so LGBTQ-friendly venues, private-bath alternatives, English-language guidance and LGBTQ-specific venues or advocacy resources are thinner than in Tokyo, Osaka or Kyoto, and everyday exposure rests on reserved social attitudes, tighter small-town networks and unfamiliarity rather than documented acceptance. Proximity to Kyoto's more visitor-experienced environment means major urban services remain reachable. 

Conditional on discovery or being outing, the likely harms are bureaucratic awkwardness, misgendering, invasive curiosity, intrusive questions, social friction and possible service refusal rather than arrest or severe punishment; ryokan, onsen and sento in lake-tourism areas may respond awkwardly or refuse trans guests, with discretion varying by establishment, and less familiarity among service providers in rural and onsen settings adds to this. Bathhouse access and document handling carry uncertainty that no Shiga-specific rule or practice resolves, and that uncertainty should not be read as a guarantee of safety; detention, exclusion or severe outcomes are not a documented concern for visitors here, and region-specific evidence beyond the national picture remains limited.

regions.name: Tochigi
regions.merged_summary:
Tochigi is a largely rural prefecture north of Tokyo, with Utsunomiya as its main city, Nikko's temple complex as the principal tourist draw, and onsen towns and ryokan culture shaping the visitor experience. It has no local law criminalising gender expression, no local ordinance or enforcement practice targeting transgender visitors, no local anti-discrimination guarantee, and no rule permitting or barring bathhouse access; no Tochigi-specific incident, police practice, border procedure or custody rule is known to worsen the national baseline, and no region-specific protective mechanism exists either. Socially, it is comparatively conservative with low LGBTQ visibility and few specialist support services outside the more international tourist areas around Nikko, so street reaction is more likely to be curiosity, staring or awkwardness than confrontation, and rural areas beyond Utsunomiya and Nikko may raise social friction modestly, though no hostile local layer is documented; Nikko's tourism economy means staff are accustomed to foreign visitors and hostile targeting is not a documented feature. Rule of law functions, and police targeting, imprisonment or lethal punishment after discovery are not credible.

Because Tochigi inherits Japan's national framework, discovery or being outed exposes a visitor to the same institutional friction: no general statutory protection from discrimination on grounds of gender identity (only a 2023 promotion act), gender-segregated onsen, sento, toilets and other facilities that customarily apply birth-sex rules, few private-bathing alternatives in smaller resorts, and document handling based on registered sex — hotel or police checks can produce awkward disclosure, custody follows the family register rather than gender identity, and documented detention practice includes misgendering and barriers to appropriate treatment. For foreign nationals, gender records are changed through their country of nationality and reported to immigration, a process that can break down bureaucratically. Private baths and alternative venues exist but are offered mainly as informal guidance and are not an enforceable traveller protection, so the likely outcome is staring, service friction, humiliation, refusal or exclusion at facilities, with limited local recourse beyond national remedies rather than arrest or violence; this sits marginally below the comfort noted in Japan's major tourist destinations, and the presence of tourism is not evidence that these institutional risks are absent.

regions.name: Tokyo
regions.merged_summary:
Tokyo shares Japan's national framework: there is no criminal penalty for being transgender or expressing gender differently, ordinary day-to-day contact is generally reserved rather than hostile, no state campaign against trans visitors is documented, and no statute or enforceable guarantee protects gender identity from discrimination or violence — the 2023 understanding-promotion law grants no such protection, discrimination remedies for visitors are slow, and no shield-type protection is documented. Bathing and changing facilities, onsen and sento (with no rule permitting trans access), hospital wards and custody or detention placement remain segregated or assigned by registered sex and the family register; a foreign visitor's own registered gender depends on their home country's record, and border screening, immigration, prisons and pre-trial detention are national matters, including documented mistreatment of a trans detainee. Document checks, bathhouse use and ward-office dealings can still force disclosure and denial — as in a 2018 case where a Tokyo ward office did not recognise a US resident's gender change, a resident-facing process not shown to create routine friction for short-stay visitors.

Locally, Tokyo is Japan's most internationally visible, tourist-facing and anonymous metropolis: it holds the country's largest LGBTQ district, dense LGBTQ-friendly venues in Shinjuku Ni-chome and across Shinjuku, Shibuya and Roppongi, a tourism economy accustomed to foreign visitors, greater familiarity among hospitality, service and medical staff, and more private rooms, private-bath and gender-neutral options than smaller communities, with less ordinary street hostility than rural areas; everyday confrontation and police targeting are reduced, and immigration and routine police interaction are not documented as profiling trans visitors. The city also has a 2016 partnership certificate system, a 2018 metropolitan ordinance on respect for gender identity and sexual orientation in prefectural administration, and other awareness measures — signals of climate rather than remedies whose effectiveness for a visitor is established. If outed or discovered, a visitor is more likely to encounter curiosity, misgendering, service friction or a bathhouse refusal than state punishment, but an arrest, detention or medical emergency can escalate sharply into the national custody, document and facilities exposures, and nothing local offsets them. Trans-specific targeting of visitors, a local pattern of violence, and special rules for travelling minors are not documented; their absence is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: North Kazakhstan Region
regions.merged_summary:
Kazakhstan does not criminalise transgender identity, cross-dressing or use of facilities matching a person's presentation, no trans-specific clothing or facility ban has been documented, and consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1998. A December 2025 law banning public and media "propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation" carries fines and arrest of up to 10 days, creating legal uncertainty for visible expression, and how it is enforced against visitors is uncertain; domestic document-change rules govern residents and do not apply to a traveller's home-issued passport. There is no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity in employment, housing, health care or public accommodation, and no hate-crime reporting system, with no hate-crime data reported to the OSCE since 2018; documented violations against LGBT people include a 2019 Supreme Court case in which two women fled for eight months over fear of harm. Legal gender recognition is medically gatekept — requiring surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation — and is effectively centred on Almaty, making it practically unavailable elsewhere. No organised state targeting or lethal pattern against trans visitors is known.

North Kazakhstan Region is rural, agricultural, small-city and predominantly Russian-speaking, bordering Russia, with deeper social conservatism and homophobic and transphobic attitudes more pronounced than in the south. Compared with Almaty and Astana it lacks LGBTQ organisational, legal-aid and medical infrastructure, has no local trans support and no functioning gender commission, so anonymity is thinner and remedies for harassment or service refusal are correspondingly sparse; local enforcement practice here is undocumented, and its location or social character alone does not establish a documented pattern of targeting distinct from the national picture. Document checks, hotel registration and police spot-checks can out a traveller. A visibly trans visitor who is outed or discovered may face staring, gossip, scrutiny in housing, services, policing and medical settings, service refusal, misgendering or refusal of care, questioning, possible detention under the propaganda law and an unsympathetic police response, with local disapproval more likely to escalate into administrative harassment and little practical recourse.

regions.name: South Kazakhstan Region
regions.merged_summary: South Kazakhstan Region — centred on Turkestan and Shymkent, also referred to as Turkistan Region — inherits Kazakhstan's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is decriminalised, and neither gender presentation nor the use of public facilities is restricted for visitors. However, the December 2025 law banning 'propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation' in public spaces and media applies here and carries fines and arrest of up to 10 days for covered expression, though how it would be applied to a transgender visitor is uncertain. Legal gender recognition is resident-facing and effectively unavailable to visitors, since document changes require surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation, and the only functioning medical commission is in Almaty. There are no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections in force, and effective remedies are limited, with their direct application to visitors undocumented. No region-specific pattern of police targeting, anti-trans violence, or a distinct trans-visitor law is documented here — an absence of evidence rather than assurance of safety — and no local protective practice is documented. The region's more conservative, religiously observant, rural and less internationally exposed character, with stronger family and community norms, very low trans visibility, few trans-specific services or advocacy, and police and public unfamiliarity with gender diversity, is a general cultural cue rather than a documented driver of trans-specific enforcement; recourse is weaker outside Shymkent's university and student milieu. If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the national regime: stigma, social hostility, harassment, outing, refusal of services, extortion, and hotel or clinic awkwardness are more likely, alongside police discretion that can bring questioning or short administrative trouble if expression is treated as propaganda. Local reaction and police handling may be harsher and more unpredictable than in Almaty or Astana, with weak recourse in practice; there is no credible local evidence of routine imprisonment.

regions.name: Kajiado
regions.merged_summary:
Kajiado has no documented county-specific law, enforcement pattern, protective ordinance or restrictive measure for transgender visitors, so Kenya's national framework governs: same-sex conduct remains criminalised under unrepealed Penal Code sections 162 and 165 and is sometimes used by police as a lever against gender-nonconforming people; there is no enacted statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination or hate crime, and no codified pathway for a visitor to change documents, so identity papers usually do not match presentation — a High Court ruling on gender recognition has issued, but no protective legislation has been enacted. Documented national risks include police detention on pretexts such as 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion, remand beyond constitutional limits and intrusive custody practices, plus an Eldoret High Court finding of abusive prison treatment; court-ordered protections exist but enforcement is uneven. A pending Family Protection Bill would make 'aggravated homosexuality' punishable by death, but it is not law. Court rulings on documents and prison conditions have not produced enacted protections, barriers to affirming care persist, and no region-specific information on entry, policing, facilities or healthcare distinguishes Kajiado — such local practices are simply undocumented, which is not evidence of safety. Overall exposure remains well below routine arrest or torture for gender presentation, but substantially above a setting with operative protections and effective remedies; no specific additional exposure for travelling with a minor is documented.

Locally, Kajiado is Maasai-majority and socially conservative, with strong patriarchal customary norms, Maasai age-set and pastoral gender segregation, small-town visibility and weaker legal-literacy and support infrastructure than central Nairobi, particularly outside Kajiado town and Kitengela. The northern commuter-belt towns of Kitengela, Ongata Rongai and Ngong offer relative anonymity and routine foreign-tourist traffic, and Amboseli's tourism economy increases exposure to visitors, but neither adds documented hostility nor documented protection, and tourism and conservancy employment do not guarantee safe facilities or privacy; trans-specific support is limited to Nairobi-linked networks. If discovered or outed, a visitor may face social scrutiny, humiliation, service refusal, and police questioning, extortion or arbitrary detention with thin and inconsistent local recourse, while sex-segregated ward or cell placement and border or document checks follow observed sex rather than identity, making emergency health and custody encounters especially exposed.

regions.name: Kiambu
regions.merged_summary:
Kiambu is a densely populated, largely Kikuyu county bordering and wrapping Nairobi, made up of commuter and dormitory towns such as Thika, Ruiru, Juja, Kikuyu and Limuru alongside a more rural interior. It is a strongly Christian and socially conservative setting, and no county-level statute, protective ordinance, policing directive, enforcement practice, documented incident involving a transgender visitor, or distinct treatment on border or document checks, facilities, custody placement or access to remedies is known to apply — so proximity to Nairobi alone does not establish safer conditions. The county operates under Kenya's national regime: colonial-era Penal Code provisions on same-sex conduct remain in force (with a 2019 High Court validation still on the books), no Kenyan statute recognises gender identity, there is no statutory gender-recognition pathway pending the May 2026 document-marker ruling, civil registration has refused most gender-marker corrections, there are no anti-discrimination protections, and the Family Protection Bill — which proposes capital penalties — remains stalled rather than enacted. Court remedies are slow and uncertain, and recent rulings on document markers and prison treatment still await implementing legislation.

For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, these conditions combine as follows. Although the same-sex provisions do not criminalise transgender identity, they are used in practice as a police lever, with documented detention on pretexts such as drunken and disorderly conduct, on-the-spot extortion and bribes, and, in reporting by Kenya's human rights commissions and 2025 High Court findings, sexual coercion and rape by security officers; a court has also found serious violations of a trans person's rights in prison, while appellate rulings against forced examinations provide limited positive evidence. Trans detainees face unresolved placement in male or female cells, sex-designated facilities and bathroom use are documented flashpoints, and barriers to gender-affirming care persist. The urbanised edges closer to Nairobi offer a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor more anonymity than upcountry rural areas and put them nearer both those documented police practices and reachable Nairobi-based legal and advocacy support, while small-town and market-centre policing remains conservative and local police stations and county hospitals provide no trans-specific recourse; there is no locally documented additional exposure for travelling families or minors.

regions.name: Machakos
regions.merged_summary:
Machakos County — a largely rural and peri-urban, closely knit Kamba-majority area just southeast of Nairobi, centred on Machakos and Athi River — operates entirely under Kenya's national framework: Penal Code sections 162, 163 and 165 criminalising same-sex conduct (upheld by the High Court in 2019, with a Court of Appeal decision still pending), no trans-specific criminal offence identified, and no gender-identity statute or codified recognition pathway for visitors, though a May 2026 High Court ruling allows changes to gender markers on identity documents and other recent court rulings have supported marker changes and barred forced anal examinations. A Family Protection Bill that would impose severe penalties has been stalled in committee for about two years and is not law, and no trans-specific killing rate is available. Locally there is no protective ordinance, no trans-specific organising, and no LGBTQ legal-aid, NGO or service infrastructure comparable to Nairobi's or Mombasa's, where most documented harassment cases originate; county courts and hospitals may be less accustomed to gender-identity disputes, social attitudes are broadly conservative with strong church influence, and there is little anonymity for visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitors, so legal and medical recourse lies with Nairobi-based lawyers and NGOs rather than locally.

For a trans visitor who is outed or discovered, national police practices apply through the same system: harassment, pretextual detention (such as on 'drunk and disorderly' grounds), on-the-spot extortion, remand abuse, unresolved questions about cell placement for trans detainees, and misgendered custody — exposure that may rise after a passport, incident or medical request draws attention. A local case in which two men were taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 Hospital, where a magistrate halted a proposed anal examination, and a subsequent Court of Appeal ruling that forced examinations are unconstitutional with compensation awarded in 2024, alongside a 2025 High Court finding recording mistreatment of a trans prisoner including nonconsensual procedures, are meaningful signs of judicial relief but do not establish reliable protection from police harassment or abuse in custody. Discovery would most plausibly produce gossip, service refusal, police shakedowns or short detention rather than prosecution for identity itself; local conditions may therefore sit slightly below the national picture, though nothing county-specific distinguishes Machakos from Kenya overall, and any recourse would be thinner than in the capital.

regions.name: Narok
regions.merged_summary:
Narok is a largely rural, pastoral, Maasai-majority county in southwestern Kenya bordering Tanzania, whose main visitor economy is the Maasai Mara safari circuit; beyond the lodges and tourist corridor it is sparsely populated with strong customary and patriarchal norms. It inherits Kenya's national regime: same-sex conduct remains criminalised under Penal Code sections 162 and 165 with penalties up to 14 years, upheld by the High Court in 2019; decriminalisation litigation is unresolved; there is no statutory anti-discrimination protection and no legal gender-recognition pathway, with a May 2026 High Court ruling on document markers unimplemented as legislation and the Family Protection Bill stalled. The national record documents police detention of gender-nonconforming people on pretexts, on-the-spot extortion, and custody placement by birth sex, with a 2025 High Court finding that a trans prisoner suffered rights violations and nonconsensual procedures. The criminal provisions do not specifically target transgender identity, but the documented treatment of gender-nonconforming people makes them a relevant secondary concern; Kenya's lack of a domestic gender-marker process is not itself a visitor-facing exposure. Narok offers no local ordinance, protective practice, documented tolerance toward trans visitors, LGBTQ organisation, or trans-specific services, and region-specific documentation of trans incidents here is limited — the absence of local reports is not evidence of safety.

Maasai customary norms include documented traditional roles for gender-variant men, which may offer some familiarity but no legal protection. County policing is thinner and less professionalised than in Nairobi or Mombasa, courts and legal aid are distant, and the tourist corridor toward Maasai Mara lodges is comparatively shielded and brings international visitors and some external scrutiny, with lodges offering a discreet setting but not a protective system; transit through Narok town and Kilgoris is not comparably shielded, and visibly gender-nonconforming strangers in small-town settings may attract immediate public attention. Conditional on being outed, a transgender visitor would combine these conditions with the national exposures, facing heightened public hostility, elder or community humiliation, more arbitrary local policing and community-level confrontation or mob exposure, reduced access to supportive services and legal recourse than in Nairobi, and heightened risk of detention or violence — with remote areas potentially worse than the national picture, though Narok-specific practice cannot be confirmed either way.

regions.name: Tana River
regions.merged_summary: Tana River is a sparsely populated, predominantly rural and pastoralist county on the lower Tana, with a partly Muslim population, strong clan and religious authority, limited tourism infrastructure, thin policing, court and legal-aid access, and a history of periodic intercommunal violence. No local protective ordinances, LGBTQ support services, clinics, or documented patterns of greater tolerance are known, and no region-specific incidents involving transgender visitors or local protective policy have been recorded for the county. Visitors inherit Kenya's national regime: Penal Code sections 162 and 165 criminalise certain same-sex conduct though transgender identity or presentation is not itself a criminal offence, no legal gender-recognition pathway was in place before the May 2026 Nairobi High Court ruling, which is not yet implemented by legislation, and police harassment, extortion and detention of gender-nonconforming people are documented nationally, alongside a court finding of severe abuse of a trans prisoner in 2025. Recent court protections against forced examinations and degrading treatment, and the 2023 association decision, exist but operate primarily through Nairobi and Mombasa institutions and do not apply locally in the same way.

regions.name: Uasin Gishu
regions.merged_summary:
Uasin Gishu operates under Kenya's national regime: same-sex conduct remains criminalised under Penal Code sections 162–165, there is no trans-specific criminal offence, no statutory gender-recognition pathway for visitors (whose documents come from their home country), no statute protecting against gender-identity discrimination, and there is documented police harassment, detention and extortion of gender-nonconforming people, together with birth-sex facility and custody-placement practices, misgendered custody, documented prison-custody abuses and barriers to gender-affirming care. A pending Family Protection Bill would, if enacted, add death-penalty and monitoring provisions. Locally, the Eldoret High Court in August 2025 found a trans petitioner's rights violated in incarceration — including torture, nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered gender determination — and directed the state to legislate trans protections and end prison abuses; no protective law has followed, and one assessment records this as a national-level finding rather than evidence of local conditions. Descriptions of the area itself differ: several assessments portray Eldoret and the surrounding Rift Valley highland as religiously conservative and church-influenced, with limited trans-specific advocacy or safe infrastructure and no local anti-discrimination ordinance, shelter, visitor-facing protection or documented police-reform practice, while another notes the record does not quantify local conservatism and so makes no adjustment. One assessment instead emphasises Eldoret's character as a large university and hospital town offering some anonymity, with privacy thinner and social hostility more likely outside the urban centre; the county is described as lacking the trans-visible community infrastructure and tourist-facing protections found in parts of Nairobi or Mombasa.

For a transgender visitor, conditions remain close to the national baseline, with local conservatism and thin support slightly reducing safety and the judicial precedent offering only a partial, slow check if detained. Because discovery or outing leaves a visitor dependent on discretionary police conduct, the consequences can include harassment, extortion, humiliation, intrusive verification and jail, with custody conditions and misgendering a documented concern. One assessment records no region-specific evidence of routine targeting of trans visitors or organised sweeps, and no capital threat beyond the stalled national bill; but with no operative visitor-facing remedy or enforcement reform, recourse for a discovered visitor rests on uneven police and court practice.

regions.name: Chuy Region
regions.merged_summary:
Chuy Region surrounds Bishkek and takes in Tokmok, Kant and the Manas International Airport corridor — the country's main international gateway — so national entry and document rules, including migration-service registration and the busy Kazakh border crossings, apply to most arriving visitors. It is the country's most urbanised, Russian-speaking and transit-oriented area, and anonymity plus proximity to the capital's small NGO, expatriate and community scene offers some discretion; at the same time, that community life is contracted (the capital's only gay club closed in 2017 and public LGBTQ venues in the wider capital area have largely disappeared), while the surrounding Chuy valley outside the immediate capital area is rural, agricultural and markedly more conservative, with family and community ostracism reported as especially acute and fewer protective networks. No region-specific enforcement practice or trans-specific exposure beyond the national picture is documented, nor is any distinct local protective effect; police and social hostility remain the main risk, illustrated nationally by an MP's call after the 2019 pride march for participants to be beaten.

Visitors remain subject to the national regime: same-sex conduct is legal, but there is no anti-discrimination protection and no legal gender recognition — marker changes barred since 2021, with a 2026 bill at first reading that would further ban marker change and gender-affirming care — while transition-related care is barred under 25, vaguely defined 2023 restrictions on promoting non-traditional sexual relations apply, and child-protection speech provisions reach the same subject matter. There is no documented trans-specific criminal offence, but police blackmail of LGBTQ people recruited through dating sites and social media, along with documented political hostility, discrimination and violence, is reported nationally. If a transgender visitor is outed or discovered — most likely at the airport, land borders, hotels, clinics or in small conservative towns — the likely consequences are extortion, humiliation, privacy exposure, service refusal or harassment rather than arrest or imprisonment; urban anonymity and community contacts soften but do not remove that exposure, and no local protection after harassment is known.

regions.name: Preah Sihanouk
regions.merged_summary:
Preah Sihanouk, centred on Sihanoukville, is Cambodia's main coastal port and a tourist and casino hub; since 2019 a Chinese-run casino and construction boom has shifted it from beach resort toward a transient, gambling-heavy economy with guesthouse, nightlife and informal entertainment work. No local trans-specific statute, facility rule or protective ordinance distinguishes the province: same-sex conduct and trans status are not criminalised nationally, but there is no legal gender recognition, no gender-marker change (documents can only be issued abroad) and no statutory non-discrimination protection, while tourism-ministry messages of welcome are not backed by law. The province has less visible LGBT community infrastructure, Pride or venue presence than Phnom Penh or Siem Reap, fewer local advocates and a less established tolerant nightlife, so discovery may hinge more on private hospitality staff, checkpoints or crime-associated settings. Cutting the other way, its beach-tourism and entertainment economy has historically employed and welcomed visibly gender-diverse people, foreign visitors in ordinary hotel, beach and nightlife settings face little identity scrutiny, and tourist-area familiarity with foreigners offers some buffer — though routine contact with international visitors is not evidence of protection, and no local safeguards or trans-specific support infrastructure are documented. Border treatment, facility access and police responses here remain uncertain.

The policing and justice environment is weakly accountable, with organised-crime presence, corruption and extortion of vulnerable visitors known concerns, and police treatment of transgender entertainment workers follows patterns documented nationally: harassment, arrests tied to presentation, sex-worker raids and extortion practices. Nationally, street harassment of transgender women is documented, roughly a third of surveyed transgender women report arrests linked to their identity, and custody placement is informally governed; how often such conduct affects visitors in Preah Sihanouk is not documented. Conditional on being outed or discovered, a trans visitor is more likely to face gossip, service refusal, extortion or humiliation than systematic prosecution or imprisonment, with thin local recourse, and ID-mismatch stops carrying a payment demand are a real risk. Local conditions differ only marginally from the national pattern, and organised crime and corruption raise trans-specific risk only where they produce targeted harassment, detention or denied care.

regions.name: Siem Reap
regions.merged_summary: Siem Reap follows Cambodia's national framework: same-sex conduct and transgender identity are not criminalised, but there is no anti-discrimination protection for gender identity, no legal gender recognition or marker-change route (which foreign visitors cannot obtain anyway), and gender-affirming surgery is not legally available — reported practice places transgender prisoners who have had surgery in the women's facility at Prey Sar. Official acceptance has not produced reliable recourse: nationally there are more than 100 reported street-harassment cases, roughly 38% of surveyed transgender women report arrest linked to being transgender, and there is no formal remedy for an outed traveller. Imprisonment or execution solely for being transgender is not documented locally. As a place, Siem Reap's large tourism economy, international hotels, visible bar and club scene, annual Pride since 2018 and publicly promoted welcome to LGBT visitors — including the Ministry of Tourism's 2011 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign — can make ordinary hospitality interactions less hostile than in less international settings. The local record cuts the other way: Cambodian Centre for Human Rights research documented Siem Reap police specifically targeting transgender women, especially sex workers, forcing them to bathe in stagnant river water, sometimes naked, and expelling them from the area, treatment not documented for cisgender sex workers; harassment of visibly gender-nonconforming people and street harassment of transgender women are reported in the city. For a visitor, the documented abuse concentrates in sex-work enforcement rather than visitor settings, and the evidence is dated rather than proof that the same treatment is routine for transgender tourists today, with current local enforcement and remedies unclear — but discovery can still bring police humiliation, document mismatches, custody, extortion or service refusal, especially away from protected tourism spaces, with little effective remedy.

regions.name: Gilbert Islands
regions.merged_summary:
The Gilbert Islands are Kiribati's main inhabited archipelago and include South Tarawa — the capital and most urbanised, institutionally dense area, with government offices, the main airport and the country's highest concentration of outsiders and visitors — along with Betio and the outer atolls, so the national regime applies directly. Penal Code sections 153–155 criminalise sex between men with penalties up to fourteen years, but they are a documented dead letter with no recorded prosecutions; sex between women is not an offence; there is no trans-specific offence, facility restriction, document-check practice, detention-placement rule or organised targeting of gender-nonconforming visitors; and no constitutional or statutory protection names gender identity, with employment discrimination law covering only sexual orientation. No assessment found region-specific evidence of harsher local enforcement, local ordinances, local protections or documented anti-trans violence beyond the national baseline. The available report of no societal discrimination or violence dates to 2015 — roughly a decade old — and current visitor-specific evidence on border checks, facilities, custody, care and violence is not documented. Kiribati's recognised gender-variant tradition, the binabinaaine, who appear in dance performance and public life, provides some local familiarity with gender variance but does not establish consistent acceptance of foreign trans people; they remain stigmatised and without legal recourse or advocacy infrastructure.

Local conditions shape how discovery would unfold.
