Society is conservative and church-influenced (Catholic and Kiribati Uniting Church), tourism is minimal so foreign visitors are conspicuous, and South Tarawa is densely populated and close-knit, with state offices and modest visitor accommodation alongside small communities where news spreads through accommodation and kinship networks; outer atolls have dense kin networks in which discovery travels quickly, and one account places social exposure sharpest outside Tarawa. For a discovered or outed visitor the likely consequences are staring, intrusive questions, awkwardness, curiosity, informal service friction and gossip rather than credible prosecution or custody. A foreign passport attracts no known scrutiny, though passport gender presentation is required in everyday document checks. Formal recourse is thin: there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime remedy, institutional capacity and anonymity are limited, and police would likely treat violence or extortion as a private or family matter. Evidence on targeted violence is thin, so the absence of reports does not establish safety.

regions.name: Line Islands
regions.merged_summary:
The Line Islands follow Kiribati's national framework: the Penal Code's provisions criminalising sex between men remain on the books but are unenforced, with no reported prosecutions and no trans-specific offence, execution risk, or documented police, border, facility, custody, or healthcare measures targeting transgender visitors. There is no general statutory protection covering gender identity, no legal gender-recognition machinery, and the narrow employment protection covering sexual orientation is not a safeguard for visitors. No distinct local law, protective practice, targeted anti-trans violence, or enforcement of the sexuality statute is known in the Line Islands, and no region-specific information indicates harsher or more protective local practice than nationally. The only cited report on social conditions, from 2015, found no discrimination or violence based on sexual orientation and so does not establish current attitudes toward transgender people; local trans-specific evidence remains thin.

Local conditions are remote, sparsely populated eastern atolls centred on Kiritimati, with very limited services, avenues for complaint, and delayed outside assistance. Kiritimati's resort, fishing, and historic military and scientific presence make foreign visitors familiar there, while Kiritimati and the smaller atolls are tiny, tightly knit, conservative Christian communities where a foreigner is conspicuous, gossip travels quickly, privacy after discovery is very limited, and an outed visitor would attract notice with essentially no local recourse, LGBT services, or discreet care infrastructure. Health and police services are thin and there is no trans-specific support or advocacy, so serious cases may require evacuation to Tarawa or abroad. Conditional on discovery, likely consequences are curiosity, awkwardness, moral disapproval, harassment, or service refusal, with friction handled informally through community pressure rather than arrest or formal exclusion; formal recourse is limited, and local border, facility, custody, care, and trans-specific enforcement practices are not documented.

regions.name: Phoenix Islands
regions.merged_summary: The Phoenix Islands — an extremely remote, largely uninhabited atoll group of Kiribati, with Kanton the only settled island (a few dozen residents and a government station, alongside Nikumaroro, Orona, Manra and others) — have no separate legal regime and inherit the national framework: Penal Code sections criminalising sex between men (carrying up to fourteen years' imprisonment) remain unrepealed but are documented as unenforced with no reported prosecutions; no offence targets transgender identity or expression; there is no legal gender recognition, no constitutional or statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity (employment protection for sexual orientation does not name gender identity); Kiribati did not respond to recommendations to decriminalise at its 2016 Universal Periodic Review; and the only recorded observation of no societal discrimination or violence dates from 2015, with no later survey available. Locally there is no police station, court, clinic or tourism infrastructure — only a small settlement on Kanton, occasional vessels, small-scale eco-tourism and research visits, and access by permit or research vessel — and no documented local targeting, hostility, enforcement, distinct local policy or restrictive practice toward transgender people is known. The climate is described as conservative but non-violent and strongly Christian, while Kiribati's recognised binabinaaine tradition gives some cultural familiarity with gender-variant people.\n\nFor a transgender visitor, discovery or outing in such a tiny community is close to certain, producing deep social exposure: curiosity, gossip, misgendering, social pressure, refusal of services and informal scrutiny are more plausible there than in Tarawa, though no documented pattern of hostility, detention or abuse exists and there is no state apparatus on hand to detain or prosecute, nor any traveler-specific ban or campaign against transgender people. The main exposure is therefore the latent criminal statute combined with absent recourse — no medical, legal or redress infrastructure and reliance on distant authorities in Tarawa — so any incident would fall on a community with almost no institutional support, and ordinary medical-evacuation limits apply.

regions.name: Christ Church Nichola Town
regions.merged_summary:
Christ Church Nichola Town is described in varying terms — as a small, largely rural parish on Nevis, and also as covering the tourism settlement of Frigate Bay or Basseterre, the capital and main tourist port, on Saint Kitts — but no parish-level legislation, enforcement practice, official posture or incident record specific to transgender visitors was identified, so the national regime governs: consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 court ruling, yet there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity, no legal gender recognition (identity documents cannot be altered locally, though visitors travel on home-issued documents), no recognition of same-sex unions, and no local statutory remedy — discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and hate speech remains lawful.

A transgender visitor who is outed or discovered faces no criminal charge and no documented trans-specific violence pattern, facility ban or campaign against trans visitors in the parish, but also no dependable recourse: LGBTQ+ organisations report that people avoid police, so an outed traveller may be refused service, questioned, mistreated or reported to authorities with social and bureaucratic friction rather than severe state punishment and no credible custodial risk. The parish's small population, conservative social climate and tourism base reduce anonymity, making a visibly trans visitor conspicuous and leaving disapproval likely to surface as gossip, curiosity or service refusal, and no local support organisation or documented local tolerance regime is recorded. Nevis's 2005 exclusion of a largely LGBTQ cruise party at the port — the federation's only documented entry-point exclusion, not recorded as occurring within this parish — remains on record, and nothing indicates that barrier has been formally withdrawn.

regions.name: Saint George Basseterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint George Basseterre is the capital parish of Saint Kitts and Nevis and its main air and sea gateway, containing the cruise terminal, most hotels and the country's government, expatriate community and visitor services. Its urban, tourist-facing economy means foreign visitors are routine and encounters are largely commercial and anonymous rather than village-based, and no trans-specific local statute, checkpoint rule, facility ban, document requirement, organised police targeting or documented incident against a trans visitor distinguishes the parish from the national picture; no region-specific evidence documents locally different enforcement, protections or attitudes. Local society remains conservative, and that urban familiarity does not amount to documented protection. The 2005 exclusion of an LGBTQ cruise ship occurred at Nevis's port, not in Basseterre, with no comparable local barring known, though it remains a dated signal of official attitudes rather than evidence of current practice here. National law, applying nationwide since the 2022 court decision, makes consensual adult same-sex conduct lawful and documents no trans-specific criminal offence, but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute covering gender identity, no spousal recognition, no legal gender recognition or local gender-marker procedure for visiting documents (trans visitors rely on home passports), and the National Gender Equality Policy is described as unimplemented. Discrimination in employment, accommodation and services is lawful with no local statutory remedy. LGBTQ people are documented as avoiding law enforcement, and police are an unreliable route after harassment or assault. Exposure through gendered facilities, border checks, custody placement or care denial is not documented, though that does not establish such encounters are safe. Conditional on discovery or being outing, a trans visitor could face harassment, service refusal, police indifference or discretionary scrutiny with no statutory recourse, while imprisonment for gender expression is not documented as routine and severe state-sponsored punishment is considered unlikely.

regions.name: Saint George Gingerland
regions.merged_summary: Saint George Gingerland is a small, mainly rural and agricultural parish made up of villages rather than resorts or nightlife, and nothing in the parish-specific record — no local ordinance, documented incident, protection, enforcement practice, or facility, custody, care or violence practice — distinguishes it from the wider national picture. It inherits the Saint Kitts and Nevis framework: consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since a 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court judgment, but there is no statute prohibiting discrimination or harassment on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, no hate-crime protection, and no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor travels on home-issued documents — the absence of a local gender-marker process is not itself a visitor-facing requirement — and has no local statutory remedy for service refusal, harassment or assault, while LGBTQ+ people are documented as avoiding police, which is not a reliable route to protection. At island level, Nevis displayed an exclusionary posture in 2005, when its port authority barred an LGBTQ cruise group and officials framed the decision culturally, stating that homosexuality is not part of local culture; this is a dated expression of official hostility rather than evidence of current trans-targeting, and it occurred elsewhere on Nevis rather than in Gingerland itself. Locally, the close-knit community, limited lodging and medical options, thinner services and police response than on Saint Kitts, and the visibility of outsiders reduce anonymity for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor, so discovery or being outing is likely to become widely known. For a trans visitor in that position, these conditions combine with the national gaps above: social disapproval, humiliation, social exclusion, refused service and denied practical access, with little reliable official protection. No criminal offence targeting trans presentation or organised violence campaign is documented, so the main exposure if discovered is social and practical rather than imprisonment.

regions.name: Saint James Windward
regions.merged_summary:
Saint James Windward is a small, rural parish on Nevis with a resort-and-estate tourism economy (Golden Rock, Pinney's Beach properties) alongside tight-knit village communities, so a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is quickly noticed, anonymity is limited and local gossip travels. It has no parish-level protective measures, local ordinances or hospitality-sector guarantees — resort staff civility is informal rather than enforceable — and no parish-specific trans-targeting, document checks, facility restrictions, or age-specific restrictions affecting travelling families are documented, nor is there parish-level data on enforcement, facilities or violence. Nevis carries the federation's only documented official exclusion gesture: a 2005 port refusal of an LGBTQ cruise ship announced publicly as a cultural decision, indicating a more conservative local posture than Saint Kitts, though it is dated and does not establish current routine targeting. No other region-specific information distinguishes the parish from the national picture.

Under the national regime, consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down the buggery and indecent-assault offences in 2022, and no trans-specific criminal offence is documented. However, there is no statute prohibiting discrimination, harassment or hate speech on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds, no hate-crime recourse, and no legal gender-recognition procedure, so a trans visitor travels on home-issued documents that cannot be altered locally. LGBTQ+ organisations report that people avoid law enforcement, and police are not a reliable route to protection. Where a trans visitor is outed or discovered, that absence of legal remedy combines with the close-knit social environment: social hostility, misgendering, service refusal or official friction may follow, with thin recourse — though no documented criminal penalty attaches to transgender status itself, and no local trans-specific protections or support infrastructure are known.

regions.name: Saint John Capisterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint John Capisterre, described variously as a small, rural, close-knit parish on northern Saint Kitts taking in Dieppe Bay, Saddler and St. Paul's with little tourist-facing LGBTQ infrastructure, and in one account as the capital on Saint Kitts, has no documented parish-level differences: no region-specific restrictions, protections, enforcement or organised anti-trans targeting are recorded, so the national framework governs. Consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling, but that ruling addressed privacy rather than trans status, and no trans-specific criminal offence or border exclusion exists. There is no legal gender recognition or local procedure to change a gender marker, so a visitor's home-issued documents cannot be altered locally, and no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment based on gender identity — discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and hate speech remains lawful, and there is no recognised same-sex partnership.

regions.name: Saint John Figtree
regions.merged_summary:
Saint John Figtree is a small, socially conservative and largely religious parish or community, and accounts differ on exactly where it sits: it is described both as a residential area on Saint Kitts just northwest of Basseterre and as a parish on Nevis around Charlestown. On either reading it inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 High Court decision, and no trans-specific criminal offence, entry ban, facility restriction or documented pattern of police targeting distinguishes it. However, there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute covering gender identity, so discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and hate speech remains lawful with no local remedy, and there is no legal gender-recognition procedure — though this is not itself a travel restriction, since a visitor simply uses home-issued documents. There is no local protective machinery. Nevis has a documented instance of official hostility: in 2005 its port authority excluded an LGBTQ cruise vessel and publicly described the decision as cultural, an incident some accounts note occurred on Nevis and do not attribute to a Saint Kitts parish; it is dated and does not establish current practice or trans-specific targeting. Against this, Nevis's tourism-dependent economy, including its port and resort districts, encourages informal hospitality and tolerance, and no recent local anti-trans enforcement, arrests or violence, and no documented pattern of trans-specific violence, is known. Accounts also differ on the local social climate relative to the capital, with the community described both as more conservative than the capital and as visitor-exposed and capital-adjacent.

In a parish of this size a visibly transgender visitor is unlikely to remain anonymous, and small-island visibility raises outing exposure. If identity becomes known, reported and plausible outcomes include gossip, misgendering, service refusal or friction, harassment, police indifference or avoidance of police by LGBTQ people for lack of remedy, and — in exceptional cases — border questioning or denial of admission, along with uncertain emergency standing for a partner; reliable recourse after harassment or assault is lacking because police are not a dependable route. Severe punishment is not documented, and no conditions are known to differ from the wider local social climate.

regions.name: Saint Mary Cayon
regions.merged_summary: Saint Mary Cayon is a small rural coastal parish on central Saint Kitts, outside the main tourist belt around Basseterre and Frigate Bay, and no local ordinance, policing practice, or documented social pattern distinguishes it from the national picture of Saint Kitts and Nevis. As a small, less visitor-facing community with limited resort infrastructure, it is likely more socially conservative than the urban tourist areas, and small-community visibility can raise the chance of being read as an outsider, though no local pattern of targeting is documented and ordinary friction rather than organised targeting is the realistic exposure; no parish-specific anti-trans law, campaign, or protective exception is known. National entry-point hostility has been recorded historically in the 2005 refusal of a cruise vessel carrying LGBTQ passengers at Nevis, a different island, alongside official statements of cultural resistance, indicating limited public acceptance, while no documented record of violence against transgender visitors exists either way. Consensual adult sexual conduct has been lawful since the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court's 2022 ruling struck down the buggery and indecent-assault offences, so there is no criminal statute to leverage against a trans visitor and no trans-specific offence or documented programme of police targeting.\n\nBecause legal gender recognition is unavailable, visitors travel on home-issued documents that cannot be changed locally, and the penal code offers no protection against discrimination or harassment based on gender identity: discrimination in employment, education and accommodation and hate speech remain lawful, same-sex partners receive no spousal recognition, the state has taken no tangible steps under its gender equality policy, and no local statutory remedy exists if a visitor is refused service or harassed. LGBTQ+ people are reported to avoid law enforcement, so police remain an unreliable route of protection after harassment or assault, leaving no realistic local redress. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, outcomes depend heavily on individual officials: informal scrutiny, discomfort, discriminatory treatment, and moderate inconvenience with denial of recourse are more credible than detention or violence.

regions.name: Saint Paul Capisterre
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Paul Capisterre is a small, rural parish on Saint Kitts' northern coast, close to Basseterre and the island's main port, airport and tourist services, with a tight-knit, church-going population and little tourist traffic. It has no local laws, border practices, facility rules, police guidance, or documented incidents that distinguish it from the national picture, and no LGBTQ-specific venues, support services, or advocacy groups. A visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to be highly visible and read as an outsider, with word travelling quickly in a community of this size and discretion and anonymity much harder to maintain than in Basseterre or the tourist belt; discovery through visible nonconformity or a document check is plausible, and the expected outcome is social or bureaucratic friction rather than dedicated enforcement or documented organised hostility, though the absence of local evidence reflects uncertainty rather than safety, and no region-specific information addresses how mismatched documents, facilities, healthcare access, or violence would affect a trans visitor here.

The national framework applies in full: consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court decision, there is no trans-specific criminal offence, facility ban, or documented police targeting of visitors, and identity documents are those issued at home. However, there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity, no legal gender recognition (so foreign-issued documents cannot be altered locally), discrimination in employment, education, accommodation, services and hate speech remains lawful, and there is no local statutory remedy for discrimination. LGBTQ people are widely reported to avoid law enforcement and policing in the parish is thin, so recourse after harassment or assault is unreliable. The 2005 cruise-ship exclusion was a Nevis decision rather than a Saint Kitts one, announced as a cultural choice; it is dated and does not establish a pattern in this parish, but it reflects past official hostility and cultural wariness at entry points.

regions.name: Saint Paul Charlestown
regions.merged_summary: Saint Paul Charlestown is a small, close-knit parish containing the port town of Charlestown, capital of Nevis, where a tourism-dependent economy of resorts and visiting yachts sits alongside conservative social norms and limited medical and support services distant from St Kitts-based organisations. The town inherits Saint Kitts and Nevis's national framework: consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since a 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling, there is no trans-specific criminal offence, and a visitor simply uses home-country documents — but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute covering gender identity, no recognised same-sex partnership, and no procedure for legal gender recognition, so documents cannot be altered locally. No trans-specific local protections, protective infrastructure or tourist-tolerance exceptions are documented here, and Nevis officials and the national government have disclaimed any mandate to reform the law. The clearest local signal is the 2005 Charlestown port incident, in which police halted and turned away an LGBTQ cruise ship and officials described the exclusion as a cultural decision or said homosexuality was not welcome in local culture; this is a dated event that does not establish present frequency, and no later local reversal is recorded. Also documented nationally are LGBTQ people's avoidance of law enforcement, which limits recourse. There is no documented local record of trans-specific violence, police extortion of gender-nonconforming visitors, or border or facility restrictions, and no current trans-specific targeting is recorded. For an outed or discovered trans visitor, the tourism economy and pragmatic commercial encounters may moderate everyday exposure, but small-town visibility means the encounter would be highly visible, with bureaucratic or service friction, discomfort in a close-knit community, and no statutory remedy if service is refused or harassment occurs — modest everyday friction, with no credible custodial or lethal exposure documented.

regions.name: Saint Peter Basseterre
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Peter Basseterre is the parish containing Basseterre, Saint Kitts and Nevis's national capital, principal cruise port and the Robert L. Bradshaw International Airport, along with the city's eastern suburbs and the Frigate Bay resort belt, so document checks, immigration questioning and port discretion are more concentrated here than in rural parishes. Its urban, tourism-dependent and cosmopolitan cruise traffic makes it more anonymous and accustomed to foreign visitors, and resort staff and other guests are generally attentive to service norms, suggesting somewhat easier everyday social friction than rural areas; the inland villages around St. Peter's, by contrast, are small, church-centred and socially conservative. No local ordinance, facility rule, exclusion pattern or practice specifically protecting or harming trans visitors is documented, and visitor document treatment and other local practices remain uncertain.

The inherited national framework governs: consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling, and no trans-specific criminal offence, facility ban or documented police targeting of visitors is known, but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity, discrimination in work, housing and services remains lawful, no legal gender recognition exists so visitors rely on home-issued passports, and there is no statutory remedy for harassment or service refusal. LGBTQ organisations report that people avoid law enforcement, so police are an unreliable protection route, and LGBTQ groups may register but told the 2025 Universal Periodic Review that this avoidance persists. A documented 2005 refusal of entry to an LGBTQ cruise ship signals official hostility at ports of entry, though it was a Nevis port decision rather than Basseterre's, predates the decriminalisation ruling, is dated and is not specific to trans visitors. If a trans visitor is discovered or outed, humiliation, service denial and administrative delay or refusal are possible, with custody and privacy risks and no dependable remedy; no trans-specific violence, organised local hostility or pattern of custodial violence against trans people is documented.

regions.name: Saint Thomas Lowland
regions.merged_summary: Saint Thomas Lowland is a small, rural, low-density parish in a small, churchgoing, socially conservative island society of roughly twelve thousand people (most descriptions place it on Nevis, one on Saint Kitts), so a visibly trans visitor who is outed faces high visibility, limited privacy and near-certain community awareness. Nevis carries a specific recorded marker at its entry point: in 2005 port officials publicly turned away an LGBTQ cruise ship, citing cultural concerns — the clearest documented instance nationally of exclusion aimed at travellers, signalling official-level disapproval but not establishing current or routine targeting of trans visitors. The parish's upscale resort economy, serving international guests, offers comparatively neutral private settings and generally works in a visitor's favour; there is no evidence of organised targeting or custodial risk, no parish-specific border, facility, custody, care or violence practice is documented, and no local protective machinery for visitors was identified. The inherited national regime applies: consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 Jeffers judgment and no trans-specific criminal offence reaches a visitor's presentation or conduct, but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity (discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and speech remains lawful), no legal gender recognition or local gender-marker change, no same-sex partner or union recognition, and no facility or custody protections. LGBTQ people are documented to avoid law enforcement, which is not a reliable source of protection, so there is no statutory remedy for service, employment or accommodation discrimination and no reliable official recourse after harassment or assault: foreseeable harms for an outed visitor are refusals of lodging or service, questioning during entry or port arrangements, misgendering and weak official follow-up, rather than prosecution for identity or presentation. Visitors travel on home-issued documents that cannot be altered locally, and how officials would handle a document mismatch, along with local enforcement practice, is not well documented, so outcomes may vary by host and authority.

regions.name: Saint Thomas Middle Island
regions.merged_summary:
Saint Thomas Middle Island is a small, rural, semi-rural parish on the west coast of Saint Kitts — generally placed around Middle Island village, Sandy Point and Half Way Tree, and the Romney Manor/Caribelle Batik visitor sites — though one account places the parish on Nevis, where authorities have previously shown hostility at the point of entry. No parish-level legislation, institution, enforcement practice, incident record, facility or custody policy, visitor document check, or protective measure distinguishes it from the national framework: consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court (Jeffers) decision struck the relevant Offences Against the Person Act provisions, LGBTQ+ organisations may register, and same-sex unions are not recognised. There is no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment on grounds of gender identity — including in employment, education or accommodation — no hate-crime provision, no legal gender recognition or procedure to change gender markers on locally issued documents (so visitors rely on home documents), and no statutory remedy for a visitor refused service, harassed or assaulted. No local transgender-specific targeting or official hostility is documented, and those gaps do not establish safety.

If discovered or outed, the practical local difference is heightened social visibility: small, tight-knit and churchgoing communities offer little anonymity for a visibly transgender visitor, the parish is not a tourism hub with the hospitality-sector familiarity that brings, and police and social services are thinner than in Basseterre, with everyday access depending on informal discretion at guesthouses and bars. Against the national record — which includes documented avoidance of law enforcement by LGBTQ people, making police an unreliable route to protection, and a past exclusion of an LGBTQ-heavy cruise ship at a Nevis port, an old and distinct incident on a different island rather than a documented local event — this combines into greater exposure to questioning, service denial and harassment with weak redress, while no documented campaign of imprisonment or lethal violence against transgender visitors exists in the parish.

regions.name: Trinity Palmetto Point
regions.merged_summary:
Trinity Palmetto Point, on Saint Kitts, has no documented local exception to the national regime: no parish-specific criminalisation or organised targeting of transgender visitors is recorded, and there is no local protective machinery, trans-specific service, or advocacy presence. The parish pairs visitor-facing resort and yachting developments on the southeastern peninsula and residential enclaves west of Basseterre with a small, close-knit rural character and little anonymous tourist infrastructure, so a visitor's status is likely to circulate through local social networks. That tourism presence may shape service interactions, but no evidence of greater acceptance and no local facility, border, custody, or care rule affecting trans visitors is documented, and nothing otherwise distinguishes the parish from the national picture.

Nationally, consensual adult same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruling, and no trans-specific criminal penalty or documented imprisonment pathway is known — but no statute protects gender identity, so discrimination and hate speech in employment, accommodation, and services remain lawful with no local statutory remedy; legal gender recognition is unavailable, so home-issued documents cannot be altered locally, and spousal or next-of-kin status may go unrecognised. LGBTQ+ organisations may register, yet the Gender Equality Policy has produced no tangible steps, and LGBTQ+ people are reported to avoid law enforcement, which civil-society submissions describe as an unreliable route if a visitor is harassed or assaulted; cultural exclusion and earlier stated official reluctance to reform, together with the 2005 refusal of an LGBTQ cruise ship at a Nevis port (outside this region), signal an ambivalent official posture. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered in the parish, this means social disapproval, possible denial of service or harassment, and no effective legal remedy, rather than a known risk of criminal punishment.

regions.name: Bokeo
regions.merged_summary: Bokeo is Laos's far-northern border province, centred on Huay Xai — the main border crossing into Thailand — and the river-trade and Golden Triangle special economic zone, with a tourism- and border-driven economy, casino-town security, and rural ethnic-minority communities. The national regime carries over: consensual same-sex conduct and transgender status are not criminalised, but there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity, official tolerance is conditional and is withdrawn where presentation is seen as indecent, disorderly or attention-seeking, media discussion is rare, and trans visibility is largely confined to entertainment, with societal discrimination prevalent and advocacy limited. Locally, social conservatism is stronger and there is no LGBTI advocacy or specialist recourse; no region-specific documentation of trans-targeted enforcement, arrest, custody, facility rules or lethal violence was found. Border and special-economic-zone policing is more opaque, discretionary and informal than in much of the country, with checkpoint scrutiny and casino-town security practices, though everyday enforcement in tourist-facing areas is also described as looser than in the capital, which may reduce routine scrutiny of visitors. A trans visitor who is outed would mainly face curiosity, gossip, social stigma, possible refusal of lodging or service, intrusive document questions, and opportunistic official shakedowns such as fines or bribery demands, plus possible eviction and police or official disapproval, but not prosecution under a sexuality or gender-based law; detention risk arises mainly if an encounter is linked to visa or nuisance allegations, recourse is uncertain, and arbitrary enforcement in border and tourist settings can make outcomes more severe than the national baseline.

regions.name: Champasak
regions.merged_summary: Champasak is a largely rural, socially conservative southern province centred on Pakse, taking in Mekong and border tourism, the Wat Phou temple complex and the Si Phan Don islands; these tourist-facing settings draw modest but regular foreign visitors and hospitality staff accustomed to outsiders, which eases everyday friction. The province inherits Laos's national position: consensual same-sex conduct and gender expression are not criminalised, no law specifically targets transgender visitors, and there is no documented local pattern of police targeting, facility exclusion or document-based detention. Offsetting this, there is no anti-discrimination, gender-recognition or hate-crime protection and no complaint mechanism reaching visitors, while distance from the capital and its diplomatic visibility or support networks leaves the province with weaker civil-society and institutional infrastructure and thinner recourse. Guesthouse passport copying and provincial officialdom are the main points of friction, and hospitals and shared lodging may fall back on observed sex; treatment of foreign documents, facilities, custody, healthcare and travelling minors is undocumented rather than protective.\n\nState practice tolerates gender-diverse people unless they campaign publicly, are politically vocal or are judged immodest, and officials may act against perceived public indecency; media discussion of trans people is rare, LGBTI-themed online content has been restricted, and organised advocacy is minimal, alongside documented societal discrimination. If discovered or outed, a trans visitor in Champasak is more likely to meet curiosity or awkwardness than organised hostility — expect misgendering, intrusive questioning and uneven hotel or clinic responses, with consequences tending toward social embarrassment, service disruption or discretionary public-order pressure rather than severe legal punishment. Internet and media restrictions suppress open discussion, so quiet-society expectations apply and there is no trans-specific advocacy or visitor-facing remedy locally.

regions.name: Aakkâr
regions.merged_summary:
Akkâr, Lebanon's northernmost and among its poorest, most rural governorates, is a predominantly Sunni, agricultural border district with weak services, a heavy security presence and frequent checks along the Syrian frontier, refugee camps including Nahr al-Bared and Beddawi, and weak, uneven state policing. It has none of the LGBT civil-society infrastructure found in Beirut — organisations such as Helem and Legal Agenda, the court rulings that have declined to apply the same-sex-conduct provision or frozen anti-assembly orders, and the local advocacy and legal-aid services on which an outed visitor might otherwise rely — while the conservative social climate, clan and family authority and tight kinship and neighbourhood networks mean a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor would draw immediate attention, with information spreading quickly through those networks and recourse correspondingly more distant than in the capital.

The national regime governs: Penal Code Article 521 exposes feminine presentation to imprisonment of up to six years, Article 534 remains on the books despite appellate reluctance to apply it, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and arrests, police raids, prosecutor-ordered anal examinations and other intrusive checks, harassment and prejudice are documented — with foreign documents providing no protection, including at checkpoints or in villages where identity documents may not match presentation. In this setting an outed visitor would face police handling shaped by conservative local mores rather than Beirut's more contested climate, plausibly including detention under those provisions, compounded by informal sanction through family and community pressure, and with enforcement likely uneven and dependent on local officials. There is no known local pattern of trans-directed arrests or violence and no documented local tolerance, but incidents here are sparsely recorded, and the absence of such evidence does not indicate safety; no region-specific mitigation is known.

regions.name: Baalbek-Hermel
regions.merged_summary:
Baalbek-Hermel inherits Lebanon's national framework: Penal Code Article 521 exposes trans feminine presentation to up to six years' imprisonment for men disguising themselves as women, Article 534 remains on the books even as courts have declined to apply it to consensual conduct, and no legal gender recognition is available, leaving document mismatch a persistent outing risk. Nationally, police have arrested and prosecuted LGBT people, including documented anal examinations, and security forces have restricted LGBT assembly, with a documented 2023 crackdown on LGBT cultural events.

Locally the region is markedly more conservative than Beirut — a largely rural, clan-structured, Shia-majority area of the Bekaa Valley where tribal and honour norms are strong and Hezbollah, alongside Amal and informal security actors, exercises dominant influence over security, everyday norms and moral authority. There are no LGBT venues, organisations, legal clinics, activist networks or tolerant tourist-facing scene of the kind found in the capital, and Beirut's reformist jurisprudence and anonymity are largely absent; a visibly gender-nonconforming stranger is conspicuous, and public discretion is harder to rely on. Security forces have enforced assembly bans there as elsewhere, and religious-police-style morality enforcement is considered plausible. If a visitor is discovered or outed, discovery is likely to reach family or clan actors as well as police, with formal recourse, NGO support, police protection, access to lawyers, courts or consular help all scarce and little expectation of impartial remedy; family, tribal or moral policing can escalate to detention, extortion, expulsion or violence, leaving consequences below the national baseline. Ordinary tourism may reduce daily visibility but does not lower the consequences once discovered. No region-specific documented cases of trans enforcement, no local protective measures, and no effective visitor-facing remedy are documented, so local enforcement intensity remains uncertain and the reading rests on the national provisions combined with the region's social character.

regions.name: Beyrouth
regions.merged_summary:
Beyrouth inherits Lebanon's national legal regime with no local exemption: Article 521 criminalises men disguising themselves as women with penalties up to six years, and Article 534's morality provision remains in force despite repeated Beirut court rulings declining to apply it to consensual conduct and other favourable rulings; these statutes have brought arrests and prosecutions, with trans women most exposed, alongside documented raids on LGBT gatherings, prosecutor-ordered intrusive anal examinations, intrusive identity checks, extortion and mistreatment by police or security forces, particularly at checkpoints, in nightlife raids and during public moral panics. Legal gender recognition is unavailable through the civil registry, so identity documents — including foreign-issued ones — may not match a visitor's appearance, and state economic and institutional collapse leaves recourse thin. Security forces have actively restricted LGBT assembly, including the 2012 cinema raid, the 2018 shutdown and pressure to cancel Beirut Pride involving the arrest of an LGBT rights activist, and the 2022 interior ministry order against gatherings that the Shura Council later froze — relief that has not removed the criminal provisions or guaranteed equal treatment. Travelling families with a child face added scrutiny through guardianship, schools and neighbourhood reaction, and no Beirut-specific exemption from national law exists.

Locally, Beirut is Lebanon's most cosmopolitan, tourism-oriented city and its most visible queer hub, hosting most of the country's LGBT venues and community infrastructure including Helem, Legal Agenda and NGO legal support; its tourist and university districts afford more anonymity than rural areas, and a degree of social familiarity with gender diversity exceeds the rest of the country, reducing everyday scrutiny in some neighbourhoods. However, the capital's visibility concentrates policing and national crackdowns where the scene exists, and documented prejudice and violence against trans and queer people in Beirut itself has risen since 2022. Local tolerance is uneven and dependent on district and authority, so consequences remain serious if an officer, landlord, club or hostile group identifies a traveller as transgender: the state regime follows the visitor at full strength, and local tolerance lowers everyday social friction but does not soften custody, prosecution or police exposure conditional on discovery.

regions.name: Béqaa
regions.merged_summary:
Béqaa operates under Lebanon's national regime: Penal Code Article 521 criminalises men disguising themselves as women (trans-feminine presentation) with up to six years' imprisonment; Article 534 on intercourse contrary to nature remains on the books, though courts have declined to apply it to consensual conduct since 2023; legal gender recognition is unavailable; and police have documented arrests, raids on LGBT venues, intrusive (including forced anal) examinations, attempts to ban LGBT gatherings, and policing and documentation barriers affecting trans people. No regional exception to these laws or documented local protection exists, and no distinct local policy or pattern of enforcement against trans visitors has been established — but thinner NGO documentation and public visibility in the valley mean the record is incomplete, so an absence of reported incidents, including no region-specific evidence of lethal violence or execution, should not be read as safety.

Compared with Beirut, Béqaa is a predominantly rural, partly town-based governorate (including Baalbek-Hermel, Zahle and Rashaya) with socially conservative communities, strong clan, family and tribal or feudal networks, heavy Hezbollah and conservative religious-party influence alongside Amal, a large Syrian refugee population, and frequent informal checkpoints operated by Hezbollah or the army. State authority is weaker in outlying districts, with poorer police professionalism and complaint handling; trans community, activist, legal-clinic and secular institutional recourse are far thinner, with limited access to Beirut-based support such as Helem or Legal Agenda, and there is little anonymity for a visibly trans foreigner. Zahle is more mixed and Zahle and parts of Baalbek have tourism economies offering some ordinary urban commerce and a degree of anonymity, though hospitality-sector and religious authorities there remain socially conservative. A transgender visitor who is outed therefore faces family and community sanction — with family or honour-based danger a particular concern — public hostility, and possible detention, extortion or communal retaliation, while police recourse is thin to nonexistent and protection after harassment or detention is limited.

regions.name: Keserwan-Jbeil
regions.merged_summary: Keserwan-Jbeil, the predominantly Maronite Christian governorate north of Beirut taking in Jounieh and Byblos, operates entirely under Lebanon's national regime: Penal Code Article 521 penalises men disguising as women with up to six years' imprisonment and reaches trans feminine presentation, while the Article 534 morality provision on intercourse contrary to the order of nature remains on the statute book despite appellate rulings declining to apply it to consensual conduct. Arrests and prosecutions have occurred, prosecutors have ordered invasive examinations, and documented police raids, detention and abuse, executive restrictions on LGBT gatherings, and the absence of legal gender recognition all persist; a visitor's foreign documents do not remove this criminal and policing exposure, and detention reverts to birth-sex custody practice. Security forces, courts and the civil registry act under national authority, and no local protective exception, sanctuary practice or region-specific enforcement pattern is documented.\n\nLocally the governorate is more socially conservative than Beirut's concentrated LGBT venues and support organisations: strong Church and family networks, smaller communities and tight village social structures reduce anonymity, so discovery or outing can quickly become community or family pressure, with escalating prejudice and thin recourse, and there is no queer infrastructure or advocacy presence to offset it. Church-linked institutions enforce this conservatism through custom rather than militia or morality-police patrols, and there is no documented local anti-LGBT campaign, region-specific pattern of trans-targeted raids, detentions or dating-app entrapment. At the same time, the Jounieh nightlife strip, Harissa and the Byblos tourism trade give the coast a large hospitality economy accustomed to foreign visitors, with no Beirut-style policing of queer venues, though that offers no specific trans-traveller safeguards. Exposure still runs through document checks and hotel registration and the national criminal provisions, and immediate access to legal aid and community networks is limited outside the capital; local data is thin.

regions.name: Liban-Nord
regions.merged_summary:
Liban-Nord operates entirely under Lebanon's national legal framework, which retains provisions reaching transgender presentation: Penal Code Article 521 penalises men disguising themselves as women with up to six years' imprisonment, and Article 534 covers intercourse contrary to the order of nature — it remains on the books despite court rulings declining to apply it to consensual conduct, with arrests, prosecutions, raids and intrusive examinations (including anal examinations ordered by prosecutors) documented, along with dating-app entrapment-style policing as a known national pattern. No legal gender recognition is available, so a visitor's foreign documents govern encounters and cannot be reconciled locally, and police or document checks create outing risks. Public assembly restrictions apply nationwide, and there is no region-specific protective machinery, local ordinance, or enforcement exemption; recourse runs through the thin national judiciary, and no separate local rule for visiting families or minors is documented.

Locally, the north — especially Tripoli, the smaller towns and the rural Akkar interior — is markedly more socially and religiously conservative than Beirut, with documented Salafist influence, a more sectarian and close-knit social fabric, and less tolerance of visible gender nonconformity. Visible LGBTQ support networks, trans-specific advocacy, and legal-aid presence are far thinner than Beirut's, police protection for a visibly transgender visitor is less reliable, and the rule-of-law environment is weaker amid a severe economic crisis; this means discovery can spread quickly through family and community networks, with fewer confidential remedies, and raises the likelihood of confrontation, refusal of service, harassment or extortion, hostile social reaction, and informal pressure, leaving few effective remedies if detained or assaulted. The Batroun and coastal tourist belt is more relaxed and familiar with foreign visitors, and coastal Christian towns may allow more discretion, though no documented local tolerance or protective practice offsets the national exposure. Region-specific trans-targeting or enforcement patterns are not documented; the region's conditions combine the national criminal exposure with a harsher communal climate and weaker local support.

regions.name: Mont-Liban
regions.merged_summary:
Mont-Liban falls entirely under Lebanon's national legal regime: Penal Code Article 521 criminalises men presenting as women with imprisonment of up to six years, Article 534 remains on the books despite successive court rulings declining to apply it to consensual conduct, legal gender recognition is unavailable apart from one documented 2015 court approval of a gender-marker change, and identity documents are governed by the civil registry. Documented national practices include police raids, arrests of LGBT people, intrusive examinations and medicalised verification, poor accountability for abuse, restricted public assembly — including a 2022 assembly-ban episode that affected this metropolitan area directly — and a recorded rise in prejudice. There is no region-specific difference in police powers, statutes or custody practice: security forces operate under national Interior Ministry authority, and no local rule suspends the penal articles or offers traveller-facing protections.

Locally the governorate is mixed. Its Beirut-adjacent inner suburbs and coastal and mountain tourism centres — including Byblos, Jounieh, Faraya and Aley — have the country's highest trans and queer visibility, a comparatively tolerant nightlife and hospitality sector, activist organisations such as Helem and Legal Agenda, and proximity to Beirut's civil-society support, giving a foreign traveller somewhat more everyday privacy and lower street-level friction than in rural governorates. Beyond those areas the governorate includes strongly conservative Christian, Maronite, Druze, Shia and mixed districts with heavier clerical and family influence, less queer visibility, fewer support and legal-aid services, and greater likelihood of local hostility to gender-nonconforming presentation; local enforcement may depend more on discretion or community complaints, and community support remains concentrated in Beirut. For a visitor who is outed or discovered, exposure is driven by the nationally enforced statutes rather than local tolerance: police stops, hotel or landlord identity checks, or complaints from family, neighbours, employers or clergy can lead to refusal of service, interrogation, possible brief detention, a morality charge or arrest and prosecution, with the region's stronger community networks and more discreet urban norms easing everyday conditions somewhat but providing no exemption from the underlying legal consequences, and recourse being thin.

regions.name: Bomi
regions.merged_summary:
Bomi is a largely rural western county centred on its capital, Tubmanburg, built around mining and farming, with deep social conservatism, strong traditional and religious norms, and far weaker institutional and advocacy presence than Monrovia. No Bomi-specific legal exception, trans-targeting practice, operative protection, hate-crime recourse or local tolerance is documented: the county inherits Liberia's national regime, in which consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under a sodomy offence carrying up to one year's imprisonment and applying to women as well as men, same-sex marriage is not recognised, enforcement is uncommon but arrests of LGBTQ people have occurred after attackers invoked their status, and criminalisation deters victims from reporting attacks to police. Public concealment is the documented norm, with LGBTQ life confined largely to private, advocacy-supported spaces concentrated in Monrovia (where groups such as SAIL and TNOL operate) and not documented in Bomi, and no gender-affirming hormone therapy or surgery is available anywhere in the country. Repeated legislative attempts to impose harsher penalties have not become law. The Decent Work Act (2015) bars employment discrimination on grounds including gender identity, though that offers little to a short-stay visitor.

For a transgender visitor, being outed does not mean trans identity itself is criminalised, but exposure in Bomi runs through tightly knit communities with little anonymity, where a visibly trans person is a rarity and social scrutiny is high, with police, landlords, clinics and community authorities the likely points of discovery. Police and judicial capacity is thinner outside the capital, with less capacity for investigation, remedy or safe custody placement and none of the sparse urban infrastructure that partially buffers queer people elsewhere, so harassment, blackmail and denunciation to family or employers are plausible, while detention or service denial are the realistic consequences rather than severe violence; the sodomy statute remains a lever attackers can invoke, and fear of police discourages reporting, leaving little effective recourse. Some accounts place outcomes here somewhat below the wider national picture because of the rural density of scrutiny and thin rule-of-law protections rather than any documented local enforcement practice, while others note that no county-level information distinguishes it from Liberia overall. No organised county-level campaign of violence against visitors is documented, and enforcement remains sporadic rather than systematic.

regions.name: Gbarpolu
regions.merged_summary:
Gbarpolu is a remote, forested and sparsely populated rural county in northwestern Liberia centred on its capital Bopolu, with a subsistence and small-scale mining economy, limited road access and tourism, weak public services, and strong reliance on customary authorities and community institutions. There is no documented local ordinance, protection, tourist tolerance, trans or LGBTQ organisation, safe venue, or incident record distinguishing it from Liberia's national picture, and local reporting is scarce. The national regime applies: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised, with the sodomy offence carrying up to one year's imprisonment and applying to women as well as men, active legislative pressure seeks harsher penalties, and there is no legal recognition of same-sex marriage, no legal gender recognition, and no domestic access to gender-affirming hormone therapy or surgery. The law does not specifically criminalise trans identity, and while the Decent Work Act (2015) bars employment discrimination on gender identity, that provision is not a documented visitor-facing remedy. Public concealment is the documented norm among LGBTQ Liberians, arrests involving LGBTQ people are uncommon but documented, and victims may avoid police; everyday enforcement of national law appears less systematic in the county than in the capital, though no lighter local enforcement offsets the national regime.

For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine as follows: the small communities and limited anonymity make a visibly trans visitor highly conspicuous, drawing intense local curiosity, conservative religious and customary disapproval, social hostility, misrecognition, service refusal, or community pressure rather than institutional accommodation. Police and judicial presence is very thin and courts are distant, and custody would likely place a trans woman with birth-sex males, with possible detention under the sodomy or public-order laws and little practical recourse. Advocacy-run safe spaces and networks concentrated in Monrovia are less likely to be reachable, and the risk of arrest under morality provisions deters reporting of victimisation. No Gbarpolu-specific evidence establishes trans-targeted enforcement, border or facility restrictions, custody practices, or local protective measures; these factors are undocumented rather than evidence of safety.

regions.name: Grand Bassa
regions.merged_summary:
Grand Bassa is a rural, tightly knit coastal county centred on its county seat and port, Buchanan, and it operates under Liberia's national framework with no documented local tolerance, targeted enforcement, exception, or protective measure that sets it apart. Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to one year's imprisonment, enforcement is uncommon but gives police a discretionary lever, and there are active legislative proposals for harsher anti-LGBTQ penalties. LGBTQ people are documented as commonly concealing their status, victims are deterred from reporting crimes, and police have been documented arresting LGBTQ people after attackers invoked their sexuality or gender identity. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically, and the Decent Work Act's protection of employment regardless of gender identity stands as the only statutory counterweight, offering limited practical protection for a short-term visitor. Advocacy organisations and private affirming spaces, including SAIL and TNOL, are concentrated in Monrovia, leaving the county with thinner institutional and community support, conservative religious norms, uneven local policing, and fewer local avenues for discreet support or rapid intervention.

For a transgender visitor in Grand Bassa, discovery or being outed can bring community scrutiny, hostile reaction, police questioning, extortion or short detention, and no reliable local medical or institutional recourse, with the sodomy provision increasing exposure even though it is not a trans-specific offence. Society's conservatism and the county's weak rule-of-law institutions make outing more hazardous than in the capital, though a foreign visitor may be treated as an oddity rather than the target of a campaign, and the resulting exposure is harassment, possible arrest, and absent recourse rather than custodial violence or lethal penalty. For a trans minor travelling with a parent, these same gaps raise the possibility of school or community outing, interrupted continuity of care, and family pressure.

regions.name: Grand Cape Mount
regions.merged_summary:
Grand Cape Mount is a sparsely populated, largely rural coastal county in Liberia's far west, centred on Robertsport and Lake Piso, where fishing and subsistence farming dominate and institutional density is very low: police posts are few and distant, courts sit intermittently, and the county has no LGBTQ or transgender organisation, shelter or clinic. Monrovia's advocacy groups, legal aid and informal private-space networks are a costly journey away. Close-knit fishing and cross-border communities, strong church and mosque authority and traditional society influence mean a foreign visitor is conspicuous in small towns, so once a person is discovered as trans it is hard to control who learns; border proximity adds routine document checks, with no evidence they treat foreign trans documents differently. Limited surfing tourism at Robertsport brings some familiarity with foreigners, and tourist beach areas may offer some everyday anonymity, but neither creates institutional protection, and the absence of documented incidents is not evidence of safety. No trans-specific local statute, official protection, accommodation standard, tolerance exception or documented local hostility has been identified for the county, so there is no basis to infer either stronger local protection or harsher local enforcement than nationally; enforcement here appears more likely to depend on informal reporting and police discretion than on systematic targeting.

The national regime therefore applies unchanged: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminalised with imprisonment for up to one year, an offence seldom enforced but one that deters victims from reporting crimes, and there are documented arrests of LGBTQ people, sometimes after attackers invoke their identity, alongside repeatedly proposed anti-LGBTQ bills and active legislative pressure to expand penalties. Public concealment of LGBTQ identity is the documented norm, and fear of police discourages people from seeking help, so a trans visitor who is outed or discovered faces the possibility of arrest once sexuality or gender identity surfaces, limited control over who learns, and weak formal recourse. Gender-affirming care is unavailable domestically (local availability is not established), and no facility or document process accommodates a mismatched marker, so a visitor's transition status may become visible through documents, medication or disclosure with limited recourse. The gender-identity employment protection in the Decent Work Act (2015) does not reach a short-term visitor's everyday exposure, and the local tourism environment offers no trans-specific protection.

regions.name: Grand Kru
regions.merged_summary:
Grand Kru County, a remote, predominantly rural county in southeastern Liberia with small, close-knit communities and little anonymity, inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under a sodomy offence carrying up to one year's imprisonment and applying to women as well as men, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and anti-LGBTQ bills have recurred in the National Assembly pressing for harsher penalties. Enforcement is documented as uncommon, yet the law deters LGBTQ crime victims from reporting to police, and LGBTQ people have been arrested after attackers invoked their status. Public concealment is the documented norm, with private and NGO-sponsored support spaces existing nationally but operating chiefly in Monrovia and largely absent here; gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically. The Decent Work Act's non-discrimination clause covering sex, gender identity and sexual orientation applies to employment, not to visitor exposure. Local conditions make discovery more consequential than in the capital: police presence and institutional recourse are weak, police, medical and legal services are thin and distant, customary Poro and Sande authority structures shape public order, and longstanding social conservatism brings close community scrutiny. No Grand Kru-specific arrests, border practices, facility restrictions, violence patterns, protective measures, sanctuary practice or documented local hostility have been recorded, and the absence of such documentation should not be taken as proof of safety.

A transgender visitor who is outed inherits the criminal sodomy framework, the strong concealment norm and no access to gender-affirming care, with no known trans-specific advocacy, health or safe-venue infrastructure and limited consular, legal or medical support to fall back on. Recourse after harassment, extortion or violence is uncertain, and reporting may itself draw attention; possible consequences include community moral enforcement, detention under morality or public-order pretexts, extortion, denial of services or informal expulsion, with little reliable protection or continuity of care.

regions.name: Lofa
regions.merged_summary: Lofa County in northern Liberia, a largely rural and comparatively remote border region with small towns, limited tourism and few signs of LGBTQ community infrastructure or private supportive spaces compared with Monrovia, inherits the national legal framework: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under a sodomy offence that applies to women as well as men, enforcement is uncommon though arrests have followed attackers invoking LGBTQ status or gender identity, anti-LGBTQ bills have recurred in the national legislature, same-sex marriage is unrecognised, and gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically. LGBTQ Liberians commonly conceal their identities in public, and reporting of crimes against them is deterred. The 2015 Decent Work Act bars employment discrimination based on gender identity, but this resident-facing protection does not reach everyday safety and has uncertain reach. No documented Lofa-specific incidents, enforcement records, hostile local ordinances, protections, or tolerance signals are known, and organised state targeting is not indicated; chiefdom-level authority provides no documented recourse. Conservative Christian and Muslim community norms, indigenous and traditional authority, small settlements, weak police and justice capacity, and the absence of trans-specific support or safe venues outside Monrovia mean a visibly transgender visitor has little anonymity and may be outed within tight local networks, facing stigma, community exposure, extortion, or morality/sodomy-related charges with thin practical recourse if police or courts become involved — a somewhat harsher environment than the national average, though low visitor traffic limits outing frequency and there is no evidence of targeting beyond the inherited national pattern.

regions.name: Maryland
regions.merged_summary:
Maryland County, in rural and remote southeastern Liberia around Harper, is governed by the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised, carrying up to one year's imprisonment and applying to women as well as men, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no statute targeting transgender presentation as such is known. Enforcement is uncommon but documented, and the law has been used to arrest LGBTQ people after attacks while deterring victims from reporting crimes; anti-LGBTQ bills have recurred in the national legislature, some proposing deeper penalties. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically, and public concealment is the documented national norm. Some LGBTQ private spaces and advocacy exist nationally — notably SAIL and TNOL — but both are capital-based and neither operates in the county, where no distinct local protective law or documented tolerance exception is known and no hostility beyond the inherited national picture is documented. The Decent Work Act's employment non-discrimination clause applies nationwide, though no traveler-facing protection is documented for Maryland.

Locally, tight-knit and highly religious communities, customary norms, limited tourism and visitor infrastructure, sparse formal policing and legal services, thin health, legal-aid and transport options, and little anonymous private space combine with distance from Monrovia's advocacy and medical services to make recourse, care continuity and official help harder to obtain; local enforcement, facilities and support access are not documented, which is not evidence of safety. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, these conditions mean that community exposure and hostile attention, questioning, humiliation, extortion, brief custody or detention under morality or sodomy provisions, denial of respectful emergency care, and a less reliable police response to harassment or extortion than in the capital become more likely, while travelers with minors or partners face added family or community scrutiny. Proximity to the Ivorian border adds no protective regime.

regions.name: Montserrado
regions.merged_summary:
Montserrado contains Monrovia, Liberia's capital, largest urban centre, most urbanised county and the location of the international airport, the government and police headquarters, and the national legislature where anti-LGBTQ bills were pursued in 2012 and 2024. National law applies without any separate local regime: consensual same-sex conduct remains criminalised under a sodomy provision carrying up to one year's imprisonment and applicable to women as well as men, same-sex marriage is not recognised, no gender-affirming care is available domestically, and proposed anti-homosexuality legislation signals continuing official hostility. Enforcement is described as uncommon but deters reporting to police, people have been arrested after attackers invoked their sexuality or gender identity, and police use LGBTQ status against victims rather than protecting them. The county is also where the country's LGBTQ community infrastructure is concentrated, including advocacy groups such as SAIL and the Transgender Network of Liberia, private gathering and safe spaces, and the largest presence of embassies, NGOs and international personnel; the Decent Work Act's protection for workers regardless of gender identity operates mainly in this urban labour market but does not reach a visitor's everyday exposure. Public concealment remains the documented norm, and no Montserrado-specific protections for transgender visitors or distinct local enforcement pattern are established.

For a transgender visitor, the capital's scale, anonymity, foreign presence, community contacts and consular or human-rights channels modestly soften everyday outing risk and may make informal assistance more reachable than in rural areas, though that civil-society presence is not a guaranteed protection. If discovered or outed, however, these advantages do not change national law, police discretion, detention conditions or social stigma: arrest leverage under the sodomy statute, police corruption and extortion, denial of care, custody or facilities following birth sex, and street hostility toward visible gender nonconformity that can escalate to mob confrontation with thin or unreliable recourse all remain plausible, and reporting abuse can itself expose LGBTQ people to further risk. Local variation is small relative to the national exposure.

regions.name: River Gee
regions.merged_summary:
River Gee is a remote, sparsely populated south-eastern county centred on Fish Town, built on subsistence agriculture with very limited police, medical and judicial capacity, no tourism infrastructure, and no LGBTQ community spaces or advocacy presence — the organisations serving trans Liberians, such as SAIL and TNOL, operate essentially in Monrovia. Local communities are strongly traditional, with conservative Christian and norms that make privacy hard to maintain in small, closely-knit settlements, so a visibly gender-nonconforming foreign visitor would be conspicuous in ways that spread quickly. There is no documented county-level legal recognition regime, protective custody practice, tourist-facing exception, or service-access safeguard, no local exception to the national regime, and no documented state targeting or violence pattern specific to the county; matters such as visitor document checks and local police practices are simply undocumented rather than established as safe. Weak or absent external oversight and thinner rural police oversight mean fewer reporting channels and less access to the private safe spaces that exist in the capital.

River Gee inherits Liberia's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to one years' imprisonment, applying to women as well as men, though enforcement is uncommon; active legislative pressure to expand penalties is underway, and the proposed harsher legislation is not enacted law. Public concealment is the documented norm, reporting of crimes against LGBTQ people is deterred by the law, and some LGBTQ people have been arrested after attackers invoked their status — so the statute can act as a secondary lever against victims. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable nationally, and no legal gender recognition or transition care exists, which matters if care is needed during a trip; the Decent Work Act's gender-identity employment clause gives little practical cover in daily life. If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed here, the national climate combines with the county's deep conservatism and total absence of protective infrastructure: expect social hostility, possible questioning, extortion, refusal of services, detention or violence, difficulty accessing help or shelter, unsympathetic police and thin recourse, while imprisonment after discovery is not highly likely and there is no indication of organised state targeting or execution.

regions.name: Rivercess
regions.merged_summary:
Rivercess is a remote, sparsely populated rural coastal county in southeastern Liberia with a logging and mining economy, little tourism infrastructure, and thin formal state presence; customary chiefly authority carries much of daily governance, police presence and judicial reach are markedly thinner than in Monrovia, and communities are small and tight-knit, offering far less anonymity. Christian churches dominate social life, where gender nonconformity is widely read as a moral offence. No county-specific protective legislation, incidents, or distinct enforcement pattern distinguishing it from the national picture is documented, and the absence of local incident records is not evidence of safety; the county offers no known exemptions, care access, or protective practices, and there is neither refuge nor added legal severity relative to the capital. LGBTQ-supportive spaces and advocacy or legal-aid networks are concentrated in Monrovia and effectively absent here, leaving no local community fallback, while medical infrastructure is minimal and serious cases are referred to Monrovia.

The national regime applies in full: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to one year's imprisonment, and the sodomy statute applies to women as well as men; enforcement, while uncommon, has followed attacks in which perpetrators cited LGBTQ status and it deters victims from reporting abuse; proposals to harden penalties recur; there is no legal gender recognition; and no gender-affirming care is available domestically. The Decent Work Act's gender-identity employment clause is a resident-facing labour rule with no realistic local enforcement and offers a visitor no protection if outed. For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, police retain sodomy and public-order levers, any detention would house them by birth sex in a facility with no protective protocols, and encounters with authorities may be mediated by weak formal institutions and informal local expectations; reduced anonymity means a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is noticed at once, while distance from legal and medical help leaves little recourse. Rural conservatism and the weight of traditional institutions make conditions less protective than in Monrovia, though county-specific police, border, facility, healthcare, and visitor-violence practices are not documented, so their absence cannot be treated as assurance.

regions.name: Sinoe
regions.merged_summary:
Sinoe is a remote, sparsely populated rural county in southeastern Liberia centred on Greenville, far from Monrovia's LGBTQ advocacy networks (SAIL, TNOL) and the capital's private safe spaces. It has conservative, close-knit communities where customary structures carry significant influence, weak and thinly spread policing, and periodic inter-ethnic violence that residents say outpaces state response; legal aid and advocacy support are effectively absent, and a visibly foreign transgender visitor would be conspicuous. No Sinoe-specific protective law, ordinance, community infrastructure, police-targeting pattern, or record of hostility toward transgender people is documented, and no local enforcement record of the sodomy statute exists — but the absence of local reports does not establish safety, and custody or prison placement for a transgender detainee remains an open question rather than a documented practice.

The national regime governs: consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to one year's imprisonment, applies to women as well as men, and is enforced uncommonly — yet it has been used in arrests of LGBTQ people after attacks in which their status served as a pretext, and legislative proposals to expand penalties remain active. The law deters victims from reporting abuse. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically, and public concealment is the documented norm. The Decent Work Act (2015), Section 2.4(b)(iii), bars employment discrimination by gender identity, though no Sinoe-specific enforcement record was found. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, Sinoe's thin, discretionary policing and conservative norms combine with that national picture to mean possible questioning or detention under sodomy or public-order provisions, community outing, extortion, denial of services or treatment, harassment with no realistic local remedy, and little practical recourse.

regions.name: Anse la Raya
regions.merged_summary: Anse la Raya is a small, rural west-coast quarter of fishing villages and modest local tourism, and it has no gender-presentation law, border regime, facility ban or policing practice distinct from Saint Lucia as a whole.
