A transgender visitor therefore inherits the national framework: consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by the High Court in July 2025, ending the principal criminal exposure; there is no trans-specific criminal offence and no documented state targeting of trans travellers; the Domestic Violence Act 2022 expressly covers sex, gender, sexual orientation and gender identity and provides gender-neutral protection orders with equal access for transgender victims; courts and protection mechanisms are available for reporting violence; and Royal Saint Lucia Police Force officers, including ports and border staff, received human-rights and LGBT-specific training in 2014-2015. Nationally there is no documented trans-specific violence pattern or trans-specific violence data, though the country was the only UN member state in the Americas to formally oppose the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity, and documented anti-gay violence includes the 2011 villa attack and the 2019 fatal stabbing; social attitudes remain conservative in parts of the island.\n\nLocally, the village is compact, close-knit and religiously conservative with a Catholic social climate, limited anonymity and few trans-aware services, and no local protective infrastructure or tolerance mechanism clearly better than the national picture. A visitor whose trans status becomes known may face staring, gossip, misgendering, possible service refusal or low-level harassment, and no local trans-specific violence pattern is documented. The Friday fish-fry and tourist traffic give foreigners some cover but do not create a trans-specific support structure, and rural isolation may mean slower recourse than in Castries, with local police less likely than Castries-based units to have practical experience handling trans complaints.

regions.name: Canaries
regions.merged_summary: Canaries is a small, tight-knit west-coast fishing village between Soufrière and Anse La Raye rather than a resort district, with limited tourism infrastructure and essentially no visitor-facing trans infrastructure; its conservative, church-centred social climate and small size mean a visibly transgender visitor is likely to be noticed, discussed and stared at, with less anonymity than in Castries, while policing, courts and medical and legal recourse are the national ones, based far away in Castries or Soufrière. No local ordinances, trans-specific local law, border practices, facility rules, service-denial patterns, protective practice or hostility specific to Canaries have been documented, the practice of its small police station is untested, and no trans-specific violence or complaint data exists for the area. Nationally, a July 2025 High Court ruling decriminalised private consensual adult same-sex conduct, though the buggery and gross indecency sections remain in the Criminal Code as amended, and the 2022 Domestic Violence Act uses gender-neutral definitions, bars discrimination on gender identity by public officers and service providers, and gives transgender survivors equal access to protection orders, while police, port, customs and prison staff have received sensitisation training, in 2014 and 2015, though implementation can be uneven and no trans-specific violence data is recorded. Against that framework stand a 2011 anti-gay robbery of visitors, a 2019 stabbing murder, Saint Lucia's opposition to the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity, and an asylum risk finding pointing to enduring social hostility and enforcement uncertainty, with no trans-specific targeting documented in Canaries. If outed there, a visitor could expect staring, intrusion, possible harassment, service friction or an awkward encounter at a guesthouse rather than organised hostility, with formal legal protection reaching the village but local enforcement and everyday services thin.

regions.name: Choiseul
regions.merged_summary:
Choiseul is a small, largely rural district of fishing villages and subsistence farming on Saint Lucia's southwest/southern coast, with little tourism infrastructure and none of the anonymity available around Castries and the northern resort belt. It has no separate local law, border rule, documented enforcement pattern or protective exception for transgender visitors, so it simply inherits the national framework: the High Court's July 2025 decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct, no criminal statute targeting gender expression or trans visitors, the Domestic Violence Act's gender-neutral definitions and gender-identity non-discrimination clause with access to protection orders, and police and port officers' human-rights sensitisation training (delivered in 2014 and 2015). The absence of Choiseul-specific incident, enforcement or border records does not itself establish safety.

A foreign transgender visitor is conspicuous in such a close-knit community, and discovery or being outed is likelier here than in the capital or resort areas; local social conservatism and church attitudes raise the chance of gossip, intrusive questions, staring, misgendering, reluctance to assist or possible service refusal rather than arrest or custody, though there is no documented local arrest, facility exclusion or severe punishment aimed at trans travellers. Low violent-crime levels and community ties moderate severity, but documented nationally recorded anti-gay violence — a 2011 villa robbery and a 2019 murder — signals underlying social prejudice, and no trans-specific violence data exists. The government's opposition to the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity is a broader climate note rather than a Choiseul condition. Because legal aid, health services, advocacy and formal remedies are concentrated in the capital, a visitor stranded in the south may find redress slower and less reliable.

regions.name: Dennery
regions.merged_summary:
Dennery is a small, predominantly Creole-speaking fishing village on Saint Lucia's Atlantic east coast — close-knit, more rural and socially conservative, with religiously rooted attitudes, less tourism anonymity, modest tourism infrastructure, little visible LGBTQ presence and fewer trans-specific support or advocacy resources than Castries or the northern resort belt. No local law, ordinance or practice distinguishing it from the national picture is known, and no Dennery-specific incident or local protection has been identified. The national regime therefore applies: the High Court decriminalised consensual adult same-sex conduct in July 2025, though the Criminal Code provisions remain on the books as amended; there is no trans-specific criminal offence; the Domestic Violence Act 2022 uses gender-neutral definitions, bars discrimination on gender-identity grounds by public officers and service providers, and provides protection orders, though its operation for trans visitors is not documented; and police and port officers received LGBT sensitisation training in 2014 and 2015. No documented pattern of trans-specific violence, targeting, detention or expulsion exists nationally or locally, while documented anti-LGBT violence includes a 2019 stabbing murder alleged to be motivated by perceived sexual orientation, and the country formally opposed the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity. The economy is tourism-dependent and generally accommodates foreign guests.

For a transgender visitor who is out or is recognised, Dennery's tight-knit character and limited anonymity raise the likelihood of gossip, staring, direct questioning, misgendering, informal disclosure and service friction, with socially conservative hostility more likely than state action. National police and courts remain the recourse, but distance from the trained units and services concentrated in Castries, plus less centralized complaint handling, means familiarity with trans issues and consistency of enforcement are likely thinner and less predictable if a situation escalated. Trans-specific treatment at local facilities or by local police, and for visitors travelling with minors, is not documented — an uncertainty that is neither evidence of safety nor of additional local exposure. Trans-specific violence itself remains undocumented.

regions.name: Laborie
regions.merged_summary:
Laborie, a small, close-knit fishing and farming community on Saint Lucia's southwestern coast near Hewanorra airport and Vieux Fort, has no documented local law, ban, checkpoint, court precedent or pattern of trans-specific enforcement distinguishing it from the national picture. Saint Lucia's framework applies unchanged: a July 2025 High Court ruling removed criminal penalties for private consensual adult same-sex conduct, though the relevant Criminal Code provisions remain on the books, and there is no trans-specific offence. The Domestic Violence Act 2022 uses gender-neutral definitions, includes gender identity in its non-discrimination clause binding public officers and service providers, and provides access to protection orders; police, port and border officers and corrections staff have received LGBT sensitisation training, documented in 2014-2015. No trans-specific violence data is documented nationally or locally; recorded bias-motivated violence concerns sexual-orientation minorities, including incidents in 2011 and the 2019 murder of Michael Pooran, alongside a 2019 UK asylum finding. Saint Lucia has historically been slow on SOGI issues internationally and formally opposed the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Laborie's small scale and traditional Creole and Catholic character mean a visibly transgender visitor cannot easily stay anonymous — gossip travels quickly and discovery through documents or talk is likelier than in Castries — while trained-officer support and any LGBT infrastructure are concentrated in the capital, far from Laborie's position outside the resort corridors of Castries and Gros Islet. The local record shows no documented trans-targeted policing, violence or service refusal, and violent crime is low, though social conservatism is strong: expect curiosity, misgendering, informal questioning and possible service awkwardness rather than state or organised hostility. Any incident would draw community attention, with recourse resting on the national protection-order machinery and thin local support, and local medical and transport infrastructure is limited. Consequences of being outed remain social and service-discretion based rather than legal exposure.

regions.name: Micoud
regions.merged_summary:
Micoud is a small, mainly rural, close-knit community in Saint Lucia — described as a quiet east-coast fishing town with strong Catholic ties, few foreign visitors and limited tourist infrastructure, and also as a largely agricultural district in the south-east near Vieux Fort and Hewanorra airport. A visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller is conspicuous there and lacks the anonymity of Castries, while police resources and trained officers are concentrated elsewhere, oversight is thinner, and hospitals and legal support are further away. There is no Micoud-specific record of police conduct, facility practice, incidents or remedies involving transgender visitors, so the area offers no documented local mitigation and no documented additional exposure; local social attitudes being more conservative than in the capital remains an open question rather than a documented fact. Everyday encounters with lodging, facilities and medical staff depend on staff discretion, and in a close-knit community discovery or outing is more likely to draw staring, gossip, misgendering, moral disapproval, pressure and uneven responses from smaller institutions than arrest or state punishment.

State protection remains available in principle through Saint Lucia's national regime: no offence targets gender expression or gender identity, the High Court decriminalised private consensual same-sex conduct in July 2025, and the 2022 Domestic Violence Act uses gender-neutral definitions, bars discrimination on gender identity and grants access to protection orders. Police and border/port officers have received human-rights sensitisation training, although the documented sessions date to 2014–2015, and there is no documented pattern of police targeting trans visitors. There is also no trans-specific criminal offence, no documented trans-specific entry, facility or custody rules for visitors, and no trans-specific violence data for either Saint Lucia or Micoud — an absence that is not evidence of safety. Documented violence against people perceived as sexual minorities includes a 2019 stabbing murder and a 2011 robbery, alongside earlier anti-gay attacks and social hostility, none of which establishes trans-specific targeting; Saint Lucia's record of opposing UN gender-identity declarations is further context.

regions.name: Vieux Fort
regions.merged_summary:
Vieux Fort is a small, close-knit southern coastal town — Saint Lucia's second town — whose main feature for visitors is Hewanorra International Airport, the island's principal international gateway, where routine immigration and document checks are encountered first. It has no trans-specific legal regime, statute, facility rule, document restriction, protective ordinance, or documented difference in police or border practice: the national framework governs, including the High Court's July 2025 decriminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct and the 2022 Domestic Violence Act's gender-neutral protection orders and non-discrimination clause covering gender identity, alongside police LGBT sensitisation training conducted nationally in 2014–2015. There is, however, no legal gender recognition or general anti-discrimination statute protecting gender identity, the country formally opposed the UN SOGI declaration, advocacy and recourse infrastructure is concentrated in Castries, and no local trans-specific protocol, events or infrastructure exists. Nationally no trans-specific violence data has been identified; documented hostility — attacks in 2011 and 2019, and the 2019 murder of Michael Pooran nearby — was sexual-orientation motivated, as was a 2019 UK asylum finding on persecution risk for gay men.

For a transgender visitor who is openly trans or is outed, the small-town setting offers little anonymity and heightened scrutiny at border clearance, with stares, gossip, service friction, misgendering, hostile questioning, harassment and possible verbal hostility plausible in streets, clubs and informal settings under the influence of social conservatism and strong church influence — outcomes turning on individual attitudes and discretion rather than formal criminal exposure, with no indication of systematic state targeting or custodial risk. Offsetting this, the tourism-facing economy of beach resorts, dive operators, visitor nightlife and hospitality staff accustomed to international guests can soften everyday friction and make gender-nonconforming travellers less anomalous than in deeply rural parishes. Facility access, custody placement, healthcare access and protections for travelling minors are not documented, and that uncertainty does not establish safety.

regions.name: Balzers
regions.merged_summary:
Balzers is a small, predominantly Catholic municipality in southern Liechtenstein near the Swiss border, home to a few thousand residents, Gutenberg Castle and vineyards, with a quiet, tourism-facing character and close practical ties to Switzerland. No local ordinance restricts gender-nonconforming visitors, no local rule excludes them from sex-segregated facilities, and no local protective measure goes beyond national law, so Liechtenstein's national regime governs: same-sex relations are lawful, marriage equality and joint adoption have been open regardless of gender since 2025, and no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity. Anti-discrimination and hate-speech protections cover sexual orientation only, with no gender-identity or gender-expression ground to invoke, and there is no procedure to change a Liechtenstein-issued gender marker — though foreign-issued documents are unaffected, entry is on the traveller's own documents, and Liechtenstein-issued marker procedures do not reach visitors. Official posture has included conservative remarks from the state religion and the Prince, the latter drawing sharp criticism from civil society and parliamentarians; police and courts are functional and there is no trans-specific criminal exposure, documented policing, exclusion, or violence directed at trans people in Balzers.

In a community of this size with modest local institutions, a visibly trans or outed visitor is more exposed to social than official consequences: small-town visibility may bring staring, misgendering, curious or conservative disapproval, awkward hotel or clinic interactions, and limited discreet recourse, with everyday friction somewhat likelier than in larger places such as Vaduz or Schaan. Because harassment and incitement protections run only along the sexual-orientation axis, there is no protected ground to invoke if such friction occurs, but no documented local pattern of hostility, targeting, or service denial toward visitors exists. The main exposure is social discomfort and institutional uncertainty rather than detention or criminal penalty.

regions.name: Eschen
regions.merged_summary:
Eschen is a small, quiet and prosperous residential municipality in Liechtenstein's Unterland lowlands, near the Austrian border and away from the capital's visitor services. No local laws, policing practices, border or document controls, or other region-specific conditions distinguishing it from the national picture are known, so a transgender visitor there is governed by Liechtenstein's national regime: same-sex relations are lawful, marriage has been open regardless of gender since 2025, sexual-orientation discrimination is banned, no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities by gender identity, and there is no documented targeting, detention or other severe consequence for transgender visitors, with functioning courts and police under a stable rule of law.

Against that, gender identity and gender expression are not covered by the anti-discrimination or hate-speech protections, and Liechtenstein has no procedure to change legal gender markers, so Liechtenstein-issued documents cannot be made to match a trans person's gender — though visitors travelling on foreign-issued documents are not directly affected, and no border or document friction for such passports is documented. Official posture has been less protective than the statutes, with public opposition to LGBT equality and marriage equality from the Church leadership and the prince, including in 2016. Locally, life is compact, Catholic and socially traditional, so curiosity, staring, awkward questioning, misgendering and gossip may be more noticeable than in Vaduz, and there are fewer specialist clinics or LGBTQ venues; a visitor refused a service would have limited recourse. There is no Eschen-specific evidence of either added local tolerance or added local hostility, so local conditions cannot be treated as either an added exposure or a demonstrated safeguard.

regions.name: Gamprin
regions.merged_summary: Gamprin is a small rural Rhine-valley commune in Liechtenstein's Oberland, described in assessments as having roughly 1,700 to 5,500 residents, an industrial and agricultural character rather than a tourism centre, no ski resort or visitor infrastructure comparable to Vaduz or Malbun, no municipal police force, and no services aimed at trans visitors; policing, border control and document checks are national. No local ordinance, enforcement practice, border screening, facility rule, custody practice or documented incident specific to Gamprin was identified, so the national framework applies in full: same-sex relations and same-sex marriage and joint adoption since 2025 are lawful, gender expression is not criminalised, no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity, and a functioning rule-of-law system with low public-order risk applies. However, sexual orientation alone is covered by anti-discrimination and incitement protections, while gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not expressly protected; there is no domestic procedure for changing a gender marker on Liechtenstein-issued documents, which does not directly affect a visitor travelling on a foreign passport. Official posture is less protective than the statutes, with conservative public statements from the head of state and the state religion (the Catholic Church) opposing marriage equality — a stance that is national rather than locality-specific. On the ground, the close-knit, conservative and Catholic village setting means a visibly trans visitor may be conspicuous and could meet everyday curiosity, awkwardness or friction, though no local pattern of targeting, exclusion, organised hostility or official mistreatment is known. If a trans visitor is outed or discovered, the combination of absent gender-identity legal protection, limited trans-specific official recourse and a tight-knit social setting leaves them with little formal remedy; severe state consequences and trans-specific targeting of visitors are not documented, and local practice remains uncertain.

regions.name: Mauren
regions.merged_summary:
Mauren is a small, largely rural and Roman Catholic municipality in Liechtenstein with no separate municipal law, police force or facilities regime, and no region-specific information distinguishes it from the national picture — the country's framework applies uniformly, and knowledge of the region is limited to confirming its small-town, rural character. Same-sex relations are lawful and marriage equality has been open since January 2025; no law criminalises gender expression, restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity, or authorises entry refusal or detention, and there is no documented local pattern of police profiling, targeting or violence against transgender people. Conversely, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not protected grounds under Liechtenstein's anti-discrimination, harassment or media law — those protections cover sexual orientation only — so a trans visitor has no protected ground for a complaint, and Liechtenstein has no procedure to change a legal gender marker on its own documents, a limit that does not affect travellers carrying foreign identification but does affect anyone relying on local identification. No local trans-specific support, and no documented account of how local officials treat trans visitors or of age-specific rules, is known; that absence of documentation is not evidence of safety.

For a transgender visitor who is out or discovered, Mauren's small, close-knit, socially conservative and strongly Catholic life — mirrored nationally by the state church's opposition to marriage equality, senior political remarks in 2016 describing rainbow families as irresponsible, and other socially conservative views from senior public figures — tends to produce lost anonymity, curiosity, awkwardness, less-experienced service staff when documents and presentation diverge, bureaucratic inexperience, service friction and informal exclusion, more so than in larger, more international towns, with no statutory remedy for discrimination on grounds of gender identity. At the same time, Liechtenstein's stable rule of law, low crime and functioning administration, together with the absence of documented police targeting, mean the consequences of discovery tend to be limited rather than serious: rule-of-law breakdown and custody are not plausible outcomes, and no trans-specific police targeting or detention practice attributable to Mauren is known.

regions.name: Planken
regions.merged_summary:
Planken is a small, quiet rural municipality in Liechtenstein's Oberland, perched above Schaan with only a few hundred residents, limited accommodation and everyday services, and policing, hospitals and larger commercial centres concentrated in Vaduz and Schaan. No local ordinance, enforcement practice, facility exclusion, violence record or special protection distinguishes it from the national picture, and none is documented; the national framework therefore applies directly. Same-sex conduct is lawful, marriage has been open since 2025, no law criminalises transgender identity or expression, no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities by gender identity, and rule of law and policing function normally for visitors. Against this, gender identity and expression are absent from both anti-discrimination and hate-speech and hate-crime provisions, which cover sexual orientation only, and Liechtenstein has no domestic procedure for changing a legal gender marker — a gap that does not affect a visitor's foreign-issued documents, which govern entry.

For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, exposure is chiefly social and administrative rather than legal. Planken's very small size, strong Catholic traditions and limited institutional infrastructure mean a visibly trans visitor is conspicuous and cannot rely on urban anonymity, and complaint or mediation resources may be sparse; the realistic local harms are curiosity, staring, misgendering and conservative disapproval rather than hostility, targeting or police interest. Official posture has been less protective than the statutes, with the Catholic Church holding state-religion status and opposing marriage equality, senior public remarks questioning rainbow families, and remarks by the Prince in 2016 signalling social conservatism — but this signals climate rather than a specific threat, and the worst documented consequences of being outed remain discrimination without clear recourse rather than arrest. Local patterns of treatment of trans visitors are not otherwise documented.

regions.name: Ruggell
regions.merged_summary:
Ruggell, Liechtenstein's smallest and northernmost municipality, is a quiet, predominantly Roman-Catholic Rhine-valley village near the Swiss border, and no local ordinances, enforcement practices or incidents are documented that distinguish it from the national picture; Schengen and Swiss border crossings impose no trans-specific gender-marker rules. The national regime therefore governs: same-sex conduct is lawful and marriage has been open to all couples since 2025, no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity, and no law criminalises gender expression. However, anti-discrimination and public-hatred provisions cover sexual orientation only, not gender identity or gender expression, so a trans visitor refused service or housing has no protected ground to invoke, and Liechtenstein has no procedure for changing a legal gender marker, though foreign-issued documents are unaffected by that absence. Official posture has been less protective than the statutes, with senior church hierarchy and the Prince having voiced conservative views on gender and family and publicly opposed rainbow families, though these past remarks are a social signal rather than evidence of current local enforcement practice.

For an outed or visibly transgender visitor, Ruggell's small, rural, close-knit character means low anonymity and possible social scrutiny or disapproval rather than state punishment; small-village visibility may raise friction, and local consequences remain uncertain. No documented police, border, facility, custody or care-based targeting, organised hostility or violence against trans visitors is known locally, and rule of law and low violent crime mean the main exposure is social friction, lack of formal discrimination recourse, and uncertainty over service rather than arrest or custody.

regions.name: Schaan
regions.merged_summary:
Schaan, Liechtenstein's largest and most populous municipality and its main commercial and transport centre, sits adjacent to Vaduz near the Swiss border. No separate local law, policing practice, or facility rule on gender identity is known; the national regime governs. Same-sex conduct is lawful, and anti-discrimination and hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation, but gender identity and expression have no anti-discrimination or hate-speech coverage. There is no criminalisation of transgender identity or expression, no law restricting access to sex-segregated facilities by gender identity, and no legal procedure to change a Liechtenstein-issued gender marker — a limitation that does not govern a visitor's foreign-issued documents, which are used as presented. Marriage equality has been in place since 2025, institutions and the rule of law function predictably, and no documented pattern of police targeting, border document friction, trans-specific violence, or organised harassment of trans visitors is known, though region-specific trans-visitor data are scarce. The state religion is Roman Catholic, and conservative remarks by royal, archbishop's, and other senior religious and political figures — including opposition to marriage equality and disparaging remarks about rainbow families — colour the official climate.

Schaan's urban, affluent, low-crime, tourism-oriented and internationally connected character is generally considered to offer a more anonymous and tolerant setting than rural communes, potentially reducing overt harassment, but it adds no protective layer beyond the national picture. For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered, the main exposure is social disapproval, service-level discretion or awkwardness, bureaucratic mismatch, and private discrimination with thin legal recourse rather than state persecution or institutional consequence.

regions.name: Schellenberg
regions.merged_summary:
Schellenberg is a small, predominantly rural municipality of roughly a thousand residents near the Austrian border in Liechtenstein, with a castle ruin and hiking traffic rather than a resort economy. It has no separate legal, border, policing or facility regime: policing and document checks are national, handled by the Landespolizei at the Swiss and Austrian crossings, and no local statute, enforcement practice or documented incident specific to the municipality distinguishes conditions for transgender visitors from the national picture. A trans visitor therefore meets Liechtenstein's national framework — same-sex relations and marriage are lawful, but gender identity and expression carry no anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage (harassment and hate-incitement protections cover sexual orientation only), no domestic legal gender-marker change procedure exists (a visitor's home-issued documents are unaffected by that), and no law in force restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity. No trans-specific violence, police targeting, arrest, custody risk or border friction is on record, and functioning police and courts remain available, though the absence of local incidents is not itself proof of safety and gender-identity-specific recourse is limited. Official posture is socially conservative: senior public figures and the Roman Catholic Church, the state religion, have voiced opposition to marriage equality and rainbow families, registering as social climate rather than a traveller-facing restriction.

Locally the difference is visibility rather than law: an unfamiliar face draws notice in a compact, traditionally Catholic, agrarian community where anonymity is low and privacy limited, and Catholic conservatism runs deeper than in Vaduz. This raises the chance of social discovery or being outed without raising its severity — the likely consequences are friction, stares, gossip, misgendering, service friction or privacy exposure rather than official action. Nothing indicates deliberate targeting, and no region-specific protective distinction or documented local hostility is known either way.

regions.name: Triesen
regions.merged_summary: Triesen is a small residential Rhine-valley municipality in southern Liechtenstein, close to Vaduz, and no region-specific conditions distinguish it from the national picture: it has no local ordinances, no municipal discrimination ordinance either protective or restrictive, no local facility bans, no trans-specific enforcement practice, protective measure, or pattern of official hostility, and no documented local incidents involving transgender visitors. The national framework therefore applies: same-sex relations are lawful and marriage is open regardless of gender (in force since 2025); there is no trans-specific criminal offence and no law restricting access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity; but gender identity and expression are not protected grounds in anti-discrimination law, and hate-speech and discrimination provisions cover sexual orientation only, leaving a transgender visitor without such a ground for complaint. Liechtenstein has no procedure to change a legal gender marker, so Liechtenstein-issued identification cannot be made to match gender, but a visitor arriving on foreign-issued documents is not directly affected by that gap, and foreign documents are generally handled under national rather than local procedures. Public life is shaped by a predominantly Catholic, socially conservative culture in which the state religion's leadership, the Prince, and senior officials have voiced disapproval of gender diversity or made dismissive remarks — an official posture less protective than the statutes — yet these statements are not documented as targeting trans visitors, and there is no record of trans-specific policing, detention, violence, police targeting, or organised anti-trans violence; institutions operate under an orderly, stable rule-of-law framework with no documented border, facility, custody, or care exposure for a visitor whose documents come from abroad. A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed in Triesen therefore faces the same conditions as elsewhere in the country: no local legal penalties or exceptional state action attach to that visibility, though as a small community, Triesen may make an outed person more noticeable and draw everyday curiosity.

regions.name: Triesenberg
regions.merged_summary:
Triesenberg is a small, predominantly Roman Catholic alpine municipality in Liechtenstein's Oberland above Vaduz, with a tourism-based economy centred on the Malbun resort. It has no local ordinances or practices that distinguish it from the national regime — no region-specific rule, targeting or pattern of violence toward transgender people is documented — and residents and visitors rely on Liechtenstein's national law, policing and courts, with borders handled under routine Schengen procedure. The local difference is mainly visibility: a compact, close-knit and less anonymous village means an outed or discovered trans visitor stands out, with staring, curiosity, conservative disapproval, misgendering, service awkwardness and informal judgment more likely than hostility. The area's tourism character neither adds protection nor raises risk, and local attitudes and specific trans visitor experiences remain uncertain. Institutions operate predictably, so ordinary travel, lodging and public presence carry friction rather than severe consequence, and the risk of detention, prosecution, violence or denial of emergency care remains low.

The national framework applied there makes same-sex relations lawful and marriage open and bans sexual-orientation discrimination and incitement, but gender identity and gender expression have no explicit anti-discrimination protection and there is no equivalent trans-specific incitement provision, leaving thin recourse in a complaint about identity-based discrimination. No law in force restricts access to sex-segregated facilities by gender identity, and no border rule aims at trans visitors. Liechtenstein has no procedure for changing legal gender markers, which affects only those relying on Liechtenstein-issued identification, so a visitor's foreign-issued documents are unaffected. Official posture is mixed: the Church's leadership opposed marriage equality, and the Prince and other senior public figures have voiced disapproval of gender-diverse or rainbow families, but this is rhetoric rather than an enforced restriction — no criminalisation of gender expression, detention practice or documented targeting of trans visitors is recorded, and national policing and courts remain lawful and generally protective.

regions.name: Vaduz
regions.merged_summary:
Vaduz, Liechtenstein's capital and principal urban, administrative and tourism-facing centre, shows no known divergence from the national regime: same-sex relations and marriage (open since 2025) are lawful, no criminal offence targets trans identity or expression, no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on gender-identity grounds, and no cross-dressing or impersonation provision is enforced against presentation. The country has no procedure for changing gender markers on local documents, so a visitor carries foreign-issued documents, though a mismatch can surface at Schengen entry or hotel registration. Anti-discrimination and hate-speech protections cover sexual orientation but not gender identity or expression, leaving a traveller without a formal ground to invoke if discriminated against in services or employment-adjacent settings. Courts, police and administrative remedies function, and the city's international visitors, cross-border and expatriate workforce, service infrastructure and anonymity compared with smaller villages ease ordinary interactions without guaranteeing a remedy.

For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, exposure is mainly social rather than official: Vaduz is a small, Catholic and socially conservative society where visible presentation can draw staring, curiosity or disapproval, and official posture has at times been less welcoming than the statutes, including public criticism of LGBT families by the head of state and archbishopric opposition to marriage equality. There is no documented pattern of police targeting, detention, extortion, custody abuse or anti-trans violence reaching visitors, and no territory-specific exposure has been identified, though that silence does not itself establish safety; social friction is considered more likely than confrontation, with limited legal recourse if discrimination occurs.

regions.name: Central Province
regions.merged_summary:
Central Province has no documented region-specific legal protections, facility rules or enforcement record distinct from Sri Lanka's national picture, and that absence of information is not evidence of safety. Nationally, Penal Code sections criminalising same-sex conduct are rarely prosecuted but give police a lever for harassment, extortion and outing of LGBT people, with forced examinations used in custody, complaints from LGBT victims routinely ignored, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection. If detained, placement defaults to birth sex, with only a discretionary medicalised exception for those holding recognised identity documents; national gender-recognition procedures do not protect a visitor carrying foreign papers. Locally, the province is anchored by Kandy, the cultural-religious heartland and seat of the Temple of the Tooth, with socially conservative Sinhala Buddhist and Tamil hill-country communities, strong temple influence, and rural and plantation districts around Nuwara Eliya and Matale where social policing runs deeper than in Colombo. Police presence is thinner and more traditional than in the Western Province, and there are fewer LGBTQ-specific services, community organisations or predictable complaint-handling channels than in the capital. Kandy's established tourism economy offers some foreigner tolerance and service-sector familiarity, but no province-specific exception or recourse against police abuse is documented.

A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed here therefore faces the national pattern — questioning, extortion, public humiliation, short or arbitrary detention, and potential custody exposure — combined with a modestly harsher local social climate and weaker support infrastructure. Kandy hosts Bogambara Prison, so an arrest there means the same birth-sex placement default and discretionary medical assessment applies. Tourist-facing normalcy does not remove document or detention mismatches. The main exposure is police-driven harassment, extortion and detention rather than routine imprisonment for identity alone; severe outcomes such as execution are not credible.

regions.name: Eastern Province
regions.merged_summary:
Eastern Province (Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Ampara) inherits Sri Lanka's national regime: Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex conduct with up to ten years' imprisonment, and although prosecutions are limited and there is no evidence of imprisonment or capital enforcement against trans visitors, police cite the provisions to justify harassment, extortion, threats of arrest, forced anal and vaginal examinations, and refusal or dismissal of LGBT victims' complaints — police being the main perpetrators of rights violations against LGBTI people. There is no anti-discrimination protection for sexual orientation or gender identity. Prison placement defaults to birth sex with only a discretionary, medicalised exception and no statutory gender rule, while gender recognition certificates have been available since a 2016 Health Ministry circular allowing certification without surgery; gender-affirming care remains hard to access, with some clinicians showing ignorance or ridicule. Public opinion is mixed.

Locally the province is largely rural, poorer and more socially and religiously conservative than Colombo, with predominantly Tamil and Muslim communities (conservative Muslim, Tamil and Sinhalese norms), stronger moral policing in Muslim-majority areas such as Kalmunai and Ampara, tighter-knit communities offering less anonymity for visibly gender-nonconforming people, and a dense post-war military and police checkpoint presence that raises document-check exposure, alongside police forces with a heavy security mandate and poor accountability culture. NGO, legal-aid and LGBT infrastructure is thin beyond national groups, with no visible trans community and comparatively limited trans-focused health and advocacy services, so an outed visitor has fewer allies and weaker practical recourse than in the capital; encounters with police, medics, prison officials or service providers can become more adversarial. No province-specific protective regime, shield practice, remedy, trans-targeted campaign, venues or documented pattern of trans violence distinguishes the region, and the absence of such documentation reflects uncertainty rather than evidence of safety. Tourist areas such as Trincomalee (with naval and tourism activity) and Arugam Bay are more used to foreigners and may offer some anonymity or foreigner leniency and moderated street friction, but this does not offset the inherited state response: discovery or being outed is likely to bring harassment, extortion, detention risk, service denial and denial of protection rather than lethal outcomes.

regions.name: North Central Province
regions.merged_summary:
North Central Province has no documented local protective exception, additional hostile measure, or province-specific enforcement pattern distinguishing it from Sri Lanka's national picture; no province-specific incidents against transgender visitors are on record, and the national police force operates here as elsewhere. It is the country's most rural and among its poorest area — a dry zone organised around the sacred Buddhist cities of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, with pilgrimage tourism bringing foreigners but little urban anonymity. Social attitudes are markedly more conservative than in Colombo, with a strong Buddhist clergy presence, modesty and dress expectations at religious sites, and none of the capital's visible queer community organisations, outreach services, legal-aid capacity, or tolerant commercial venues; services are concentrated in provincial centres. While a functioning gender-recognition certification process and active community organisations exist nationally, and public opinion is broadly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex unions, locally there is little of Colombo's support infrastructure to turn to.

A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed therefore combines that thin local support and heightened social scrutiny with the full national regime: Penal Code sections criminalising same-sex conduct — though transgender identity itself is not a criminal offence — which police cite to justify harassment, extortion, assault, moral policing and refusal to take LGBTQ complaints, with police identified as the foremost perpetrators of rights violations against such people, and forced medical examinations used as evidence-gathering. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, legal gender recognition depends on an onerous, medicalised certificate process, and prison placement defaults to birth sex under a discretionary medicalised exception, leaving detention placement uncertain. Provincial health facilities offer no gender-affirming care, and staff have been reported as uninformed or ridiculing. Imprisonment or lethal harm is not the typical outcome for a discovered visitor and would be less common than in more severe jurisdictions, but custody, extortion and assault risks are real, and outed visitors should expect elevated social attention with minimal community support or informal recourse.

regions.name: North Western Province
regions.merged_summary:
North Western Province (Kurunegala and Puttalam districts) has no separate statutory regime or documented local protections for transgender visitors; it is governed by Sri Lanka's Penal Code, whose Sections 365 and 365A criminalise same-sex conduct with up to ten years' imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions structure policing, and police are documented as the foremost perpetrators of harassment, extortion, moral policing, assault and forced physical examinations against LGBT people, with complaints from LGBTQ people sometimes ignored. There is no sexual-orientation or gender-identity anti-discrimination law, and no local protective ordinance or documented trans-specific programme offsets this exposure. If discovered or outed, a transgender visitor therefore faces the national policing and detention framework: prison placement defaults to birth sex, decided case by case with a discretionary medicalised exception for holders of a gender recognition certificate (available through a bureaucratic 2016 circular). Legal gender recognition, gender-affirming care and certificate access concentrate in Colombo; where care is available, patients report ignorance and ridicule from medical staff, and family and community rejection remains common. Public opinion is largely opposed to same-sex unions.

Locally, the two districts are markedly more rural and socially conservative than Colombo, with fewer LGBTQ organisations, legal-aid providers, advocacy bodies and international-facing services. Foreign visitors are uncommon, so a visibly transgender traveller may be more conspicuous and less likely to find local support or anonymous recourse, and small tourism pockets such as Kalpitiya are the only notable visitor-facing exception and carry no institutional safeguards. Some assessments find no documented province-level additional hostility or enforcement difference from the national picture, while others indicate that the conservative social climate makes societal hostility somewhat more pronounced and police scrutiny somewhat less tolerant than in Colombo; the province has no evidence of either better recourse or harsher local targeting. On balance, discovery here is generally considered somewhat more consequential for a transgender visitor than the national average, with no documented local variation in border, document, policing, detention, facility or care exposure.

regions.name: Western Province
regions.merged_summary: Western Province — centred on Colombo, Gampaha and Kalutara — applies Sri Lanka's national regime with no documented local legal divergence: Penal Code sections 365 and 365A criminalise same-sex conduct and remain available as a policing lever, police are documented using them for harassment, extortion and forced examinations, complaints from LGBTQ victims are often ignored, and there is no anti-discrimination law. Detention defaults to birth-sex wards with a discretionary, medicalised exception, prison and remand facilities in Colombo apply that default directly, hospital staff often lack trans-awareness, and gender-recognition certificates are resident-facing and irrelevant to a visitor's passport. Border screening or document treatment specific to the province is not documented. Colombo is the country's most urban, cosmopolitan and tourist-facing area, hosting the largest concentration of LGBTQ organisations (including Equal Ground, Companions on a Journey and Women's Support Group), most NGO and police sensitisation activity, international hotels, and a visibly larger trans and gender-diverse community, alongside urban anonymity and hospitality-sector norms that reduce casual service discrimination and everyday friction compared with rural districts. Street-level curiosity toward a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is more likely to be friction than confrontation, though social conservatism and routine moral policing persist. For a transgender visitor, these local conditions modestly raise everyday comfort and support access but supply no operative protection once authorities are involved: police stops, hotel identity checks and nightlife policing remain documented exposure points, misuse of section 365 against gender-nonconforming people is documented within Colombo itself, and recourse is weak.

regions.name: Berea District
regions.merged_summary:
Berea District, whose seat is Teyateyaneng, sits alongside (though one account places it within) the capital Maseru, and mixes small-town, peri-urban and mountain-rural terrain with regular visitor traffic. No district-specific legislation, ban, incident or official hostility is known to distinguish Berea from Lesotho's national picture: consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since 2012 with no trans-specific offence, but there is no general anti-discrimination or hate-crime law covering gender identity (workplace protection under the Labour Act 2024 covers employment only), no process to change a legal gender marker, and same-sex partnerships receive no recognition. National reporting, including a 2024 UN review submission, documents community discrimination, rape and assault alongside barriers to health, education and other services, with stigma and taboo driving underreporting; a legal analysis has warned that a passport marker not matching presentation could invite questioning or charges, though actual enforcement against visitors is not documented.

For a transgender visitor, discovery or being outed would most likely mean social friction, discrimination or refusal of services in a largely small-town and rural district with low anonymity and conservative attitudes, where local services and police have less specific experience and most LGBTI support is based in Maseru. There is no documented Berea-specific pattern of anti-trans enforcement, organised targeting or violence. Mitigating the picture, the Matrix Support Group operates across all ten districts and police have sometimes worked cooperatively with LGBTI organisations, assisted pride marches, and provided reported escorts and intervention at annual Pride gatherings; the district's proximity to the capital and its local civic infrastructure suggest somewhat greater tolerance than in rural areas, though document mismatch, service discrimination and stigma remain possible, and formal recourse is limited. Historical reports of police cooperation do not establish current, district-specific protection.

regions.name: Butha-Buthe District
regions.merged_summary: Butha-Buthe District, a small rural, mountainous northern district and border town, inherits Lesotho's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised and no trans-specific offence or statute criminalising gender expression is documented, but there is no general anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity (the Labour Act 2024's protections are employment-only), no legal gender-marker change, and same-sex unions are unrecognised. Documented societal discrimination, rape and assault, with under-reporting, apply nationally, as does an official warning — echoed in a 2017 constitutional analysis — that a passport whose marker does not match a traveller's presentation can attract scrutiny or possible charges, though enforcement against visitors is not documented. No district-specific hostile incidents, organised anti-trans targeting, custodial campaigns, lethal violence, border or police targeting, or facility restrictions are documented here, and no district-specific protective exception is known; the absence of a local incident record should not be read as evidence of safety. Nationally there is a registered, functioning LGBTI organisation and police cooperation, including reported operation across all ten districts and supportive pride escorts, though documented cooperation is concentrated around Maseru and cited examples are dated, with one source noting constructive police relations supplying some recourse. Locally, strong traditional and church influence, a conservative social climate and small-community visibility mean limited anonymity: an outed or discovered visitor is highly exposed to gossip, service refusal, misgendering, inadequate care and insensitive police handling more so than in the capital. The district's limited local legal, health and support services, weaker institutional footprint and distance from Maseru — with LGBTI-specific support thin outside the capital — mean police, clinics, hotels and community leaders may have less familiarity with transgender visitors, recourse is slower, and the South African border post adds a further document-check point, so discovery is more likely to become community-facing and to raise serious social and administrative friction than formal punishment.

regions.name: Mafeteng District
regions.merged_summary:
Mafeteng District — a small, predominantly rural lowland district centred on an agricultural town — inherits Lesotho's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct is lawful, there is no trans-specific criminal offence, no procedure for changing a legal gender marker, no recognition of same-sex unions, and no general anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity (the Labour Act 2024 addresses employment only, leaving visitors without general protection). A passport whose gender marker conflicts with a visitor's presentation may invite scrutiny or fraud-type questioning or charges, although the extent of such scrutiny is uncertain and no visitor-specific enforcement is documented. Nothing in the district's own record distinguishes it: no local ordinance, documented raid, targeting or trans-specific enforcement is known, and police conduct there is not documented as differing in character from the national service. The registered national LGBTI organisation, the Matrix Support Group, operates freely in all ten districts including Mafeteng and has a cooperative relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service — including cooperation in 2015 and 2016 and escorts for pride events — though its reach into everyday district-level policing is weak, and the district lacks Maseru's services and support infrastructure.

Because Mafeteng is more rural, socially conservative and closely knit than the capital — with limited anonymity, greater social scrutiny and gossip around a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner, fewer accommodation-oriented practices and heavy reliance on family and community networks — a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered faces a greater likelihood of invasive questioning, social or familial confrontation, service refusal, harassment and uneven police responsiveness, with thin practical recourse in local institutions. These conditions compound nationally documented community discrimination, rape and assault against LGBT people (recorded in an October 2024 Universal Periodic Review submission), a 2016 US State Department account of taboo and underreporting, and documented official insensitivity. Arrest, custody or state-directed lethal punishment remain unlikely and no district-specific hostility is recorded, but the absence of documented district incidents is not evidence of safety, and existing reports do not establish how often visitors are affected or whether local recourse is effective today.

regions.name: Mohale's Hoek District
regions.merged_summary: On discovery or being outed, a transgender visitor inherits Lesotho's national regime: consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2012 sodomy ruling and gender identity is not criminalised, but there is no legal procedure to change a gender marker, no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, and no general anti-discrimination protection outside employment, where the Labour Act 2024 covers gender identity and sexual orientation. Documented conditions include societal discrimination, taboo around same-sex relationships, community-level SOGIESC discrimination, rape and assault recorded in the October 2024 Universal Periodic Review submission, barriers to health and education services, and under-reporting driven by stigma, alongside documented official insensitivity. A mismatch between a foreign passport's gender marker and presentation could raise document questions at entry, and one legal analysis warned it could prompt charges, though actual enforcement against visitors is not documented. Police are not recorded as targeting trans people, no local anti-trans criminal enforcement or organised targeting is documented, and there is no credible imprisonment, execution or routine arrest risk: exposure is mainly social, bureaucratic and service friction — staring, intrusive questions, service hesitation, harassment, service refusal, extortion or assault — with thin practical recourse. Older accounts of supportive police interactions do not establish current district-level protection, and the absence of district-specific evidence is not evidence of safety. Cross-border travel into South Africa from Mohale's Hoek is routine.

regions.name: Quthing District
regions.merged_summary: Quthing District — a remote, rural and mountainous southern district bordering South Africa, with a small district town, limited tourism and health infrastructure, strong customary and church norms, fewer public-facing institutions and less accommodation, and a small town ranked among the country's more conservative and economically marginal areas — inherits Lesotho's national framework: consensual same-sex conduct and gender expression are not criminalised (the common-law sodomy offence was struck down in 2012), but there is no legal gender-marker change process and no general anti-discrimination statute, with protections limited to employment and workplace harassment under the Labour Act 2024. Same-sex relationships are described as taboo, and national submissions from 2024 document discrimination, rape and assault against LGBT people alongside official insensitivity and underreporting driven by stigma. A legal analysis warns that a mismatch between a visitor's foreign documents and presentation could prompt charges, though actual enforcement against visitors is not documented. No district-specific protective legislation, incident data or evidence of harsher local enforcement, armed-group control, trans-specific violence or local tolerance is known, and there is no known local LGBT community infrastructure, service or pride presence; socially conservative communities offer little anonymity to a visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitor, and the district's low-resource setting likely sharpens the health and education discrimination documented nationally. The country's only known LGBTI organisation, the Matrix Support Group, has operated freely across all districts with a generally cooperative working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service, which has provided supportive escorts at pride events, but that support and documented police liaison are concentrated in Maseru, leaving district-level capacity thin and legal aid distant, with current local enforcement and the effectiveness of support undocumented rather than established as safe. Conditional on discovery or being outed outside tourist or urban settings, a transgender visitor faces societal stigma, stares, service hesitation, family or community pressure and inconsistent or unpredictable official handling, with recourse distant from any support structure, while police encounters are more likely to reflect unfamiliarity than hostility and no documented local targeting exists.

regions.name: Klaipeda County
regions.merged_summary:
Klaipėda County has no county-level entry, document, facility or policing rules of its own, and no local ordinance, enforcement pattern or trans-specific incident targeting visitors is documented, so conditions track Lithuania's national picture. The county is coastal, port- and tourism-oriented — taking in Klaipėda, Lithuania's third-largest city and a major seaport, the resort of Palanga, the Curonian Spit and a university centre — with a tourist-facing economy, port-city cosmopolitanism and greater anonymity, so visitor-facing services have some familiarity with foreign travellers and everyday friction is somewhat lighter than in rural districts; it is nonetheless smaller and more socially provincial than Vilnius, with weaker trans-specific support and complaint practice, and for a visitor accompanying a minor, schools or clinics may be slower to accommodate than in the capital. None of this local character is documented as evidence of either greater safety or greater danger.

Under the national regime, no entry or visa screening touches gender identity, no gender question is asked at the border, visitors carry home-country documents, no law criminalises gender expression, and consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since 1993, with courts and police operating under ordinary rule of law; public incitement against LGBT people is banned, same-sex partnership registration now operates under constitutional and court-ordered arrangements, and a 2024 constitutional ruling struck down limits on expression concerning minors. Against this, there is no working legal gender recognition procedure, no implemented Civil Code Article 5.1 route and no administrative way to change document markers, and the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson records the absence of any strategic framework for trans people; hate-crime victim support is thin, the Seimas Ombudsperson found in 2024 that police failed to secure an LGBT assembly against hostile provocateurs, and the wider public remains broadly socially conservative, with reported workplace ridicule and labour-market discrimination alongside growing but heavily policed Pride participation. A trans visitor's marker is therefore not tested locally and official outing is unlikely; if discovered or outed, the exposure is bureaucratic friction, possible scrutiny of mismatched documents, awkward questioning, service friction or misgendering, social disapproval and limited local recourse, rather than a distinct legal or custodial threat.

regions.name: Telsiai County
regions.merged_summary:
Telsiai County inherits Lithuania's national framework: there are no border, visa, residence or accommodation checks tied to gender identity, no entry questioning on gender expression, and no criminal offence targeting transgender identity, presentation or medical transition — foreign visitors travel on home-issued documents, and the absence of a working domestic gender-marker change procedure is not itself a visitor-facing restriction. However, that same gap means a mismatched foreign passport cannot be remedied locally, leaving any document discrepancy to individual official discretion. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised and public incitement against LGBT people is banned, but support for hate-crime victims is recorded as systemically lacking, police were found in 2024 to have failed to adequately protect an LGBT assembly, and workplace discrimination and ridicule against LGBT people are documented nationally. There is no documented region-specific hostile legislation, official hostility, violence record, county ordinance, or local campaign of arrests, facility bans or forced outing, and no distinct traveller-targeting or detention regime is recorded here.

Locally, Telsiai is a smaller, rural, strongly Catholic Samogitian county centred on Telšiai town, with a more religiously and socially conservative climate than Vilnius or Kaunas, no Pride presence, no documented local LGBT organisations or trans-specific support infrastructure, no dedicated LGBT services, few anonymous urban spaces and thinner community infrastructure overall. Rural police and healthcare staff have no trans-specific training, and the national failures in protecting assembly and supporting hate-crime victims apply with extra force outside major cities. As a result a visibly trans visitor is more conspicuous and has less institutional anonymity, so discovery or being outed would more likely bring curiosity, disapproval, staring, intrusive questioning, cold or inconsistent service — especially outside the main town — rather than organised targeting or severe legal punishment, while local police and municipal practice are not documented as specifically hostile.

regions.name: Canton Capellen
regions.merged_summary:
Canton Capellen is an affluent, largely residential and commuter canton west of Luxembourg City — including Mamer, Steinfort, Käerjeng, Capellen and Kehlen — with a quiet, rural-suburban character and a large international and cross-border population, though some smaller villages may be more socially conservative. No cantonal or communal ordinances restricting facilities, expression or services are known, no divergent policing, tourism or service-refusal practices exist there, and there are no documented trans-specific incidents or patterns of local hostility; policing, health regulation and equality enforcement are national, so no commune operates separate rules. Practical friction in the canton rests on ordinary rural-urban variation in familiarity — occasional curiosity or misgendering rather than hostility — and there is no local acute hospital, sending routine and specialist care to the capital, where the Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale and the CET equality body are based.

Across Luxembourg, gender identity and expression are not criminalised, legal gender change is available by declaration through the civil register without surgery, sterilisation, divorce or medical treatment (a procedure that does not apply to visitors, whose documents come from their home countries), and discrimination based on change of sex is prohibited in employment, education, health care, social security, goods and services, with bias-motivated offences treated as aggravated. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2015, and there is no facility-exclusion regime. National gaps remain: no nonbinary marker is available, gender expression and sex characteristics are not protected grounds, and the 2025 LGBTIQ+ Action Plan omits depathologisation. If a transgender visitor is discovered or outed in the canton, conditions combine so that the realistic outcome is discrimination or social awkwardness rather than custody or violence, with recourse functioning through Luxembourg's national institutions, equality body and LGBTIQ+ centre.

regions.name: Canton Clervaux
regions.merged_summary: Canton Clervaux is a sparsely populated, predominantly rural canton in northern Luxembourg's Ösling region, centred on Clervaux town and its castle and Christmas market, and it inherits Luxembourg's national framework in full: gender identity is recognised through a declaration-based civil-register procedure without medical requirements; discrimination on grounds of change of sex is prohibited in employment, education, healthcare and goods and services; change of sex is an aggravating factor for hate-motivated offences; same-sex marriage and adoption have been available since 2015; and an equality body and national LGBTIQ+ centre offer recourse through functioning courts and complaints routes. No local ordinance, facility rule, entry restriction, enforcement practice or documented pattern of trans-specific targeting, police hostility or organised hostility is known in the canton, but neither is there documented region-specific evidence about how trans visitors are treated in facilities, at border encounters or in local enforcement, and that absence of information is not evidence of safety. Nationally, gender expression and sex characteristics are not protected grounds, and the 2025 national action plan omits depathologisation. Clervaux's Catholic-influenced, relatively conservative and traditional social climate, tight-knit communities and limited anonymity compared with Luxembourg City mean visibility and outing are more likely to be noticed; for a travelling minor or family, tight-knit social circles can make discovery more exposed socially, though not legally. Conditional on discovery or being outed, the realistic consequences are social friction, curiosity, staring, misgendering, awkward conversations at small hotels, parish events, markets or with community groups, isolated service awkwardness or bureaucratic friction and private prejudice at worst — with no criminalisation, facility bans or custody exposure, and no expectation of refusal of entry, arrest, detention placement or violence linked to being trans, while national legal protections and complaint mechanisms remain available. Local conservatism in this rural area amounts to social friction rather than a threat, and these protections do not guarantee that every local encounter will be free of friction.

regions.name: Canton Diekirch
regions.merged_summary:
Canton Diekirch is Luxembourg's small, largely rural northern canton around the town of Diekirch and Vianden, covering the Éislek and Oesling, with an older and more socially conservative population, a traditionally Catholic surrounding area, a modest local trans community and less anonymity than Luxembourg City. It is an administrative and judicial district with no separate legislative layer, so it operates entirely under the national regime: gender-marker and first-name changes by declaration without medical requirements, prohibition of discrimination on the ground of change of sex (and of sex and gender identity in employment, education, healthcare and goods and services), change of sex as an aggravating factor in hate crimes, and same-sex marriage and adoption since 2015 — all enforced by national police, the courts and the equality body CET, with Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale available. Gender expression and sex characteristics are not protected grounds, nonbinary markers are unavailable, and the 2025 action plan omitted depathologisation. No canton-specific restrictions, local ordinances, police practices, documented incidents or patterns of targeting transgender visitors, or harsher enforcement depart from the national picture, and public hostility is not documented as organised or state-directed.

The practical local difference is one of service depth and social familiarity rather than legal exposure: support organisations and visibly LGBTIQ+ infrastructure concentrate in Luxembourg City, while care is available locally through the regional hospital, and some frontline staff in smaller local offices may need guidance. A visibly trans visitor may attract ordinary curiosity, awkward bureaucratic handling, misgendering or conservative social friction if discovered or outed, but documented national protections and recourse remain fully operative and no additional legal or enforcement exposure arises from the canton itself.

regions.name: Canton Echternach
regions.merged_summary:
Canton Echternach, a small rural eastern canton in the Mullerthal centred on the town of Echternach, its lake and abbey, operates under Luxembourg's national framework: gender recognition by simple declaration in the civil register without medical requirements, discrimination on the basis of change of sex prohibited in employment, goods and services, housing-related services, healthcare and public services, hate crimes motivated by change of sex treated as an aggravating factor, marriage and adoption equality for same-sex couples, complaints handled by the equality body CET, and an LGBTIQ+ centre providing support. No cantonal or communal ordinance restricts facilities, documents or service access, and no local pattern of anti-trans enforcement, violence, visitor-directed hostility or documented anti-trans incidents is recorded here; trans-specific border or document problems and custody policies are likewise not documented, though this should not be taken as proof that they cannot occur. The area's tourism economy brings routine contact with foreign visitors, and police and communal services are the country's functioning institutions, so a trans visitor's exposure closely tracks the national picture.

Conditions that do differ locally are social and practical rather than legal: the canton is small and low-anonymity, with a population of roughly nineteen thousand and a historically Catholic, more rural character, so an outed or discovered visitor is more conspicuous and everyday visibility of trans people, specialized community services, and institutional familiarity with gender-identity paperwork are lower than in Luxembourg City. The resulting risks on discovery are discomfort, curiosity, awkward or misgendering remarks, service friction and bureaucratic unfamiliarity rather than legal punishment, and the small-community social conservatism can make acceptance less smooth than the national average; national rule-of-law remedies and equality bodies remain operative, and the general climate in this polite, tourist-oriented border area is broadly tolerant, though quieter about LGBT matters than the capital. At national level, gender recognition remains binary with no nonbinary marker, gender expression is not expressly protected, LGBT services are concentrated in the capital rather than locally (affecting service access more than traveller-facing exposure), and the available information does not establish how consistently protections operate in every local encounter.

regions.name: Canton Grevenmacher
regions.merged_summary: Canton Grevenmacher, a small, largely rural eastern canton along the Moselle and Sûre on the German border, taking in Grevenmacher, Remich, Wormeldange and Echternach, has no separate rules for gender recognition, documents, detention, policing, facilities or care: it inherits Luxembourg's national framework unchanged, including gender recognition by administrative declaration through the Ministry of Justice with no surgery or medical requirement (binary markers only, with no nonbinary option available nationally), discrimination protections covering change of sex in employment, education, healthcare, and goods and services, an aggravating factor for gender-motivated hate offences, same-sex marriage and adoption, a functioning equality body (CET) and community support through the Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale. National gaps remain: no protection for gender expression or sex characteristics, no measures addressing conversion practices or intersex interventions, and a 2025 action plan that omitted depathologisation. Locally the canton is a quiet Moselle wine and tourism region with cross-border commuters and visitors; its villages are rural and traditionally Catholic, and outside Luxembourg City anonymity is lower, so everyday curiosity, staring, mild friction or awkward service encounters in wine-village settings are more plausible than in the capital. No documented local hostile measures, targeted incidents, police hostility, service refusal, violence or enforcement differences from the national picture are known, though local incident and service-access evidence is limited and how consistently the national protections operate locally is not established, so that absence should not be taken as proof of safety. For a transgender visitor, conditional on discovery or being outed, the operative regime remains national: stable institutions, accessible remedies, no credible imprisonment or lethal punishment, and no known local pattern of police targeting, facility exclusion or organised hostility, leaving the practical exposure centred on social friction and possible interpersonal awkwardness rather than state or violent threat, with residual uncertainty reflecting rural conservatism and thin data on local attitudes.

regions.name: Canton Mersch
regions.merged_summary:
Canton Mersch, a semi-rural central canton of small towns and commuter villages on the main rail line to Luxembourg City — including the grand ducal residence area — has no separate legislation, civil-registry rules, border, detention, healthcare or policing regime of its own, and no local ordinances restricting gender expression or documented pattern of police, official or organised hostility toward transgender visitors. The national framework therefore applies in full: gender recognition by civil-register declaration to the Ministry of Justice without medical requirements, equal-treatment protections covering change of sex in employment, healthcare, education, goods and services, hate-crime aggravation for anti-trans motivation, a functioning equality body handling complaints, community services through Centre Cigale, active government LGBTIQ+ action plans, and same-sex marriage and adoption lawful since 2015; gender expression itself is not a protected ground, and gender change is not criminalised. Hospitality and tourism are ordinary features of the canton, policing, courts and equality recourse operate through the national system, and the canton sits on well-trafficked routes with quick access to Luxembourg City's services.

For a transgender visitor who is outed or discovered there, these protections carry through, with the canton differing mainly in scale rather than in exposure: smaller, less international suburban and rural communities offer less anonymity and fewer visible community venues and trans-specific services than the capital, so staring, misgendering, cautious service reactions, everyday curiosity or awkwardness, and a degree of local social conservatism are more plausible than in Luxembourg City.
