Under that inherited regime, a 2023 law bans gender-reassignment surgery and changes to document markers, and no route to legal gender recognition exists; the "international LGBT movement" carries an extremist designation (with documented raids, arrests, prosecutions, over 101 related convictions by June 2025, and 2025-era outlawing of major LGBT organisations), while propaganda statutes reaching all ages are enforced at roughly eighteen times prior rates, with fines and venue raids. There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection and no recognition of relationships, and public attitudes are broadly hostile. A trans visitor discovered orouted — at document checks, lodging, or medical settings — faces document-mismatch scrutiny and exposure under the extremism and propaganda measures, with detention carrying documented lethal risk nationally, plus official hostility, extortion, and violence and no reliable recourse; a highest-level government travel advisory is in effect.

regions.name: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
regions.merged_summary:
Nenets Autonomous Okrug is a sparsely populated Arctic district of roughly 44,000 people centred on Naryan-Mar and scattered oil and gas settlements, with traditional hunting and reindeer-herding communities and a large indigenous Nenets population; it is reachable mainly by air. There are no LGBTQ venues, no visible queer community infrastructure, and no known local trans-specific protections, sanctuary, complaint mechanism or support organisations, and local legal aid, healthcare and police services are limited. The okrug's own enforcement practice, venue presence and police conduct are not documented in the record, and there is no basis to infer either milder or harsher local enforcement than the national picture; no documented local protection exists in either direction. Federal Russian law applies directly through local police, courts and federal security services: gender recognition and the 2023 ban on transition-related surgery and marker changes do not affect a visitor's foreign-issued documents, which remain as issued at home; the 'international LGBT movement' is designated extremist, with over a hundred convictions, documented raids involving searches and photographs, extremism arrests and a death in pretrial detention in 2024; and propaganda statutes reach ordinary expression across all ages. There is no anti-discrimination protection on gender identity and no recording or aggravation of bias-motivated violence, so such violence carries no added legal consequence.

If discovered or outed, a visitor faces this same national exposure — official hostility, possible extremism or propaganda charges, and detention carrying documented lethal risk — with no local mitigation. Small, close-knit settlements sharply reduce anonymity: a visibly transgender outsider is highly noticeable, draws attention rather than finding cover, and has less community support than in Moscow or St Petersburg. Public attitudes are conservative and broadly hostile, unlikely to be more accepting than the national baseline, while remote placement provides no independent remedy; the practical local difference is a lower likelihood of safe public life and less formal recourse rather than any reduction in severity.

regions.name: Novgorod Oblast
regions.merged_summary:
Novgorod Oblast is governed in full by Russia's national regime for a transgender visitor: there is no legal gender recognition, a 2023 law bars transition and changes to gender markers (a visitor's foreign-issued documents are not part of Russia's resident marker process), the 'international LGBT movement' has been designated extremist and has drawn over a hundred convictions including prosecutions for symbols, and propaganda statutes restricting discussion of LGBT people and gender transition are enforced across all ages through fines, raids and extremism-related cases. There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, no trans-specific visitor safeguard and no reliable recourse, while national surveys and official attitudes show substantial social disapproval and large majorities rejecting non-traditional identities. No oblast-specific rule, local protective law, tolerance exception, distinctive enforcement pattern or visitor-facing recourse is known, and nothing establishes either greater protection or harsher enforcement here than nationally; the top-tier US travel advisory applies nationwide, and Veliky Novgorod's heritage tourism economy provides no documented shield.

The oblast is small, provincial and socially conservative, and Veliky Novgorod is a mid-sized city with underdeveloped queer infrastructure compared with Moscow and St Petersburg, no documented LGBT-friendly venue scene and few dedicated queer venues — meaning fewer organised raids on venue districts than in the capitals, but also no community cover and no local advocacy or legal-aid infrastructure (the main groups are based in St Petersburg or Moscow, and the recently outlawed organisations operated far from here). A visibly trans visitor is conspicuous to police, hotel staff and strangers, and street stop-and-check discretion is exercised with little accountability; provincial visibility and small-city familiarity may reduce casual encounters, but they do not lessen exposure at passport checks, police stops, detention-facility placement or detention. Extremism and propaganda enforcement runs through federal police and courts that are at least as compliant in provincial settings, so a visitor who is discovered or outed faces police profiling, potential extremism or administrative charges, and custody carrying documented lethal risk, as in the 2024 death of a man held on extremism charges. Provincial geography offers less anonymity and less community support than the federal capitals, and the absence of local incident records is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Oryol Oblast
regions.merged_summary:
Oryol Oblast is a conservative, inland, socially conservative oblast with no significant tourism-facing economy, low presence of international institutions, no known transgender-specific protections, community infrastructure, or trans-friendly venues, and no local exception to the national picture — in its smaller cities a visibly trans visitor attracts attention and has little anonymity. The region therefore inherits Russia's national regime: gender reassignment and document marker changes are prohibited under the 2023 ban, so the home passport and visa govern and any mismatch invites scrutiny; the state's designation of an alleged international LGBT movement as extremist can expose anyone displaying LGBT symbols to extremism charges; propaganda and extremism statutes are enforced through fines, venue raids, police searches involving photography and wall-lineups, arrests and detentions. There is no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, no hate-crime aggravation for anti-LGBT bias, and official hate-crime recording does not cover such bias, while public attitudes are strongly hostile, with 74% disapproval recorded nationally, and pretrial detention has proven lethal.

Conditional on discovery or being outed, a transgender visitor in Oryol Oblast faces forced document scrutiny, questioning or discretionary detention — with local police and officials unlikely to offer protection and potentially treating disclosure as grounds for an administrative or extremism inquiry — as well as denial of ordinary services and harassment or extortion by hostile individuals or officials. These consequences combine with the national regime's weak recourse and no documented local mitigation, leaving serious risk of detention, harassment, extortion, or charges with no effective remedy.

regions.name: Primorsky Krai
regions.merged_summary:
Primorsky Krai inherits Russia's national framework: legal gender recognition does not exist, a 2023 law bars gender transition and changes to official gender markers, and there is no anti-discrimination protection or official recording of hate crimes against LGBTQ people. Extremism and propaganda laws are enforced through venue raids with mass searches and photographing, arrests and convictions for displaying LGBTQ symbols, an extremist designation of the "international LGBT movement" with over 101 convictions and the 2025 outlawing of major groups, propaganda fines that have escalated eighteenfold and now reach all age groups, and a documented 2024 pretrial detention death following an extremism-related arrest. Visitors keep their home-issued documents, so any mismatch between papers and presentation remains a route to scrutiny, and families travelling with minors face added sensitivity around discussion or material concerning gender transition. Public attitudes are broadly hostile.

No local protective practice is documented in the krai: there is no regional shield, sanctuary, exemption, or identity-respecting facility, health, or police protocol to offset federal rules, and limited local reporting does not establish that enforcement is absent or safer. Vladivostok's tourist core is somewhat more cosmopolitan than the interior, with historic cross-border tourism, foreign visitors and a small underground queer venue scene, but it operates under the same national raids and extremism prosecutions within a socially conservative, militarised border region with conservative authorities, limited queer infrastructure, weaker police oversight in the Far East, and a record of nationalist violence against gender-nonconforming people; the port city's security-sensitive character adds no protective layer. Heightened document scrutiny at ports and checkpoints, hotel registration or police stops raises discovery risk for someone whose documents, visa and appearance conflict, while Vladivostok's distance from Moscow and St. Petersburg means less visible trans support infrastructure or consistent institutional recourse. For a trans visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the federal framework to expose them to detention, custody or housing assigned by birth sex, exposure under extremism or propaganda statutes, violence in custody, discrimination, and a documented lethal risk in detention; outcomes follow the harsh national rules, with no documented local remedy.

regions.name: Sakhalin Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Sakhalin Oblast operates under Russia's national regime: since 2023 gender-marker changes and transition-related care are barred, so foreign-issued documents remain as issued; the 'international LGBT movement' is designated extremist, with related convictions, raids, searches, arrests and prosecutions at LGBTQ venues; and federal propaganda statutes covering non-traditional relationships and changing sex apply to all ages, alongside a regional-level propaganda ban adopted in 2013. There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on gender identity and no recognition of same-sex partnerships, and pretrial detention carries documented lethal risk. Local conditions add to rather than soften that framework: the oblast is remote, sparsely populated and island-based, with no visible trans or LGBT infrastructure, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor is more conspicuous than in a large metropolis; it contains border-zone districts where foreign nationals face additional document controls and police contact, increasing the chance a passport mismatch escalates to official scrutiny; and limited nightlife in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk plus ferry and air links to the mainland and Japan add exposure at ports and checkpoints. Social attitudes track the national pattern of strong public hostility toward gender diversity, and federal courts, security agencies and registration systems operate throughout the oblast. No local protective exception, official tolerance or distinct enforcement practice is documented, and this absence of local information is not evidence of safety. Should a transgender visitor be discovered or outed, the same consequences as elsewhere in Russia apply — document mismatch, refusal of services, police scrutiny, detention, and prosecution for perceived association with LGBTQ expression — including where a minor's transition-related needs or expression draw official attention for adult visitors and travelling families alike.

regions.name: Smolensk Oblast
regions.merged_summary:
Smolensk Oblast inherits Russia's national framework without any documented local mitigation: gender transition and changes to gender markers on Russian documents are prohibited by a 2023 law barring both marker changes and gender-affirming surgery, and there is no route to legal gender recognition, though a foreign visitor's own documents remain as issued. The 2023 designation of an alleged 'international LGBT movement' as extremist has brought raids, searches, arrests, criminal and administrative cases and over 100 related convictions, while expanded propaganda statutes restrict expression and have produced fines and venue raids. Pretrial detention in extremism cases has carried lethal risk, including a documented custody death. There is no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, no hate-crime recognition, and hate crimes are not officially recorded. Public attitudes are broadly hostile.

Within the oblast, Smolensk is a provincial, socially-conservative city with no known LGBTQ venues or trans/LGBT infrastructure, no documented local protections or shield policies, no record of lighter enforcement, and no documented local incidents, acceptance or exceptions; police practice follows national directives, and smaller cities and towns offer little anonymity compared with Moscow. Its position as a western border area adjoining Belarus brings additional document and identity checks on roads and at checkpoints, raising the chance that a mismatch between appearance and documents will be examined by officials, while visibility of a foreign trans visitor is plausibly higher outside larger-city anonymity. Should a trans visitor be discovered or outed, these conditions combine with the national regime so that the likely result is bureaucratic friction, hostile attention or police involvement and detention rather than accommodation.

regions.name: Tver Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Tver Oblast offers no exception to Russia's national regime. There is no legal gender recognition, and a 2023 law bars gender-reassignment surgery and changes to gender markers, so a visitor's foreign documents remain as issued and any mismatch may surface during checks. The 'international LGBT movement' extremist designation exposes anyone displaying symbols or attending LGBTQ venues to administrative or criminal charges, with documented arrests, raids — including searches and photographing of patrons — and extremism prosecutions; the expanded propaganda statutes on 'non-traditional relationships' and material affecting minors reach everyday expression, enforced through fines and criminal charges. There is no anti-discrimination protection, hate-crime aggravation, or working legal recourse, pretrial detention has proved lethal in extremism cases, national polling indicates deep public hostility, and the US State Department advises against travel to Russia. In the oblast itself there is no local statute, court practice, police protocol, or service provision creating a protective exception, no trans-specific advocacy or refuge, and little anonymous queer infrastructure outside limited urban venues; federal security services and courts operate uniformly and local authorities follow rather than mitigate federal enforcement. Accounts describe the oblast variously as a conservative Volga-region oblast and as a central Russian province on the Moscow–Petersburg corridor; either way, its smaller cities, heavy transit character, heritage-tourism areas, and conservative climate can heighten social visibility, document checks, street confrontation, and discretionary police questioning, while adding no distinct formal penalty — though a smaller visible scene than Moscow's may also mean somewhat less everyday exposure, which is not documented. No region-specific information establishes separate border treatment, facilities, policing, detention conditions, access to care, venue-raid record, or a local enforcement pattern, so Tver cannot be characterised as either more protective or more punitive than the national picture. For a trans visitor whose identity is discovered or who is outed, the principal danger remains state detention and prosecution under this inherited federal framework, compounded by social hostility and the absence of documented local recourse or a safe haven.

regions.name: Tyumen Oblast
regions.merged_summary: Tyumen Oblast operates entirely under Russia's national framework, with no region-specific law, tolerance practice, protective exception, sanctuary provision or trans-specific visitor resource documented. The 2023 law bars gender reassignment and changes to Russian gender markers, so a visitor's foreign-issued documents remain as issued with no legal route to align them, making any passport or ID check a moment of possible discovery, even though those marker rules do not themselves alter a foreign document. The Supreme Court's designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as extremist has produced over 100 convictions along with raids, arrests, searches, photography, fines and criminal proceedings; propaganda statutes amended in 2022 are actively enforced and reach expression and identity at all ages. There is no anti-discrimination protection or hate-crime recognition, and public attitudes are documented as hostile, with about three-quarters expressing non-acceptance. Locally, the oblast is a conservative oil-and-gas province and Tyumen a prosperous Siberian administrative city with conventional conservative politics and a sizable security- and church-influenced public climate; its oil-industrial character brings some stability and monitoring but no trans-specific safeguards. Local authorities align with federal enforcement, no known regional rule or practice materially changes a visitor's national exposure, and enforcement geography is ordinary with minimal discretion. At the same time, compared with Moscow and St Petersburg, social attitudes are more conservative, trans visibility is lower and organised LGBTQ venues or advocacy networks are limited, reducing practical recourse; Tyumen's university population may offer some urban anonymity. The oblast's large, partly rural geography and distance from major legal-aid centres in Moscow and St Petersburg increase isolation if police intervene, and federal security and local police retain discretion. A visitor discovered as transgender faces police attention, arrest, extremism or propaganda charges, raid exposure and detention under conditions that have proved lethal, including a 2024 pretrial death linked to an LGBTQ-related extremism charge, with no established remedy.

regions.name: Red Sea
regions.merged_summary: The Red Sea region has no documented divergence from Sudan's national regime, and nothing in its record points in a protective direction: Sudan's Penal Code outlaws wearing clothing of the opposite sex under Article 152, which applies regardless of sexual conduct and can catch a transgender visitor whose presentation appears incongruent with their documents, while Article 148 criminalises anal sex with up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence, seven for a second and life for a third following the 2020 amendment that removed capital punishment and lashing. There is no legal gender recognition, gender-affirming care is legally constrained, and documented state violence against LGBTQ people — including torture, extrajudicial killings, official discrimination and vigilante abuse — continues with little public tolerance and no effective recourse. The region's own record on these exposures is not documented beyond this inherited picture, and there is no known evidence of softer enforcement or local acceptance of transgender visitors. Port Sudan, the state capital, has since 2023 been the army-held de facto seat of government and the country's main maritime and air gateway, with functioning airports, a large humanitarian and diplomatic presence, some tourism around Suakin and Red Sea diving sites, and police, courts and morality enforcement operating directly — meaning the national provisions are the operative regime rather than a gap in authority, and state presence concentrates enforcement. This brings foreign officials, aid workers and visitors modest anonymity, greater visibility and consular access, and a more functional city administration than elsewhere, but Port Sudan is also the main entry point, so repeated border and security checks raise the chance that mismatched documents or visible presentation prompt questioning, secondary screening or referral to police. Local society remains conservative, shaped by tribal Beja and Sunni, Sufi-rooted religious norms, with little or no LGBTQ community infrastructure or documented tolerance, while armed conflict and wartime displacement have strained policing, border control and the courts without creating protective recourse; conflict also leaves visitors exposed to a hostile security climate in which discovery can bring official humiliation, detention, extortion or violence, with punishment severe and remedy unavailable.

regions.name: Sennar
regions.merged_summary:
Sennar falls under Sudan's national regime: Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises wearing clothing associated with the opposite sex, so a transgender visitor whose presentation conflicts with their documents can be arrested and imprisoned for presentation alone, enforced through public-order policing. Article 148 separately criminalises anal sex, with penalties up to five years for a first offence, seven for a second and life imprisonment for a third after the death penalty was abolished in 2020, though this sodomy law is a secondary concern for a trans visitor. Sudan offers no legal gender recognition, gender-affirming care is constrained (including by fatwas), and documented state violence, extrajudicial killings, torture, official discrimination and vigilante abuse against gender-nonconforming people leave little prospect of protection, alongside strong social stigma and only 17 percent public acceptance of homosexuality recorded in 2019.

Sennar adds no local protections, exceptions or tolerant tradition: it is a rural, less urbanised than Khartoum, deeply conservative central Sudanese state with little international visitor economy, no protective institutions, community infrastructure or tourism-facing practice, and no known local pattern of trans arrests or violence - a gap that is not evidence of safety. Since 2023 the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces have contested the state, with Sennar city changing control amid heavy fighting, RSF control and mass displacement; police and court function are degraded, militia authority operates as the de facto regime, and checkpoints, armed actors, detention and extortion add exposure, while enforcement by security forces and public order police becomes less predictable and current territorial control and enforcement practice remain uncertain. This breakdown removes routine remedy and, combined with the national criminalisation and documented violence, means discovery or being outed can bring arrest, mistreatment, family questioning or service denial with little reliable recourse; facilities such as hospital wards and detention place people by birth sex, and a family or accompanying minor may draw moral policing and heightened scrutiny.

regions.name: West Darfur
regions.merged_summary: West Darfur applies Sudan's national framework: Penal Code Article 152 criminalises wearing clothing deemed to belong to the opposite sex, so a visitor whose appearance conflicts with their documents falls within its scope; Article 148 criminalises sodomy, with penalties up to life imprisonment; there is no legal gender recognition; and documented state and vigilante violence against LGBTQ people includes torture, extrajudicial killing and official discrimination, with gender-affirming care constrained. Locally, the region has been the epicentre of armed conflict since 2023, with fighting centred on El Geneina and around El Fasher, mass displacement and camps for internally displaced people, Rapid Support Forces/Janjaweed and allied militia control, ethnic violence and documented mass atrocities including ethnically targeted sexual violence and killing with near-total impunity, collapsed policing and courts, militia checkpoints, well-attested custody abuse in ad hoc facilities, a rural and conservative character offering little social tolerance, minimal tourist infrastructure and formal recourse, and conflict-degraded access to gender-affirming or emergency care. Unlike stable state-administered parts of Sudan, authority is exercised by armed actors at checkpoints and in settlements rather than by functioning courts or police, leaving no protective civil society, no safe reporting route, no functioning complaint mechanism and no reliable consular protection. For a trans visitor, discovery at an identity check, camp gate or checkpoint, or questioning of documents or presentation, therefore risks arrest under Article 152 alongside arbitrary detention, extortion, beating, sexualised assault or lethal violence by armed actors who informally enforce conservative norms, with abuse going unremedied and no realistic recourse. Region-specific trans arrests, targeting, border practices and facility rules are not documented, and that gap is not evidence of safety; no distinct rule for travelling minors is documented, though the same criminalised presentation and lack of protection affect families; and neither a pathway to execution for trans identity nor effective protection is established, with no documented systematic execution regime.

regions.name: Diourbel
regions.merged_summary:
Diourbel contains Touba, the Mouride holy city, and the region is the religious heartland of the Mouride brotherhood, making it among the most religiously conservative and closely supervised parts of the country. Religious authority shapes public life, dress and comportment are publicly policed by community and religious authorities, and denunciation to police is common; there is none of Dakar's urban anonymity or cosmopolitan character, so anonymity for a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is thin and such a visitor attracts conspicuous attention. Tourist-facing infrastructure and international visibility are weaker, police and neighbourhood reporting pressures documented nationally apply with at least equal force, and rural settings have historically produced the extralegal violence recorded elsewhere in the country. No region-specific enforcement record distinguishes Diourbel from the national picture, and there is no documented local protective mechanism, queer community infrastructure, reliable independent complaint mechanism or tourist-facing tolerance exception; local religious authority does not replace or soften national law.

Senegal's penal code (Article 319), as amended in March 2026, punishes same-sex acts with five to ten years' imprisonment and a heavy fine and bans the promotion, financing and support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality, although it does not expressly criminalise transgender status itself. Enforcement is documented and ongoing, including arrests on second-hand reports, convictions, border detention of those trying to leave, torture and invasive treatment in custody, extortion, and physical and mob violence against LGBT people — including lethal violence and, in Kaolack, the exhumation and burning of a body — while no legal gender recognition or broad protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists and LGBT groups keep an exceedingly low profile. For a transgender visitor discovered or outed in Diourbel, this combines risk of detention, prosecution or extortion, abusive custody, community violence and limited recourse with heightened stigma and moral denunciation, at least as hostile as the national climate, with local institutions and crowds unlikely to offer protection and few visible safeguards. No distinct local pattern of presentation-based arrests is documented here, but the law's terms and the region's conditions leave little room to assume tolerance.

regions.name: Fatick
regions.merged_summary:
Fatick is a largely rural, conservative Serer-majority region in southwestern Senegal, with fishing towns such as Joal-Fadiouth and administrative centres far from Dakar's legal aid and support networks, less formal tourism infrastructure, and far less urban anonymity. A visibly transgender visitor would stand out in its small towns, where close-knit social control and community reporting make discovery more likely to reach police or a hostile crowd; rural areas and thinner oversight typically leave less recourse, not more, and family or community outing and pressure from traditional or religious leaders are additional exposures. No local trans organisation, protective practice, or institutional exception is known to exist, and travellers with minors gain no additional safeguard.

Under the national regime that governs here, same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 319, with penalties raised in 2026 to five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 10,000,000 CFA francs, and with promotion, financing, support of transsexuality and promotion of LGBT content now explicitly targeted; there is no legal gender recognition and no broad anti-discrimination protection. Enforcement is documented nationwide, including mass arrests in 2026, detention of people trying to leave the country, and abuse in custody, while no Fatick-specific incident is documented — but the 2023 lynching and burning of a man outed as gay in nearby Kaolack, and dismemberment-style public desecration of his remains, indicate the regional climate. Conditional on discovery or being outed, a transgender visitor faces arrest, prosecution, imprisonment, police mistreatment, mob or community violence, and little local recourse, with national institutional recourse weak and inconsistent; no local exception or documented tolerance distinguishes Fatick from this national picture beyond its rural conservatism and weaker institutional support, leaving the situation marginally worse than the country overall.

regions.name: Kaffrine
regions.merged_summary:
Kaffrine has no region-specific protections or documented local exceptions, so the visit is shaped by Senegal's national framework. Article 319 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct; a 2026 amendment raised penalties to five to ten years' imprisonment with higher fines and targets promotion or support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality, though the explicit ban on promoting transsexuality is described in at least one account as still pending. Senegal provides no legal gender recognition and no broad anti-discrimination protection. Enforcement is documented nationally through arrests, prosecutions, mass detentions and torture in custody, detentions at the Senegal–Gambian border of people attempting to leave, and state impunity for anti-LGBT violence, including the 2023 exhumation and burning of a man outed as gay in neighbouring Kaolack. Reporting from outside Dakar is sparse, so local enforcement and social conditions in Kaffrine remain undocumented, and the lack of regional incident data is not evidence of safety.

As an inland, predominantly rural agricultural region far from Dakar's international gateway, Kaffrine is a small, tightly knit, strongly religious and socially conservative area with little public LGBTQ visibility, minimal tourism infrastructure, no visible LGBT community infrastructure, and fewer protective civic channels, legal aid, advocacy and consular support than the capital; police may act on community reports, and local religious and social disapproval is strong. A transgender visitor who is discovered or outed would face criminal exposure under an actively enforced statute, conflation with same-sex conduct and moral-policing risk, arbitrary police or gendarmerie intervention, social hostility and limited recourse, in a setting offering little anonymity and no community networks or protective institutions. Transgender identity itself is not a stated offence under these provisions, but documented anti-LGBT violence and hostility make discovery consequential, and no Kaffrine-specific trans incidents or protective measure are known.

regions.name: Kaolack
regions.merged_summary: Kaolack, a major central Senegalese city and important religious centre, falls under Senegal's national regime: Article 319 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct, and a March 2026 amendment raised penalties to five to ten years' imprisonment plus fines of up to 10 million CFA francs and introduced an explicit ban on promoting homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality (reported in one account as a proposed ban). Transgender identity itself is not an offence, but gender-nonconforming presentation is policed as immorality and discovery can draw scrutiny under the wider enforcement climate, with arrests, prosecutions, mass detentions (including 99 men detained in 2026 and detentions at borders), documented police-custody abuse, and police acting on second-hand reports of same-sex conduct. Senegal provides no legal gender recognition and no LGBTQ anti-discrimination or broad anti-discrimination protection, leaving a trans visitor whose documents or presentation conflict with little recourse. Kaolack-specific conditions intensify this: in October 2023 the body of Cheikh Fall, a man outed as gay, was exhumed and burned in the street before a crowd of hundreds in the city, with four suspects apprehended (their later prosecution or conviction is not documented), alongside a prior corpse-disinterment case pointing to escalation of local hostility into posthumous, public mob violence. The city is a strongly conservative, close-knit maraboutic centre with a low-visibility LGBT population, minimal visible LGBT organisation, strong social surveillance and low anonymity, a small tourist economy with few foreign visitors, and limited protective or institutional infrastructure relative to Dakar. A trans visitor who is discovered or outed therefore faces arrest and prosecution atop credible mob and community hostility, with weak police protection, potential denial of services, and no documented local tolerance buffer or mitigating infrastructure — a reality that applies equally to elderly travellers or those accompanied by a minor. No trans-specific visitor incidents, local facility or border practices, or other local mitigating conditions are documented, and the 2023 case should not be read as a measure of how frequently visitors face such harm.

regions.name: Kolda
regions.merged_summary: Kolda is a largely rural, predominantly Muslim and Fulani southern region of Casamance bordering Guinea-Bissau and near The Gambia, with a small, tightly connected population, very few foreign visitors, limited tourism infrastructure, and far fewer services, advocacy or support networks than Dakar. News travels quickly through family, neighbourhood and religious networks, so a visitor's transgender status becoming known would spread fast and leave little anonymity, and strong customary and religious authority combined with thinner police and legal recourse than in Dakar raises the likelihood of denunciation. The Guinea-Bissau border offers an exit route, but border, checkpoint and transport controls increase document scrutiny and the possibility of secondary screening where presentation does not match documents. No region-specific evidence documents local tolerance, protective institutions, or any mitigation from the national picture.\n\nKolda inherits Senegal's national framework: same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 319, with a March 2026 amendment raising penalties to a range of five to ten years' imprisonment and adding an explicit ban on promoting homosexuality and transsexuality, while no legal gender recognition and no broad anti-discrimination protection exist. Enforcement is documented and ongoing — arrests on second-hand reports, 22 men detained in February 2026 including one arrested at a border crossing, 99 arrested in August, and 2026 arrests and sentences — alongside recorded physical violence, including custody abuse, communal violence against gender-nonconforming people, and a 2023 killing in Kaolack. Being transgender does not itself establish a criminal offence, but discovery or outing in Kolda's close-knit setting, where a foreign visitor is highly visible, could lead to denunciation, police detention, prosecution where conduct is construed as same-sex, extortion, family or community outing, and street hostility; the risks are at least as severe as those faced nationally, with local conservatism reducing practical safeguards and limited legal aid or recourse available.

regions.name: Sedhiou
regions.merged_summary:
Sédhiou is a small, rural, predominantly Muslim area of lower Casamance where foreigners attract notice, community gossip travels quickly, and limited anonymity, social surveillance and routine identity checks compound discovery risk; border-adjacent movement and thin local LGBT infrastructure add to exposure. No Sédhiou-specific incidents involving transgender visitors, local tolerance regime, exception, or protective infrastructure are documented, and visitor-specific border checks, facility placement and care denial are also not documented — these gaps do not establish safety. The inherited national regime therefore governs: Article 319 criminalises same-sex acts, with a 2026 amendment raising penalties to five to ten years' imprisonment and adding (or proposing) bans on promoting or supporting homosexuality and transsexuality. Senegal provides no legal gender recognition and no broad anti-discrimination protection, while enforcement is documented and ongoing, including mass arrests in 2026, arrests at the Senegal-Gambian border, arrests on second-hand reports, custody abuse, and mob violence such as the 2023 burning of the body of a man outed as gay in Kaolack. Transgender people are described as facing prosecution, arrest, discrimination and violence, though precisely how the sex-based criminal offence is applied to a transgender visitor is uncertain; recourse is thin and local LGBT groups keep an exceedingly low profile.

Conditional on discovery or being outing, that combination means a transgender visitor here faces being reported to police or exposed to community hostility, followed by arrest, abuse and stigmatised detention in custody, prosecution under national practice, and possible violent community reaction, with little effective remedy.

regions.name: Ziguinchor
regions.merged_summary:
Ziguinchor, regional capital of Casamance in southern Senegal, operates under the national regime: Penal Code Article 319 criminalises same-sex conduct, and the March 2026 amendment raised penalties to five to ten years' imprisonment with added fines and explicit bans on promotion of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality or transgender status. Senegal provides no legal gender recognition and no broad anti-discrimination protection, and enforcement is documented through arrests, prosecutions and police custody abuses (including 2026 arrests at the Senegal–Gambian border), alongside mob violence, attacks and grave desecration targeting people perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming. For a transgender visitor, discovery or being outed leaves exposure to detention, lengthy prosecution and family or community violence, with no region-specific evidence of lighter enforcement, effective recourse or a documented local remedy; there is also no region-specific information distinguishing Ziguinchor from the national picture on border practice, facilities, detention or remedies.

Local conditions differ in ways that neither create protection nor alter that baseline. Ziguinchor's largely Christian, more rural and partly tourism-oriented coastal economy may reduce everyday friction and visible policing in visitor-facing resort settings, but tourism does not translate into legal or practical safeguards. As a close-knit regional capital it is, by some accounts, more socially conservative and less anonymous than Dakar, with pronounced community scrutiny, noticeable foreigners, fewer specialised support services, and local religious and traditional authority reinforcing disapproval of gender nonconformity. Conflict-era movement checkpoints, military and security checks, tight village social surveillance, and a southern border crossing policed by the same national apparatus add ordinary document and exposure risks; the MFDC insurgency is a general security concern rather than a trans-specific one. Overall, local conditions modestly cushion but do not offset the inherited national regime.

regions.name: CENTRAL REGION
regions.merged_summary:
The Central Region is Singapore's densely urban downtown core, taking in Orchard, Marina Bay, Bugis, Suntec, the wider Marina area and Hong Lim Park, where the annual Pink Dot gathering draws large crowds. It is one of the country's five planning regions and carries no separate criminal, civil, gender-marker or facility law, no distinct local policy or documented practice targeting transgender visitors, and no known local campaign, police profiling of transgender tourists or facility ban; public-order, immigration and document rules apply territory-wide. Everyday life here is markedly cosmopolitan and tourist-facing, with international hotels and services, a visible LGBTQ venue scene, nightlife and commercial districts, professional hotel and service staff, dense CCTV, rapid police response, orderly and rule-following commercial environments comparatively accustomed to foreign visitors, orderly non-violent policing and functioning courts — and no documented violence against transgender visitors. Gender-neutral facilities are nonetheless rare, and the 2023 provision of gender-neutral toilets at Suntec drew organised, contested public backlash with no enforcement following, evidencing social friction rather than institutional hostility.

The national regime governs: Section 377A was repealed in 2022 and same-sex conduct is no longer criminalised, and no specific offence covers transgender identity or presentation, though public-order provisions covering obscene acts and soliciting can still reach conduct read as obscene. Legal gender recognition requires genital surgery, giving a traveller with mismatched documents no route to recognition; gender identity is not a protected ground under workplace law, LGBTI organisations cannot register, and media restrictions on depicting LGBT lives persist, leaving thin formal recourse if a service is refused. Because this core area is dense with hotels, transport nodes, international events and routine document checks at borders, hotel check-in, MRT stations and convention venues, discovery or being outed would more likely bring bureaucratic scrutiny, awkward questioning, possible refusal of service or accommodation, and social disapproval rather than arrest, detention or lethal harm; no region-specific remedy or facility rule is documented, and outcomes in such situations remain uncertain.

regions.name: EAST REGION
regions.merged_summary:
Singapore's East Region — covering Changi and its airport belt, Tampines, Bedok, Pasir Ris and the East Coast Park area — is largely residential HDB heartland and business parks with conservative Chinese and Malay communities, but it has no separate legal regime: national law, border practice and public-accommodation rules apply uniformly, with no region-specific protections or local exceptions. Same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 repeal of Section 377A, there is no trans-specific criminal offence and no documented pattern of police targeting or official hostility; institutions, including Changi's border and police staff, are orderly, professional and procedurally bound. Public-order and obscenity provisions such as Section 294 of the Penal Code can still be applied to public conduct, while legal gender recognition requires genital surgery, leaving a trans visitor's foreign documents without a local route, and gender identity is not a protected ground under the 2025 workplace fairness law; LGBTI groups cannot register and media rules restrict positive representation, though Pride events and gay venues operate openly and Pink Dot is held annually.

Because Changi Airport is the country's main entry point, routine immigration and security screening can make any mismatch between a visitor's documents and presentation salient, and can prompt secondary questioning or document-mismatch checks, though no detention as policy and no documented pattern of friction for visitors whose papers diverge are recorded; any custody or hospital encounter would likely be arranged by recorded sex. Gender-neutral toilets and changing facilities remain limited and contested, illustrated by the backlash against a temporary gender-neutral toilet in 2023, and public facilities are a recurring friction point. Beyond that, a visibly trans visitor is more likely to encounter stares, misgendering, service awkwardness or bureaucratic friction than confrontation — documented hostility is social rather than violent — with thin statutory recourse and no visitor-specific remedy for intrusive questioning or service problems, and no East Region-specific conditions that differ from the wider national picture.

regions.name: NORTH REGION
regions.merged_summary:
North Region — including Woodlands, Sembawang, Yishun and Admiralty — has no separate ordinances, morality patrols or distinct enforcement practice; it operates entirely under Singapore's national framework, where police and courts are effective and complaint channels function. Under that regime, same-sex conduct has been lawful since the 2022 repeal of Section 377A, though public-order provisions covering obscene acts remain and can reach visible conduct, and conservative media regulation restricts depiction of same-sex life. There is no criminal penalty for being transgender, but legal gender recognition requires genital surgery, leaving mismatched documents a persistent exposure, and neither workplace anti-discrimination law nor statutory protections cover gender identity. No same-sex relationship is recognised. Pink Dot's annually permitted gathering indicates a degree of official tolerance, and the conservative climate documented in some anti-Pink Dot backlash is centred elsewhere rather than in this region.

Locally the area is residential HDB heartland rather than a tourism or business district, with a large Malay-Muslim population, fewer nightlife venues, no queer venues or community infrastructure, fewer gender-neutral facilities and generally binary public facilities, plus less familiarity with visibly gender-diverse people than in central districts. There is no documented trans-specific police enforcement, venue raids or anti-trans incidents here, and no evidence of hostility or protection beyond the national picture. For a visitor who is outed or discovered, this social texture is the main difference: expect staring, curiosity, misgendering, awkward inquiries, service friction and administrative difficulty rather than confrontation or violence. Woodlands Checkpoint, the land crossing to Malaysia and Johor Bahru, is the region's main document encounter, where routine passport checks make a marker or presentation mismatch more likely than at Changi to prompt secondary questioning, delay or entry difficulty under ordinary national practice.

regions.name: NORTH-EAST REGION
regions.merged_summary:
The North-East Region — the residential HDB heartland taking in Ang Mo Kio, Hougang, Serangoon, Sengkang and Punggol — sits within Singapore's unitary legal system, and no region-specific law, enforcement pattern, policy or incident distinguishes it from the national picture; knowledge here is effectively national. Same-sex conduct has been lawful since 2022 and no criminal offence targets transgender identity or expression, though public-order obscenity rules can still reach conduct in public places, and police and courts function in an orderly, rule-bound way with no record of state-directed targeting of trans people. Gender recognition depends on genital surgery, so a visitor's foreign documents, presentation or recorded sex have no straightforward local counterpart; gender identity is not a protected ground (the January 2025 workplace fairness law omits it), same-sex relationships receive no recognition in any form, and LGBTI organisations cannot register, while media depiction of LGBT life is restricted and Pink Dot SG continues annually. Gendered facilities remain the norm — gender-neutral toilets appear mainly on university campuses — and toilets and wards are binary in practice.

Because the area is a dense, orderly and heavily policed urban environment rather than the central tourist belt, everyday exposure arises in neighbourhood, mall, clinic and MRT interactions rather than nightlife settings. Social attitudes in these family-centred towns are more conventional than downtown, illustrated by public backlash against a temporary gender-neutral toilet at a 2023 convention, and trans-aware facilities are fewer, so a visitor who is discovered or outed should expect bureaucratic friction, misgendering, staring, awkward service or document and healthcare questioning, and possible uncertainty at verification checkpoints rather than criminal prosecution. Violent targeting is not a documented local pattern and remedies through ordinary channels generally function, but the absence of a documented pattern of targeting, facility exclusion or violence reflects uncertainty rather than established safety.

regions.name: WEST REGION
regions.merged_summary:
West Region is an administrative part of Singapore with no separate legal system, border or enforcement authority: national rules govern here, and no local policy, protective exception or campaign specific to transgender travellers is documented. Nationally, sex between men was decriminalised in 2022 and no statute criminalises gender expression or cross-dressing, with no documented pattern of arrest, imprisonment, extortion or targeting of transgender visitors by police, and policing and courts remain stable and low in direct violence, processing complaints through functional institutions. Section 294 of the Penal Code on obscene acts still reaches public conduct. Against that, legal gender recognition requires genital surgery and offers no route for a visitor whose documents and presentation differ, gender identity and expression are not covered by the January 2025 workplace fairness law, no same-sex relationship is recognised, and a media regulator discourages LGBT visibility, though gay bars and clubs operate openly and Pink Dot SG draws large annual crowds citywide rather than here. Gender-marker mismatches may prompt questioning at document checks, and how officials or venues handle a particular document mismatch, facility question or complaint is undocumented and should not be assumed safe.

The West is largely HDB heartland and industrial land — Jurong East and West, Bukit Batok, Choa Chu Kang, Tuas and Clementi — with a socially conservative residential base, few LGBT-specific venues, and fewer visitor-facing hotels, nightlife venues and LGBTQ support services than central Singapore, so everyday administrative encounters such as bathroom or lodging checks may be less practiced; the Tuas land checkpoint sits here, offset slightly by the large student and international populations around NTU and NUS. No local incidents, activism friction or enforcement differences are documented, and no distinct regional protection or restriction is established, so an outed visitor faces little prospect of custody or state-sanctioned harm, while friction, misgendering and curiosity remain credible and practical friction is modestly greater than in central Singapore.

regions.name: Capital Territory (Honiara)
regions.merged_summary:
Honiara is governed by Solomon Islands' colonial-era Penal Code provisions criminalising consensual same-sex activity between men and between women, which carry a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment; these are reported as unenforced, with no arrests or prosecutions documented, though that absence does not establish safety. The statutes target sexual conduct rather than transgender identity, and whether they could be applied to visibly gender-nonconforming visitors is uncertain. There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage for sexual orientation or gender identity, no legal gender recognition, and no relationship recognition, while senior officials have publicly opposed legal change on religious grounds. Society is broadly conservative and Christian, and gender variance is little understood outside a small NGO circle.

As the capital, Honiara is the country's most urban, most anonymous and best-served setting, holding the national referral hospital, the courts, police headquarters and a small advocacy sector, with greater exposure to foreign visitors and more professional accommodation than rural provinces, along with NGO and diplomatic familiarity with gender diversity — factors that give trans visitors somewhat more anonymity. The operative risk is nonetheless social rather than statutory: for a visitor who is outed or discovered, church, neighbourhood or police scrutiny in a conservative Christian society can produce intense curiosity, misgendering, moral commentary from church-influenced bystanders, intrusive questioning, refusal of services, extortion, brief administrative detention, placement in custody according to documents or perceived birth sex, and possible friction at guesthouses, clinics and churches. No Honiara-specific trans-specific policing pattern, facility rule, detention practice, violence record or incidents involving transgender visitors are documented, and no organised campaign targeting trans travellers is recorded; whether the statutes could be used against gender-nonconforming visitors remains uncertain, and the absence of documented incidents is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Central
regions.merged_summary: Central Province forms part of the Solomon Islands, inheriting its national framework: colonial-era Penal Code provisions criminalise consensual same-sex activity between men and between women with a maximum penalty of 14 years, though the law is recorded as unenforced, with no arrests or prosecutions of LGBT people in the available record — much of that enforcement information being dated. These provisions do not criminalise transgender identity or gender expression, and there are no explicit cross-dressing, gender-expression or travel-screening restrictions targeting trans people. No protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity is in place, trans people have no legal recognition, same-sex relationships are not recognised, and senior officials have publicly opposed legal change. No region-specific information documents border or document problems, facility restrictions, police targeting, violence or effective visitor remedies in Central; such factors are undocumented rather than shown to be safe, and there is no documented local exception or additional facility, policing or care regime.

regions.name: Choiseul
regions.merged_summary:
Choiseul is a remote, sparsely populated and largely rural province with negligible tourism infrastructure, small village communities and little anonymity. Isolation reduces routine encounters with state officials, but anyone read as gender-nonconforming is likely to become known quickly through local networks rather than formal checks. Strong Christian authority — Anglican, Catholic and Adventist — and customary chiefs shape social discipline, and there is no LGBT organisation, visible trans community or support network. Policing and court presence are thin outside the provincial centre, medical and consular recourse is remote, and any detention would be at birth sex with no trans-specific safeguards. Discovery therefore rests on communal rather than official scrutiny, and the likelihood of being outed is higher, with remedy far thinner, than in Honiara.

The province inherits the national regime: the colonial-era Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct with a maximum penalty of 14 years, though the provisions are reported as unenforced and no arrests or prosecutions are on record; there is no non-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity, no legal gender recognition and no relationship recognition, and senior officials have publicly opposed legal change. No province-specific legal exception is known, and no trans-specific criminal offence, police or border-official targeting of visitors, facility restriction, trans-directed violence or routine detention is documented in Choiseul — the conditions described reflect the province's rurality and governance structure rather than recorded incidents, and such gaps do not establish safety. If outed, a visitor is more likely to face communal shaming, ejection, hostile questioning and customary or church pressure than documented state action, with no institutional recourse beyond those responses and little practical support locally.

regions.name: Guadalcanal
regions.merged_summary:
Guadalcanal includes Honiara, the national capital and principal tourism hub, concentrating government, churches, diplomatic missions, NGOs and most visitor services, and it operates under the same Solomon Islands Penal Code that criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between males and females with a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment; that colonial-era provision is recorded as unenforced, with no arrests or prosecutions documented. There is no legal gender recognition, relationship recognition or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, senior officials (including the Prime Minister and Governor General) and church leaders have publicly opposed legal change on religious grounds, and no trans-specific criminal offence, police or border targeting, facility restriction or registration requirement is documented. No local rule or practice is known to distinguish the island protectively from the national picture, and the evidence base is thin rather than indicating organised targeting.

For a transgender visitor, discovery or being outed would combine these conditions with a socially conservative, Christian province where conservative Anglican and evangelical norms shape public attitudes, gender diversity is little understood, and a visibly trans visitor may attract intense scrutiny, gossip, staring, intrusive questioning, misgendering, family or community pressure, service refusals or other street-level friction, with limited recourse if harassed or extorted. Honiara's larger anonymous and expatriate community, the presence of international visitors and external scrutiny, and foreign nationality in hotels and business settings may offer somewhat more privacy and tolerance than remote areas, but this confers no formal protection; police capacity is limited, public order is fragile, and in smaller settlements discovery could bring ostracism, threats or violence with little protection, while how officials or service providers would respond to an outed visitor remains uncertain.

regions.name: Isabel
regions.merged_summary: Isabel is a largely rural outer-island province with Buala as its administrative centre, and no known local rule, border or document practice, policing pattern, facility or custody rule, or health-care response distinguishes it from the Solomon Islands as a whole, so conditions reflect the inherited national framework. That framework retains colonial-era penal code provisions criminalising consensual same-sex activity with a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment, but the provisions are reported as unenforced, with no arrests or prosecutions recorded, and senior officials frame their opposition to legal change in religious rather than enforcement terms. There is no relationship recognition and no non-discrimination protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and nothing in the record documents trans-specific criminalisation of gender expression, police or border targeting of transgender visitors, or documented violence against transgender people locally or nationally. Isabel is small, remote and close-knit, with predominantly Anglican and devoutly religious communities that are among the most socially conservative in the country, strong church and customary authority in community life, no visible LGBT or trans community infrastructure, few tourist services, and thin formal police and court capacity.

regions.name: Makira
regions.merged_summary: Makira-Ulawa is a remote, sparsely populated and predominantly rural province reached by small domestic aircraft and boat to Kirakira, with very low visitor numbers. Small, closely observant communities are shaped by village kinship, wantok obligation and dominant Christian churches — particularly the Anglican Church of Melanesia, which carries strong social and moral authority — alongside customary structures. Gender nonconformity has no established local traditional role and would likely be read as foreign and remarkable. Policing is thin outside Honiara, courts sit infrequently, and public facilities and health services are limited to small clinics; guesthouses and clinics are informal and unfamiliar with trans guests and patients. There is no local trans community, advocacy body or legal-aid capacity, and no documented local protection or tourist-facing tolerance. No province-specific rule, trans-specific incident, targeting pattern, facility rule or document check is documented for Makira itself, and international entry screening occurs at Honiara rather than locally, where ordinary identification checks apply rather than dedicated trans screening.\n\nThe province inherits the Solomon Islands national regime: a colonial-era penal provision criminalising consensual same-sex activity with a maximum 14-year sentence, recorded as unenforced with no documented prosecutions, no legal-gender recognition, and no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, with senior officials and prominent leaders publicly opposing legal change on church grounds. This is indirect legal exposure rather than a trans-specific offence, and no pattern of arrest for presentation is documented. Conditional on being outed, however, the combination of close-knit settlements with little anonymity, strong church and customary moral pressure, and minimal state presence points to conservative community reaction, social friction, ostracism, intrusive questioning, refusal of service or informal sanction rather than state action. Because police presence is limited, courts sit infrequently, and there is no local advocacy or legal-aid infrastructure, recourse in these isolated areas is weak, leaving a visitor with effectively no local remedy.

regions.name: Malaita
regions.merged_summary: Malaita inherits Solomon Islands' national framework: a colonial-era Penal Code criminalising consensual same-sex conduct with a maximum 14-year sentence that is documented as unenforced, with no recorded prosecutions or arrests in recent years, no trans-specific criminal offence, document rule, facility policy or border restriction, no legal gender recognition, and no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity — while senior national leaders have publicly opposed legal change and, on record, condemned liberalisation. Documents are normally examined at international entry rather than on domestic travel to Malaita. Malaita is the country's most populous but overwhelmingly rural province, among the most customary (kastom) and church-influenced, with a stronger public moral posture than Honiara, low transgender visibility, small closely-knit communities, chiefly and church authority, a largely non-tourist economy with sparse tourism, and no known trans community infrastructure or protective institutions. Civil-society, legal-aid and NGO presence is far thinner than in the capital, and policing and judicial reach are weaker outside Auki since the end of the regional mission, with customary authority often resolving disputes and interpersonal violence attracting slow state response. For a transgender or visibly gender-nonconforming visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine to make social disapproval the greater concern: local leaders, church authorities or accommodation operators may challenge, ostracise, expel or refuse service, with gossip, harassment, extortion or assault plausible and little reliable recourse, while police involvement could mean placement in custody according to birth sex and poor detention conditions, plus police discretion under the latent criminal statute. There is no documented pattern of trans-targeted police action, organised state targeting, service denial, arrests or anti-trans violence in Malaita; the absence of such records reflects limited documentation rather than evidence of safety, and everyday social hostility and limited recourse would likely be greater than in Honiara.

regions.name: Rennell and Bellona
regions.merged_summary:
Rennell and Bellona is a remote outer-island Polynesian province of the Solomon Islands with a few thousand residents, overwhelmingly church-going (Anglican, Seventh-day Adventist and South Seas Evangelical) and socially guided by clergy and chiefs in tight villages where a stranger becomes known within days. It inherits the national framework: colonial-era penal provisions criminalising consensual same-sex conduct with a maximum of 14 years, reported as unenforced with no recorded prosecutions, no trans-specific criminal offence, no legal gender recognition, no non-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and official opposition to legal change on religious grounds. The province adds its own conditions — very little tourism and few visitors, minimal police presence and medical facilities, no local advocacy or complaint mechanism, no trans-specific police training or health infrastructure, and health or legal recourse that requires travel to Honiara. Ecotourism does bring some foreign visitors, but there is no documented local record of either acceptance of or incidents against transgender people and no region-specific protective machinery is known; the pervasive church-led conservatism and absence of protective infrastructure give the province a distinctly more conservative local character than the national picture, and no local information indicates tolerance beyond it.

Conditional on discovery or being outed, a visitor's limited anonymity means news would spread quickly through village networks, making outing highly probable, especially for anyone with mismatched documents or visible gender variance. A transgender visitor could then face intense local scrutiny, social hostility, exclusion, service refusal, humiliation, pressure or confrontation, and a delayed official response; any detention would be in small local cells. Because policing, courts and care are thin and distant, practical recourse is limited and would largely depend on Honiara. There is no documented trans-specific policing, raids, violence, prosecution or detention pathway, and state pursuit of gender expression itself is not documented — an absence of records that reflects uncertainty rather than evidence of safety.

regions.name: Temotu
regions.merged_summary:
Temotu is Solomon Islands' remote easternmost province, centred on Lata in the Santa Cruz Islands: tiny, scattered island communities with almost no tourism infrastructure, no resident advocacy organisations, no consular presence, minimal policing and health capacity, and limited transport links. It is a sparsely populated, deeply Christian, largely rural province where churches and customary norms strongly shape local life, and where a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner would be conspicuous immediately in settlements where everyone knows everyone. At the same time, Melanesian culture recognises gender-variant roles (akavaine), general hospitality toward visitors is high, and no record of Temotu-specific violence, official hostility, trans-specific enforcement, border targeting or facility restrictions is documented — the available evidence does not establish a distinct local policy or pattern of treatment of trans visitors, leaving uncertainty beyond the thinness of the local information itself.

The province inherits Solomon Islands' national framework unchanged: a colonial-era prohibition on consensual same-sex conduct carrying a maximum of 14 years, documented as unenforced with no recent prosecutions and no documented enforcement of that statute against a visitor; no legal recognition of same-sex relationships or gender identity; no non-discrimination protection covering gender identity; no province-specific protective regime; and a history of senior officials publicly opposing legal change and framing LGBT identity in religiously condemnatory terms. Because the state framework is unenforced, the principal exposure for a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed is informal rather than legal: community pressure and social hostility, outing, stigmatised questions, harassment, accommodation or service exclusion, and police attention, with disputes handled informally and no realistic legal aid, discreet services, or means of leaving quickly. Remoteness and scattered settlement make timely assistance harder — a practical inference from geography rather than evidence of local targeting — so while the record shows no documented imprisonment or targeted enforcement, absence of recorded targeting is not proof of safety.

regions.name: Western
regions.merged_summary:
Western Province — centred on Gizo and Munda and taking in New Georgia, Ranongga, Choiseul, the Marovo Lagoon and the Marovo–Solomon lagoon corridor — is largely rural and remote, with services concentrated in Gizo and Munda, and it inherits the national framework: the Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, including between women, with a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment, although reporting describes those provisions as unenforced and records no recent arrests or prosecutions, so enforcement remains uncertain rather than following a documented pattern. There is no trans-specific offence, no legal gender recognition, and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity, while senior political, official and church leaders have publicly opposed legal change on religious grounds. No provincial law targeting transgender travellers is documented, and there is no record of police targeting trans or gender-nonconforming people in the province, nor documented trans-specific enforcement, violence, border scrutiny, facility restrictions or visitor incidents; public documentation of trans visitors to the province is sparse, so local exposure and any difference in enforcement remain uncertain.

On the ground, Gizo's and Munda's dive, resort and lagoon visitor economies bring expatriate contact and customary familiarity with outsiders, making foreigners unremarkable and offering some anonymity and discretion in tourism centres and facilities. Against this, small, closely knit island communities and dominant church congregations mean a visibly transgender visitor becomes known quickly, with limited privacy in guesthouses, clinics and transport; everyday reactions run from curiosity and staring to conservative disapproval, gossip, refusal of service, social censure, exclusion or pressure from hosts and villagers rather than organised hostility, and formal arrest is less likely than such community response. Church, chiefly and village authority carry strong social weight, while provincial police, courts and health facilities are thinly resourced — health care is basic with no trans-specific services and anything beyond routine treatment requires referral to Honiara — so a visitor outed through documents, a police stop, an emergency or discovery in a remote community would face conservative reaction with little practical recourse, and the unrepealed statute plus absent protections leave the inherited national regime operative, giving an overall picture broadly similar to the country's.

regions.name: Western Area
regions.merged_summary:
Western Area, centred on Freetown, is Sierra Leone's capital, main port and most urban, internationally connected and tourism-oriented area, with beach resorts, main hotels, universities, a diplomatic quarter, and a large expatriate, humanitarian and NGO presence. Its greater urban anonymity, denser civil-society and media activity, and social attitudes somewhat more moderate than the provinces modestly reduce everyday scrutiny, and concentrated NGOs, embassies and clinics may make assistance and advice more accessible. However, the capital concentrates police checkpoints, the security apparatus, and crowded markets and transport hubs, so passport, hotel, document and presentation checks make discovery more routine than in remote provinces; conservative public attitudes remain operative, and no local sanctuary policy, protective ordinance, trans-specific enforcement data or region-specific enforcement pattern that clearly reduces visitor risk is documented. One assessment notes document mismatches as a trigger for stops, while another reports that local tolerance softens everyday encounters without altering official practice.

The area inherits Sierra Leone's national regime: consensual sex between men is criminalised under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act with penalties up to life imprisonment, though prosecutions are rare and not the usual enforcement route, and there is no statutory non-discrimination or hate-crime protection or reliable remedy. More directly relevant, police practice targets presentation itself — people perceived as LGBT, especially men presenting in women's clothing, are stopped, detained, beaten, harassed and publicly humiliated, often without any formal charge being filed; these reports are dated, and current frequency is uncertain. An outed or discovered visitor therefore faces documented harassment, detention, public humiliation or assault with little effective recourse, though routine imprisonment is not established. The 2004 murder in the capital of lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy — with police declining to treat it as a hate crime and the accused later escaping custody — indicates lethal violence against LGBT people with weak accountability, alongside other known violence against LGBT activists in the capital.

regions.name: Departamento de Usulután
regions.merged_summary:
Usulután is a rural, socially conservative eastern/southeastern department with beaches and small-scale surf tourism, higher religiosity and machismo, and small towns where a visibly trans outsider draws attention rather than anonymity. It inherits El Salvador's national framework with no local addition: there is no gender-recognition law and no usable way to align a foreign passport, while hate-crime and bias-motivation provisions exist on paper but are weakly enforced — a 2020 conviction of three officers for a transgender woman's killing is an isolated example, and police have refused to investigate LGBT deaths, with impunity common. Compared with San Salvador the department has thinner legal-aid, NGO and LGBT organisational coverage, little trans-specific infrastructure, limited trans-competent health care, and local authorities, hospitals and security forces offer no known protocols or reliable complaint route; no documented local protective practice, tolerance or tourist-facing safeguard is known. Heavy police and military presence in border and anti-gang operations, plus gang control in parts of the department — where gangs have engaged in extortion, sexual assault and forced recruitment of LGBT people — further reduce oversight and discreet support, and local incidents are poorly documented, leaving real uncertainty about conditions.

Under the state of exception in force since 2022, mass-arrest sweeps have placed trans women in the ordinary male prison system with birth-sex custody, forced shaving, punishment drills, extortion, violence and denial of care, alongside hostile prison rules targeting effeminate presentation; gang withdrawal under the exception has eased some street exposure, but the custodial pathway remains, and the state's response has been raids and detention without gender accommodation rather than protection. For a transgender visitor who is discovered or outed, these conditions combine into questioning or refusal at lodging, checkpoints or clinics; detention in male facilities with humiliation, extortion and violence risk; community or gang hostility in small-town settings; and, for a transgender minor, additional outing or denial of school and medical access. Outside San Salvador, needing care or medication refills means facing the national pattern of dismissive or discriminatory treatment with fewer alternatives, while foreign status may reduce visibility somewhat without offsetting these consequences. There is no known local exception where police or courts have worked for trans people.

regions.name: Acquaviva
regions.merged_summary:
Acquaviva is one of San Marino's nine castelli — a small, socially familiar and socially conservative western hillside municipality taking in the Gualdicciolo area, adjoining the capital and the Italian border — with no tourism-facing infrastructure, policing character, or local statutes, ordinances, facility rules or enforcement practices of its own; national law governs. The land route through Italy remains open with no documented identity screening or entry friction, so a transgender visitor's foreign-issued documents govern identity throughout the stay, and visitors travelling alone or with children encounter the same administration. Same-sex conduct and gender identity and expression are not criminalised, no statute regulates bathroom or facility use, and no Acquaviva-level border, facility, health-care, document or policing restriction affecting transgender guests, and no local trans-specific violence or official hostility, is documented.

Nationally, legal gender recognition does not exist — a gap that falls on residents rather than travellers — while anti-discrimination and hate-crime protections enacted in 2008 cover sexual orientation but not gender identity; a 2019 constitutional amendment and Universal Periodic Review recommendations likewise stop at orientation, and a 2019 recommendation to extend coverage to gender identity has no recorded implementing text, leaving trans visitors without formal protection machinery. Occasional violence against LGBTQ people is reported without published figures for comparison, and attitudes and responses in Acquaviva are not specifically documented, though a 2019 referendum and civil-union framework signal moderate social tolerance.
